Salutations to the venerable Gurus.
The Śrī Śaktisaṅgama Tantra. The Tārākhaṇḍa. Part Two.
The First Chapter. Ādinātha said:
O Kālī, Kālī, Mahākālī, O beloved Dakṣiṇakālikā!
To the sovereign of the systems beginning with *ka* and *ha*, who displays the sixty supernatural powers (*siddhis*). || 1 ||
O Śivā, whose form is identical with Brahman, let even the secret be told;
O Goddess, that which was previously hinted at was not explained by you to me.
Tell that to me, O Queen of the Gods, if you have compassion for me.
Śrī Kālī said: Listen, for that which is a secret to be hidden from all shall now be told.
One, ten, a hundred, O God, a thousand, and likewise ten thousand; a hundred thousand is called a *niyuta*, O God, and that same term denotes a *lakṣa*.
And from that, O Lord, there arise prayuta (ten lakhs), daśalakṣapravācaka (one hundred lakhs),
koṭi (ten million), daśakoṭi (one hundred million), arbuda (one billion), and daśārbuda (ten billion).
Kharva, kāṣṭhakharva, nikharva, diṅikharvaka, jaladhi, anta, madhya, vṛnda, and abja follow after that.
And then, O Maheśāna, Laya was proclaimed, as well as Mahālaya;
likewise Śaṅkha, Mahāśaṅkha, Padma, and Mahāpadmaka. || 7 ||
Mukunda, Kunda-nīla, Mahānīla, Śaṅkara, Makara, and Kacchapa; after that is Parārdha. || 8 ||
Beyond the parārdha and likewise beyond that, no number exists;
it is stated in the Kālikāgama that "the infinite (ananta) shall follow after each of those."
O Maheśvara, this numerical sequence should be understood as increasing by tens;
now hear as the number of the scriptural texts is being told.
The number of verses is proclaimed to be fifty thousand;
one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, and likewise a hundred thousand (niyuta) should be known [in this sequence]. || 11 ||
Prayuta, arbuda, kharva, vṛnda, khārva, nikharvaka, śaṅkha, padma, samudra, then madhyama, and antya. (12)
Parākhya, Parame, Parārddha, and Tatparārddhaka—
these are the designations of numbers in the compendium of numerical characteristics, following a sequence of increasing by tenfold at each step.
That which consists of thirty-two syllables is called a *grantha*;
that very same [unit] arising from the eyes of Tārā is declared to be a *śloka*. (14)
Within this, O Maheśānī, are all the Yāmalas and Ḍāmaras,
the Tantras, the Ocean [of Tantra], and the three hundred Cūḍāmaṇis.
The wish-fulfilling gem, the celestial desire-tree, all the kalpas, the cow of plenty, the pārijāta tree, the nectar, and likewise the mirror— all these are established in you.
Also the Sopānasaṃhitā and those beginning with the Upasaṃhitā;
likewise the Sāṃkhyāyanāvartana and the Mūlāvatāraka. (17)
There are many Purāṇas to be enumerated and numerous secret doctrines;
there are the Bṛhadrahasya and Ujjābāla, as well as many Hṛdayas.
O Lord of Gods, likewise Kaumudī and others, O Śiva, as well as Candrikā; and those beginning with Pātañjala, and those beginning with Sārasvata. (19)
O Lord of Gods, all the Upatantras, as well as the Paryāyas, Āmnāyas, and Āgamas, bear the designation "Bṛhat" according to their respective order of application.
The prefix *upa* possesses great power and pertains to the *Tantrayāmala*.
Śrī Śiva said: "You have stated the name of the work; tell me, how many [verses] does it contain and where is it situated? (21)
"How much [is it] in the worlds of the immortals, and how much in heaven and the netherworld?
Śrī Kālī said:
"On earth, there are indeed fifty great weights, numbering thirty-six. (22)
The human count is tenfold in the heavenly world and likewise in the netherworld (pātāla). Thus, this entire collection of traditional scriptures has been recounted by me to you. 23.
The Śaiva, the Śākta, the Gāṇapatya, the Saura, and the Vaiṣṇava;
as well as the Mahāvīra, the Pāśupata, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Vīravaiṣṇava. || 24 ||
Vīraśaiva, as well as Cāndra, Svāyambhuva, Anantara, Pāñcarātra, Gāruḍa, Kerala, and likewise Śābara. (25)
O Lord, [there are] Śrīsiddhaśābara, likewise Kālaśābara, O Lord, Kumārīśābara, and likewise Vijayāśābara. || 26 ||
O Lord, [I offer] the Śābara of Kālikā, the divine Śābara, the Vīra-Śābara,
the Śrīnātha-Śābara, and the supreme Tāriṇī-Śābara.
The Śrīśambhu-Śābara and the Rudra-numbered Śābara castes;
likewise the Rakta-ghora, the Śukla, and the Ghoraviṇmūtraka.
Then there were Vīṇāghora, Nīla, and the one named Sarvabhakṣa. || 29 ||
The Ghoras, Aghoras, and Siddhas are likewise remembered as the eleven Ghoras;
furthermore, there are the Māyika, Kāpālika, Vīra, and Bauddha Āgamas. (30)
The Jaina Āgamas consist of the classes related to the red and white garments;
however, the various types of Cīna are proclaimed to be many, numbering two hundred. || 31 ||
There are one hundred divisions among the Buddhists, ten are recorded for the Pāśupatas,
eight divisions for the Kaulas, and the Vaidika-śāstra is the Avadhūta.
One should diligently apply [the ritual] according to the specific characteristics of each caste;
for whatever dharmas have been proclaimed for whichever castes among those to be meditated upon. (33)
In each of those [stages], those respective duties must be diligently applied;
a Brāhmaṇa should act accordingly so that his Brāhmaṇahood is not lost. (34)
Now, this is how it should be done for those of other castes: "O Mṛḍa, O Śaṅkara, O Īśvara!
He who knows this secret of the text is indeed Īśvara. (35)
Indeed, because of the great length of this text, I have not spoken of it here for you.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O sweet-spoken one, tell me that which was indicated within the Śiva-tattva."
The accomplished vidyā, the great vidyā, and likewise the minor vidyā are thus considered;
though described as threefold, they are not revealed again among mortals.
"O Goddess, let that very thing be told; first, O beloved, tell me the number.
Śrī Kālī said:
"The Great Vidyā consists of ten syllables; I shall state its names. (38)
(4) Siddhavidyā, Mahāvidyā, and Vidyā—such is the sequence of qualities.
How is she perfected, and of what nature is she, in the form of the four ages and so forth? (39)
Who were the perfected ones (siddhas) in the Satya Yuga, or what was the accomplishment (siddhi), O Maheśvara?
Who were the perfected ones in other ages? Everything is being told; listen. (40)
In the Satya Yuga, the Siddhavidyās are proclaimed to be Sundarī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Kālī, and Tārā, O Lord of Gods. (41)
O Maheśvara, Kālikā is a perfected lore (siddhavidyā) at all times;
likewise are Chinnamastā, Bagalā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalā. || 42 ||
O beloved, listen well to these very great vidyās;
Dhūmāvatī and Bhairavī are established as vidyās. (43)
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Cinnamastā, and likewise the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī. || 44 ||
Bagalā, Siddhavidyā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalātmikā—these alone are proclaimed as the Great Vidyās, the perfected Vidyās. || 45 ||
O Lord, according to the doctrine of Vīranātha, there are three ways [of classification] due to the division of the ages (yugas):
Kālī, Cinnā, Sundarī, Siddhavidyā, and Tāriṇī. || 46 ||
Bagalā, Kamalā, Dhūmā, Mātaṅgī, Bhairavī, Tripuṭā, and likewise Śūlinī—these shall be among the Mahāvidyās. (47)
O Maheśvara, Vanadurgā, Tvaritā, Totalā, Tripuṭā, Māyā, Kānheśī, and Bhramarāṅkikā are [to be known] as Vidyās. || 48 ||
Bhogavatī, Klinnā, Haṃsārūḍhā, Kukkuṭī, and Trikaṇṭakī, O Lord of Gods, are proclaimed as the Mahāvidyās. (49)
This doctrine of Nityā has been proclaimed; now hear, O Śiva, the doctrine of Kubjā:
Vajraprastāriṇī, Bhogavatī, and likewise Padmāvatī. (50)
Mahāmadhumatī-siddhi, as well as Mṛtasañjīvinī, Aghorā, Rājamātaṅgī, Mātaṅgī, and Hiṅgulāmbikā. || 51 ||
"O Lord of Gods, these great vidyās are proclaimed as Kālarātri.
Śrī Śiva said: "The general [form] of Chinnamastā has been told; however, there are many particulars regarding her."
"I have been recognized by you, O Sovereign of the Universe; O Beloved, assume the state of being my disciple.
O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the definitive teaching regarding the perfected sciences (*siddhavidyā*) and so forth. (53)
Śrī Śiva said:
The Siddhavidyā and Mahāvidyā are proclaimed as two-fold according to the sequence of the three divisions and according to the sequence of the Vidyā-mantras. (54)
O Śivā, the genus is proclaimed to be threefold— female, male, and neuter— and through the sequence of the four yugas, there arise further internal divisions within these distinctions.
O Maheśānī, O Śive! In Satya [Yuga] you are Kālī, Śrīvidyā, Kamalā, and Bhuvaneśvarī; you are Siddhavidyā, Triśakti, and Bagalā. || 56 ||
O Śivā, Mahāvidyā is Mātaṅgī-Bhairavī in the Satya Yuga;
and Dhūmāvatī shall be the Vidyā in the Tretā Yuga—listen, O Pārvatī. || 57 ||
Kālī, Tārā, and Sundarī are proclaimed as the Siddhavidyās; Mātaṅgī, Bhuvanā, and Lakṣmī are proclaimed as the Mahāvidyās. || 58 ||
O Maheśvarī, Dhūmāvatī and Bhairavī exist as Vidyās;
likewise, in the Dvāpara age, Kālikā, Tārā, Rocinī, and Bhairavī [are the Vidyās]. (59)
Siddhavidyā, Maheśānī, Sundarī, Bhuvanā, Ramā, Dhūmāvatī, Mahāvidyā, Mātaṅgī, and likewise Kamalā—[these are the ten Mahāvidyās]. || 60 ||
O Maheśānī, O Śivā, Dhūmā and Bagalā are [manifested] as Vidyās;
O Maheśānī, in the Kali age, Kālī alone is the Vidyā.
Kālī, Tārā, Cinnamastā, Siddhavidyā, Sundarī, Bhairavī, Lakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, and Bhuvaneśvarī are considered the accomplished vidyās in the Kali age. (62)
O Maheśānī, O Śivā, Mahāvidyā, Dhūmā, and Bagalā have been proclaimed by me as the Vidyās in the Kali age. (63)
In the doctrine of Unmattabhairava, another classification is stated; listen:
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (64)
Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and likewise Vidyā Dhūmāvatī;
Bagalā, Siddhavidyā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalāmbikā. (65)
The thirteen great vidyās are also threefold according to the division of the ages;
these very great vidyās remain pervading the three ages.
In the Kali age, Kālī; in the Kali age, Kālī; in the Kali age, Kālī alone prevails.
In the Kali age, Kālikā has been realized as manifest by Kālanātha.
In the Kali age, whoever desires spiritual accomplishment while abandoning Kālī is like one who wishes to see a form in a mirror without eyes. (68)
In the Kali age, whoever desires sovereignty while abandoning Kālī is like one who seeks the snowy mountain for relief from the cold. || 69 ||
In the Kali age, whoever desires liberation while abandoning Kālī is surely like one who seeks to end hunger without food. (70)
O Goddess, whoever in the Kali age seeks power while abandoning Kālī is like one who desires to obtain a power without the means, even in his mind.
In the Kali age, whoever desires devotion while abandoning Kālī is like one who,
having rejected prepared food, wishes to eat mere grass.
In the Kali age, whoever abandons Kālī and desires some other object of desire, he always commits sins for the sake of ending suffering.
O Goddess of gods, he is truly a pauper, a great fool, and a traitor to me, throughout the three ages beginning with the Kali, according to the reality of things.
A human being attains perfection even by practicing another lore;
however, in the Kali age, Kālī is the touchstone, and no other lore ever achieves this.
The Śrī Mahākālikā Vidyā bestows full fruit in the Kali age, whether through ignorance or knowledge, and whether performed with ease or playfulness. (76)
O Maheśvarī, even when remembered but once, Kālī bestows perfection;
indeed, Kālikā is proclaimed as the sovereign queen of the four yugas. (77)
The Queen of Wisdom (Vidyārājñī) is a perfected lore that bestows swift results in the Kali age;
she is celebrated as the Great Lore (Mahāvidyā) because of the identity of her name and the similarity of her form. (78)
O Maheśvarī, Kali indeed becomes a servant to her who performs worship at her feet, and by whom the name of Kālikā has been remembered even once.
For one who is devoted to his service, there is indeed no affliction from Kali;
for Kali bestows upon him wealth, gold, beautiful mountains, and trees.
Coming in person, he bestows it with effort every single day;
indeed, this abundance of spiritual accomplishments cannot be fully described by me. (81)
And because she is devoted to granting boons, she is remembered as Dakṣiṇā;
this very Dakṣiṇakālī is proclaimed to be the ground of spiritual accomplishment (siddhi). || 82 ||
Kālikā, Ṣoḍaśī, and Tārā are considered fond of the left-hand path (vāmācāra);
likewise, Chinnamastā and Bagalā are the presiding deities of the Vāmamārga.
O Great Goddess, Mātaṅgī and the others grant accomplishment through the left-hand path;
likewise, O Śivā, are Kamalā, Bhuvanā, Bālā, and Dhūmāvatī. (84)
Through the practice of the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra), one certainly attains success; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, one also attains success through the left-hand path (vāmācāra). 85.
Bhairavī is satisfied with the left; Bālā resides on the right and the left;
likewise are the Vidyās Vasantasundarī and Saṅgītasundarī.
Through the practice of the left and the right, one certainly attains success; of this there is no doubt.
Reṇukā follows the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra), as do the other goddesses who are of the right-hand tradition.
The Mardinī becomes manifest through the left-hand path (vāmamārga) with certainty;
likewise, for Bālā and Śrīvidyā, there is the practice of both paths (ubhayācāra). 88.
Lopāmudrā is renowned throughout the three worlds as Dakṣiṇā;
she alone is the goddess Vāmā, beloved of the Left, who bestows swift fruit through the Left path. 89.
Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Sundarī, Bagalāmukhī, Bhairavī, and Mātaṅgī—she is always fond of the left-hand path (vāmācāra). || 90 ||
In Vagalāmukhī, who is Mātaṅgī, there exists the one called Dakṣiṇā;
in Mātaṅgī, who is Laghumātaṅgī, there is Sumukhī, who is devoted to the Left (Vāma).
In some [traditions], Vāmācāra is found among Gaṇeśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Saura, and Svayambhū; even within the Vedic fold, there are Bhairavas who are devoted to the Vāma path.
The Kṣitrapālas, the Vāmaparāśvins, and likewise the Kāpālikas,
as well as the Pāśupatas, O Lord, are established in the Left-hand Path (Vāmamārga).
O Goddess of gods, the Buddhists, the Keralas, the Vīravaiṣṇavas, the Śāmbhavas, the Cāndras, and the Atighoras are devoted to the Vāmadvāra.
Other divisions such as the Bārhaspatyas are also devoted to the Left-hand path (Vāma);
O Goddess, the Cīnas are likewise devoted to the Left-hand path and dedicated to the Buddhist way of life.
The Gopālasundarī Vidyā, likewise the Nṛsiṃhasundarī, the Śrībrahmasundarī Vidyā, and similarly the Vāmasundarī. || 96 ||
O Goddess, Sundarīgaṇapa is also preceded by Hayānana;
[so too are] Yakṣiṇī and all the Vidyās, as well as Kāminī and Yoganāyikā.
They are accomplished by the left-hand path (vāmamārga) and not otherwise; nowhere else do they bestow accomplishment.
And so it is with Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Hayagrīva, and Gaṇeśa. (98)
Through the union of the left and the right, she is devoted to both modes of practice (ubhayācāra), [whether] in the Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, Saura, or likewise the Svāyambhuva [traditions]. (99)
O Maheśānī, whether in the Cāndra, Cīna, Pāñcarātra, Vaiṣṇava, Vaidika, or even the Kāpālika traditions, the Vāmārga is the underlying cause here.
Everything is accomplished by way of the Left Path (vāmamārga) and not otherwise;
O Goddess, without the Left Path, the deities are certainly not accomplished. (101)
Totalā, Tulajā, Durgā, Tripuṭā, and Trijaṭāsurī are accomplished through the left-hand practice (vāmācāra); in the right-hand practice, they cause agitation.
In this matter, O Goddess, the proof is Siddhabhairava himself;
otherwise, this man wanders in delusion, and not otherwise.
Sundarī resides on the left and right; Kālikā follows the left-hand path;
and there are Kālī, Tārā, Cinnamastā, Sumukhī, and Mataṅginī. (104)
O Goddess of the lords of gods, Bagalā is devoted to the Vāmamārga;
having abandoned the Vāmācāra, she then [worships] Kālī, Tārā, and Bhairavī. (105)
O God, for one who desires to perform the worship of Mahāpiśācinī, especially Chinnamastā, his downfall will surely occur.
He becomes a poor man, a traitor, and a stealer of children;
especially among all mantras, the family tradition (kulācāra) is thus proclaimed.
Then all the vidyās are perfected; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
O Maheśvarī, all the great vidyās belong to Śakti within you, O Sovereign Goddess. (108)
The Vidyās residing within the mantra-maṇḍala grant accomplishment through the left-hand practice (vāmācāra).
Indeed, O Śivā, the hosts of Apsarases and others attain success through the left-hand practice.

O Goddess, without the left-hand path (vāmamārga), one certainly does not achieve success anywhere; the practice of the left (vāmācāra) is preeminent here and in all philosophical systems (darśana). 110.
First the Śākta, then the Śaiva, the Vaiṣṇava, and likewise the Gāṇapa;
then the Saura, the Cāndra, the Jainadharma, and immediately after that the Svāyambhuva.
And these various types of births will indeed be included within the left; likewise, even on the paths of vision, he does not perform [the rite] on the left. (112)
O Goddess of the Gods, he has no success; he is proclaimed to be my enemy.
The Vāma path is said in the Kula scriptures to be superior to all others.
Even there, in the ritual of Kālikātārā, he is considered most beloved who, having abandoned the left-hand path (vāmamārga), worships Kālī with devotion. (114)
(9) And his ritual action is fruitless; he is called a "great beast" (mahāpaśu).
In that tradition as well, O Mistress of the Gods, there is a division into superior and middling [levels]. (115)
The third would be the lowest; thus there are three groups of three in the three [categories].
Listen now to how the highest among them is determined in due order.
The application of the mantras of the six philosophical systems and so forth to the six locations;
therein, the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is indeed proclaimed to be of a complete form. || 117 ||
In that regard, there is also a distinction of synonyms based on the predominance of the Left-hand path (vāmamārga) within the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Saura, and Buddhist systems. (118)

O Dear One, even in Buddhism, Pāśupata, Sāṃkhya, and the systems beginning with Mantra and Kāla, as well as in the Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, and Vaidika traditions, the left-hand practitioners attain perfection.
Without wine and meat, however, worship shall be fruitless.
Thus, among the ten sciences, there is the "left-handed" (vāmatā) tradition within the sixfold transmission (ṣaḍāmnāya).
The Middle Tradition (madhyamāmnāya) has been declared; now listen, O beloved, to the Lower (kaniṣṭha).
O Goddess of gods, the arrangement of the Eastern Tradition and the others is according to the divisions beginning with Kubjā. 121.

The youngest [deity] among them has been described to you here; it was previously proclaimed that the one beginning with 'Ka' is the great power Kālī, and the one beginning with 'Ha' is Tripurasundarī.
The synthesis of the meaning of the two traditions (āmnāya) is divided according to the [groups] beginning with *ka* and *ha*;
this is taught in the Kularṇava, the Tantrakaula, and also in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
In the Siddhānta and in that which is called Traipura, likewise in the two Jñānārṇavas, in the Śrīmūrtisaṃhitā, and similarly in the Samayārṇava; 124.
In this Tantra, the primary doctrine is the Vāmāmnāya, which is the cause of liberation.
By virtue of beginning with the letter *ka*, it possesses the nature of Brahman; by virtue of beginning with the letter *ha*, it possesses the nature of Śiva.
O Beloved, in this great conduct whose form is movement, there is neither day nor night;
there is no exertion to be performed, nor is there any requirement for ritual purity and the like. (126)
Indeed, all this proceeds from her own will; therefore, she is the most excellent of the two-fold [nature].
Beginning with the statement "Kādi is Kālī and Śakti," it has been proclaimed. (127)
In the Kali age, Kālikā consists of the *kādi* [ka-series] and the *hādi* [ha-series]; indeed, in the Kali age, Kālī alone prevails.
O Pārvatī, hear now how Sundarī possesses the nature of the *hādi* series and attains the state of Śiva. 128.
Having realized the state of being Śiva through the nature of bliss, one should cultivate the contemplation of that Śiva-nature;
[otherwise], bodily mortification, ritual bathing, the performance of *nyāsa*, worship, and so forth are merely manifold formalities. (129)
And thus, due to the great abundance of sequential stages in the Kali age, one may or may not attain success;
therefore, in all ages, Kālī and Tārā bestow their fruits even from heaven.
(10) In the case of Sundarī, however, the family tradition is proclaimed to be rājasa;
the divine [tradition] is also proclaimed, O Goddess, while Kālī is both rājasa and tāmasa. 131.
Even though divine, it yields fruit quickly because of the abundance of heroic [mantras];
for the Kādi is indeed the Kāmarāja, while the Hādi is proclaimed by others as the Lopāmudrā.
This has been declared as a technical convention by the approval of Vaṭeśa.
O Supreme Goddess, there are many Manavas beginning with Ka. (133)
Therein, no *kādi* [consonants] are found anywhere, nor even the *hādi* [consonants], O Great and Most Excellent Lord;
for the *mantras* beginning with *ha* are thirty-six in number, equal to the lotuses. (134)
In that [state], there is no delight anywhere; delight exists only in the sixteenth [digit].
And because the state of *kā* exists in *Kālikā*, it is therefore declared to consist of *ka* and *ha*.
Even in the *kālyā* [vowels], there are indeed many distinctions such as those beginning with *ha* and so forth;
however, in that case, while the status of beginning with *ka* is subject to elision, the status of beginning with *ha* is not.
In Lopāmudrā, there is a division of Sundarī, such as Kāmarāja and the others;
thus, there is the nature of beginning with 'ka' and beginning with 'ha', while the supreme Śrīṣoḍaśī begins with 'ha'.
However, the restraints (niyamas), such as the yamas and saṃyamas, are prescribed for those beginning with the letter *ha*;
but for those beginning with the letter *ka*, there is no restraint, and one may practice dharma according to one's own will.
O Śivā, the Kādimata is eternally embraced; it is considered to consist of technical definitions (paribhāṣā). It is named Śaktisaṅgama, the great Kādimata. 139.
Wherein those three— the *kādi* group, the *hādi* group, and both of them— reside,
the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) takes the form of the *kādi* group, while the *vādi* group is the object of the knowledge of consciousness.
The Great [Principle], known as the very nature of consciousness and bliss, consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti;
and the predominance of Śakti is always proclaimed in the case of Kālī. (141)
In some places, however, Sundarī is the primary one among all [the goddesses];
whereas in Kālī, having set aside Śakti, whoever might perform the recitation (japa), [that is the rule]. 142.
That poor man, though experiencing great suffering, is indeed one who relishes the Yoginī;
his state of celibacy is with Sundarī, and in due time, he attains the nature of bliss.
Thus, O Maheśvarī, the designations for the letters beginning with *ka* and *ha* have been declared;
this is for the sake of accomplishing all worldly manifestations and for the sake of secrecy, O Maheśvarī. (144)
In accordance with the traditions of Gauḍa, Kerala, and Kashmir, initiation should be performed during the ritual of the Vidyā, especially in the case of Tārā. (145)
In Jākukā and Sundarī, there are twenty [initiations] beginning with the full initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā).
In the two systems of Kādi and Hādi, one should perform the rite of the Hā-abhiṣeka.
One should practice in accordance with the names of one's own branch of knowledge and those of the gurus, through the various extensive divisions known as Dakṣa, Kāśmīra, and Gauḍa. (147)
One should cause the command (ājñā) to be bestowed with a name ending in "Amukānandanātha.
The full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is proclaimed for Sundarī alone, as well as for Ṣoḍaśī. 148.
In the absence of the Laghuṣoḍaśī, even when the Paribhāṣā is not present, the fifth [vidyā] is the Rājarājeśvarī, the Supreme Sundarī. || 149 ||
The Śrī Mahāṣoḍaśī is complete and bestows fulfillment upon those previously initiated;
even in other divisions, it should be performed, as has been briefly proclaimed. (150)
Likewise, Kāmakalā Kālī is also remembered in the Dakṣiṇā [tradition];
indeed, among all the Mahāvidyās, initiation brings auspiciousness. (151)
In that regard, the bestowing of names has been proclaimed according to their respective traditions;
O Pārvatī, Kālī, Tārā, and Chinnamastā are indeed one in form. (152)
Likewise, the nine-syllable mantra is taught for Kālī in the ritual procedure of emanation;
that very Vidyā is Guhyakālī, joined with the nine principles (tattvas).
Seated upon seven corpses, the supreme Mahāguhyeśvarī has ten faces; here, her name should be meditated upon according to one's own ritual manual (kalpa). 154.
In the manner instructed by the Guru and in accordance with the tradition, just as there are Gurus arranged in rows for each of the ten sciences (vidyās). || 155 ||
Likewise, the sixfold nyāsas for the ten sciences (vidyās) have been proclaimed;
they are to be worshipped at the beginning of every rite, as they bestow all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). || 156 ||
O Goddess of gods, [this applies] likewise to Sundarī, to Kāmarājā and the others, to Svapnāvalī, to Lopāmudrā, and according to the divisions such as Madhumatī and so forth. || 157 ||
Gurus are proclaimed everywhere by their various names;
Kālikā, as taught in the Kālīkramāgama, certainly bestows the fruit [of practice]. 158.
In some cases, Sundarī bestows the fruit [of practice] through the true path taught in the Kulārṇava;
the Ārṇavas are common to all, for that is the way in all dharmas. (159)
O Goddess, those men who recite the mantras of Kālī, Tārā, or Sundarī without having received the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) are but servants of Yama.
Therefore, O lady of pure smiles, the consecration must by all means be performed;
one should certainly carry out the consecration of the Gādikas and others according to the traditional scriptures. 161.
O Maheśānī, regarding the two with limbs (sāṅga), I have already spoken before;
O Deveśī, even in the case of Parā, it is there through the application of the Prāsāda [mantra].

Even within the eightfold division [of the Kula], the procedure for consecration (abhiṣeka-vidhi) is declared according to the tradition; for it is remembered that [this procedure] applies even when there is a difference in the Vidyās of the sacred tradition (āmnāya). || 163 ||
The Kālī-vidyā exists in the Kali age with ten million distinct divisions;
Sundarī is proclaimed on earth with seven million and ten thousand [divisions].
Tārā consists of three nikhārvas; Chinnā is merely one kharva, together with five hundred and eighty-five thousand and five lakhs. (165)
Listen with reverence to the great vidyā of Bhuvaneśī and to Bagalā; Bagalā consists of one hundred thousand and ninety thousand [mantras] according to the principles of reality. 166.
Dhūmāvatī is the great vidyā; Bhairavī consists of eighty-six [lakṣas]; Mātaṅgī has one hundred thousand eyes, and Kamalā has five hundred thousand. || 167 ||
These [initiations] have emerged from the expansion (prastāra) through the application of the chain (śṛṅkhalikā-yoga);
although there is a distinction between the general and the primary, they are proclaimed by the name "Initiation" (dīkṣā). || 168 ||
Sundarī is established through seventy-seven divisions, while Bhairavī is celebrated on earth through forty divisions. (169)
Bhuvaneśī has eight divisions; Mātaṅgī is remembered as being fivefold;
Kamalā has a hundred divisions; and Bagalā is remembered as having thirty-six. (170)
Dhūmāvatī has five divisions; Tārā is threefold or thirteenfold;
Kālikā is tenfold; and Cinnā is likewise remembered as sixteenfold. (171)
The initiation for the ten divisions of Śrīkālyā is proclaimed;
Dakṣiṇā, Sūryayugmā, and Śmaśānā are recorded as being tenfold.
Bhadrakālī is sixteenfold, and likewise Kālakālī is eightfold;
Guhyakālī is ninefold, and Kāmakālikā is sevenfold. (173)
Dhanakālī has nine divisions, Siddhakālī thirteen, Candrakālī twenty, and Haṃsakālī seventy; in this manner the classification should be made—what else do you wish to hear? (174)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Terminology," in the second section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 1 ||
The second chapter.
The Goddess said: O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the supreme hymn of consecration.
The illustrious Śiva said: Sundarī, Tāriṇī, and Kālī—these three proceed through the Krama initiation.
O Great Goddess, one who is perfected in the Krama will become Śambhu through the Krama;
for one whose soul is purified by the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), even if they die anywhere at all— || 2 ||
That very place would become blessed if it were to possess the form of the Goddess;
for even Śiva, in the form of a bound soul (paśu), [is not so] without the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka). || 3 ||
Without the full consecration, the deity is not pleased;
he who recites the mantra of Kālī or Tārā without the full consecration [reaps no fruit]. (4)
I shall take away his ritual efficacy; that man becomes deranged.
Whatever may be the nectar belonging to one who is endowed with the full consecration, [that too I shall take]. || 5 ||
His ritual action becomes fruitful and the deity is well-pleased;
for one who is endowed with the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), O Śivā, having beheld the mantras, he should recite them.
At that very moment he attains perfection; there is no need for deliberation on this point, O Pārvatī, even without the full initiation, O Lord of the Guru’s Dharma.

O Goddess, there is no recitation, nor likewise fire-offering, nor worship that reaches fulfillment anywhere without the Guru; yet, O Goddess, even without [the Guru], one should perform the consecration and whatever recitation [is prescribed].
Having established that [mantra] along with its divisions, one is then worthy to bestow accomplishment;
for one who is endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) should not cause a salutation to be performed.
O Pārvatī, where the teaching of the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya) remains ever awake,
there resides the supreme Śrī Mahāṣoḍaśī, the sovereign queen of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) and the rest.
In the Kālyā [Tantra], she is Kāmakālī; therein also, in the Dakṣiṇeśvarī [Tantra], she is Guhyakālī, the source of auspiciousness within the Śāmbhava tradition of the six Āmnāyas.
The sacrificial fee is Kālikā, the knowledge that is the perfected science, higher than the highest;
she is Kālī, the sovereign of the four ages, who alone is to be worshipped in the Kali age.
O Goddess of the Gods, this [mantra] belonging to all the deities and times grants success through the four watches;
other vidyās as well, O Mistress of the Gods, bestow many fruits. (13)
In the Kali age, however, there is no *sundarī* at all, nor even the utterance of a *kūṭa* in the Kali age.
A *kūṭa* arises from combinations [of phonemes]; one should always meditate upon that *kūṭa*.
In the Kali age, because of impurity of the mouth and other organs, the correct pronunciation of the seed-syllables (kūṭa) does not arise;
therefore, one should apply a vowel to each syllable and master it with great effort. || 15 ||
Alternatively, one may recite either Kāmarāja or Lopāmudrā;
in the Kali age, Kālī always bestows success and grants the fruit of memory.
O Goddess, O Śivā, by the mere remembrance of her, whether with ease or with playful grace, one becomes a master of the sixty supernatural powers (siddhis) and assumes the form of the Goddess.
The Śābara, Kerala, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Gāṇapa, Cāndra, Svāyambhuva, and Cīna [traditions], having merged together, became merely a lotus [in size]. || 18 ||
O Maheśānī, the limb-mantras number ninety arbudas and doṭis, thirty nikharvas, six vṛndas, and thirty-five padmakas. (19)
O Maheśānī, the mantras have been declared according to the numerical arrangement of the *bindu*,
and according to the distinctions of languages, the distinctions of regions, and the distinctions of the seven synonyms.

Through the different traditions of the scriptures (āgama), according to the divisions of the Nāthasiddhas and others, and with great effort within the Śaiva, Saura, Vaiṣṇava, and even the Gāṇeśa [traditions], || 21 ||
One should perform the primary consecration (sekha) and bestow the respective names;
likewise, the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), the sixteenfold [consecration], the minor preliminary, and the great [consecration].
When the five and sixfold [categories] have been fully understood, what need is there to mention the means for attaining perfection?
One has attained the sixfold Śāmbhava state, along with the Vidyā together with its limbs and its various divisions.
Having understood [the disciple] together with the mantra, initiation should be performed by one who desires his welfare.
First is Kālikā, who is black; thereafter is the beautiful one, who has a reddish luster. (24)
O Pārvatī, Kālī is the primary form of these two, radiant blue and the bestower of perfection;
she is the source of the ten Vidyās and even of the gods.

O Goddess, it has been declared in the Sūkta, according to the two divisions of the Āmnāya, in the Pātañjala, the Vimarṣiṇī, and the Sāra, which is accepted as the established doctrine (siddhānta). || 26 ||
O Goddess, [it is taught] in the Kulacandrodaya, the Bhāskara, and likewise the Śekhara;
O Goddess, in the Taraṅgiṇī, the Arṇava, the Prakāśa, and the Saṃhitāvidhi.
O beloved, the *Amnya*, *Ḍāmara*, and other [tantras] are also proclaimed therein;
furthermore, there are tantras corresponding to each individual power (*śakti*), numbering sixty-four.

O Great Goddess, there are likewise well-spoken hymns (*sūkta*), as well as the *Smṛtis*, *Śrutis*, and so forth; likewise in the six Vedas (*ṣaḍāmnāya*) and in the six systems of philosophy (*ṣaḍdarśana*), and so on. (29)
O Dear One, there are various distinct tantras, including the Saṃhitās and others;
listen now to the thirty-two Śaiva tantras and the Upatantras.
O Maheśvarī, there are three hundred and twenty-five [mantras], and they are said to be innumerable; such is the sequence according to the order of the ten Vidyās.
Mahāvidyā is the perfected lore, and likewise within the sequence of lore;
by the very sequence of Mahānīla, Kālī bestows swift results.
Tārā bestows the full fruit only through the Mahācīna method;
the ritual of Chinnamastā is likewise prescribed only through the Divya-cīna method. (33)
By the sequence known as Gandharva, the fifth [stage] is indeed difficult to attain on earth;
by the path of Mahāgandharva, the sixteenth bestows its fruit. (34)
In the Kali age, Bagalā bestows fruits through the sequence known as Saubhāgya;
Bhairavī is celebrated on earth through the sequence of Jīvacakra. (35)
Dhūmranāyikā bestows fruits precisely through the sequence of the Great Smoke;
Mātaṅgī grants all desired objects precisely through the sequence of the Royal Road.
Mātaṅgī and Kamalā are always present through the sequence of the state of Brahman, through the sequence of the divine path, and also through the sequence of the path of the bound soul (paśu).
O Goddess of gods, the ten Vidyās grant their fruits through a sequence of ten;
O Goddess, even though only one is proclaimed for the triad beginning with Kālī, [the others follow].
O Goddess, you are of one, two, or three kinds, yet you possess infinite forms numbering in the millions; through various limbs, sub-limbs, and distinctions of names, you bestow manifold names.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Praise of Consecration," in the second section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 2 ||
The third chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
"O Mahātārā, your form was previously of a blue hue."
Then indeed [appeared] the form of Sundarī, red in color, higher than the highest. || 1 ||
And in another world, she is Tvaritā; in Vasudurga she is Śārabhā;
she is Dhaneśī, Kālacāmuṇḍā, and Vārāhī preceded by Kṛṣṇā. || 2 ||
Aṇṇapūrṇā is the great vidyā who, in the Kali age, grants the most excellent boons;
she is pleased by the kula-practices and bestows the fruits of the kula-practices. (3)
Vanadurgā, Ugradurgā, likewise Sarvamaṅgalā, Vajraprastāriṇī, Kālī, and Tārā— these are the names that express her.
She is conjoined with infinite forms as the sole Mistress of the South;
she is also present in the *Ḍāmara*, in the *Vāmabheda*, and in the *Uttarāmnāya-Ḍāmara*.
O Goddess, in the tradition of Vaśinī, ritual action is prescribed as being solely on the left;
Kālikā is she who bears the garland of Brahmā and the garland of severed heads.
A garland made from coconuts is proclaimed as the Siddhamālā;
the Śaiva-mālā, however, is composed of Rudrākṣas arranged in triplets.
Due to the predominance of Śiva, it would be Śaiva; it is proclaimed as Śāmbhava.
Due to the predominance of Śakti, it would be Śākta; I am of the nature of consciousness, whose form is the void (Śiva). || 8 ||
O Śāṅkarī, because of the loss of this [practice], this Vidyā is called Lopa-mudrā; it is so named due to its diminished observance, its unrighteousness, and its state of decline.
The beautiful Śrī Mahāvidyā, the Queen of the Queens of Kings,
is accomplished in the Kali age with difficulty through the networks of ritual assignments (nyāsa) and right conduct.
In the Kali age, O Goddess, each person's own most sinful days occur;
due to the abundance of sin, Sundarī does not become pleased.
Because it bears the garland of Brahman, it is proclaimed as the Brahma-vidyā;
and because it is dear to Śiva, it consists of the nature of Mahāparaśiva.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, there are two systems of thought, Kādi and Hādi. O Śāṅkarī, O Goddess, these two systems, Kādi and Hādi, belong to him.
He who is certainly initiated into the dual form consisting of Kālī and Tārā—know such a system to be the Kādimata; [in it] Nityā Klinnā is not seen.
(17) In the Dvitaya [Tantra], initiation is not obtained by one who has reached the limit of fortune;
in that Kādima[tantra], O Śivā, a garland of severed heads (muṇḍamālā) is to be worn around the neck. 15.
In the ritual of Tāriṇī, one should wear a garland of skulls together with Rudrākṣas;
however, a garland of skulls alone belongs to Sarvasiddhiparāmbikā.
A garland made of coconut [seeds] is proclaimed as the alternative in its absence;
O Goddess, by merely wearing this, what is there that does not come into one's hand? (17)
"One should eat in the cremation ground and wear its ashes, O Śivā.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"Now tell me, how should the wearing of a garland of skulls be performed? (20)
Śrī Śiva said:
The wearing of Rudrākṣas is supreme; Kālī consists of skulls.
With Rudrākṣas and Rudra-mantras, and with skull-beads, the mantra of Kālikā [is effective]. (21)
Because the shaven head of Śiva rests upon his neck,
for that reason this garland is perfected as the very form of Rudra’s ornament.
According to the *Sundarīmata*, practitioners should never wear rudrākṣa beads;
rather, a rosary made of coconut shell is to be worn during the performance of all vidyās. (23)
In the Kali age, this Muṇḍamālā alone remains awake;
she is Kālikā, this Brahma-vidyā, devoid of qualities and whose nature is consciousness.
By whatever means the Supreme Mother may be propitiated, that person becomes a perfected one who bestows perfection upon the world; what more need be said, O Paracaṇḍikā?
O Pārvatī, on this earth, there is indeed no one capable of describing its greatness, whether by means of numbers beginning with a parārdha or even ending at its limit.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Rosary," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṃgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the illustrious Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 3 ||
The Fourth Chapter.
The Goddess said: O Lord of Gods, please explain with effort the definitive determination of the Āmnāyas and so forth.
The venerable Śiva said:
The tradition (āmnāya) is declared to be ninefold, according to the distinctions of "excellent" and so forth.
In the three divisions, there is a manifold variety; among the three groups, there are three [subdivisions] each.
First, listen to the highest [division] therein, according to the systems of Śaivism and so forth. (2)
O Goddess of the God of Gods, the philosophical systems (darśanas) are sixfold in sequence: Śākta, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Gāṇapa, and Bauddha.
The six mantras of the six philosophical systems are proclaimed in the Ūrdhvāmnāya;
by this very method [are established] those in the east, south, and west.
The six Āmnāyas are proclaimed as having the designation "Uttarārdha" (the upper half);
this most excellent one is said to shine resplendent in the world of the gods.
The middle one resides somewhere or other; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, the middle one has been indicated through the divisions of the ten vidyās and so forth.
In the Ūrdhvāmnāya, Mahāṣoḍhā is remembered; in the Uttara, Tāriṇī;
and in the Kaniṣṭha, likewise, through the piercing of the six cakras—thus it is threefold, O Śivā.
This has been declared according to the Hādima system; now hear [the procedure] according to the Kādima system.
The previously mentioned [method] alone shall be considered superior among the ten Vidyās and the rest.
In this Ūrdhvāmnāya, the deity is Mahākāmakalākālī;
she is proclaimed as having divisions such as Daśakālī and others, and is celebrated as the youngest (kaniṣṭha).
The Śākta, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Gāṇapa, and Saura [mantras], O Pārvatī,
are located respectively above, in the east, in the south-eastern conjunction, and in the west and north.
O Goddess, by virtue of being joined in sequence, that other [group] is proclaimed;
and in the Buddhist tradition, there are the Indrakas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and so forth. (11)
O Goddess, [practices such as] *indrajāla* and the like belong to the middle tradition (*āmnāya*) of Pātāla;
in the Eastern Tradition (*pūrvāmnāya*) are Vāmaka and Kaula, while Divya and Dakṣa are in the Southern [Tradition].
O Maheśānī, in the west are the Vīra-kaulas, and in the north the Vāmas; in the zenith are the Divyas, while in the netherworld (pātāla) is the path of the Pāśus.
(19) However, by her will, that path is proclaimed as the most supreme:
Brahmakālī, who is the perfected form, and Hāniruddha-Sarasvatī. (14)
O Pārvatī, listen now to the yoga of Śrīmadgandharvasundarī, who is of the nature of Śiva and the nature of consciousness, and who is also the heroic Brahmā. 15.
She is to be worshipped in succession within the midst of the thirty-six powers;
the Northern [tradition] (Uttarā) is recorded as being twofold due to the difference of opinion regarding the *kādi* and *hādi* systems.
The mountain-born goddess is the form of Kādi; Hādi is Mātaṅginī, the supreme. If that woman is indeed Mātaṅginī, then she is [the true] woman.
If she too should be such,
and if she is unmarried up to the age of sixteen, she is declared to be the most excellent of all.
Such a maiden from the mountains is known as the exclusive Kālikā;
having brought such a beautiful woman, who was full of longing... (19)
Having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) of Śakti and the others upon all the limbs of that beloved one,
one should thus worship the wheel of the living force (jīvacakra).
O Goddess, having first performed the ritual installation of the water-offering (arghya),
and having completed the rites up to the offering of the strength-food (bali), one should gaze upon the mandala.

O Supreme Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] preceded by meditation and worship. O Goddess, from its root, one should worship a flowering Pārvatī plant; O Mistress of the Gods, in its absence, even a woman is sufficient.

Having perceived any one of those previously mentioned [powers] through the practice of equanimity (*sāmarasya*), I, who am devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), become endowed with attributes (*saguṇa*) when united with her. 24.
Endowed with qualities, I am joined with her; devoid of qualities, I manifest as myself.
Through the knowledge of Brahman, one becomes liberated and becomes that very form itself.
He is a pauper, a great sinner, and a slayer of heroes; he is regarded as such. || 26 ||
Through the abundance of practice in this, what is there that is not within one's grasp?
In that regard, there is the Muṇḍāsana as well as the twenty-two āsanas.
Among these, one should select a single [mantra] and, having recited it there for Tāriṇī,
assume the hero’s posture (vīrāsana) while holding a hero’s garland in the lotus of one's hand.
One should then recite the Vīra-mantra, the Vīra-śakti, and the Vīra-vidyā.
Holding the Mahāmohana-mālā as far as the tips of the nails, and having thus assumed that very form, one becomes identical with Brahmakālī. (29)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Traditions and Other Matters," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 4.
The Fifth Chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
"O Śaṅkara, tell me how it was stated that [you] possess the nature of Brahmā."
Śrī Śiva said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare it; listen to that, O Priyaṃvadā.
Liberation is proclaimed by the Sāṃkhya school to be the essence of supreme bliss.
O Goddess, due to this identity, He is Brahman—devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and formless (nirākṛti).
"O Goddess, how is He devoid of qualities? Listen as that very point is explained. (4)
Then, O Goddess, as it was being performed, the intellect became dull;
that very state, O Ambikā, is what is called "freedom from qualities" (nirguṇatva) and "formlessness" (nirākāratva).
Though described in manifold ways, there exists only the One alone;
however a person’s intellect conceives it, so by that [intellect] is it described.
And that Brahman is proclaimed to be of the nature of the power to manifest colors;
whereas that which was previously described as possessing qualities (saguṇa) is now declared to be that very same [Brahman]. || 7 ||
O Great Goddess, that which is indescribable is proclaimed to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa);
yet even that which is qualityless is seen as the source of the bliss of Brahman.
The equality that is devoid of qualities is not a partial equality within the parts;
rather, such an equality of flavor is designated as liberation. || 9 ||
The great bliss arising from that is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman. || 10 ||
The bliss born from perceiving the Power (Śakti) is designated as heaven;
the bliss of that bliss becomes liberation—thus it is stated in the Kālikāgama.
The pleasure of coming and going is proclaimed as detachment;
the opposite is the reality of Brahman, and from that arises great bliss.
Beholding is the touching of the state of Brahman; it is the vision of Brahman. O Goddess, union is grasping, and separation is known as transference. (13)

O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, sound— such as that of musical instruments— is considered in brief to be always within the Supreme Reality, which is the power of one's own self, the auspicious Śiva whose form is one's own self.
When [the deity] resides within the body, a state of aesthetic unification (*sāmarasya*) is perceived.
For the purpose of accomplishing this through practice, there is the contemplation of union with Śakti. (15)
O Goddess, as this bliss is, so is Kuṇḍalinī Śivī;
when the bliss of supreme happiness has arrived, it is considered to be beyond all qualities (nirguṇatā). || 16 ||
This [practice] known as the "Vow of the Sword's Edge" is proclaimed on earth as Kālikā;
through the union with Śakti, the nature of Brahman in Śiva has been proclaimed by me. (17)
Having first cultivated the contemplation of being one with Brahman, Paraśiva remained;
having performed the act of universal dissolution and having established [the world] as a staff (uddaṇḍa).
Then, having set aside his great staff, Śiva became intent on meditation;
from that meditation, a resonance arose which attained the state of Brahman-realization.
For the purpose of practicing that [meditation], he performed the summoning of power;
the Goddess perceived that Śiva had fallen away and was intent on straying from the path.
The remembrance of Śiva was bestowed by the Goddess, and her grace was extended; thus was the intellect directed by the Goddess: "May Śiva come to my rescue. (21)
As soon as it was held in my mind, Śiva performed the act of attraction;
this act of Śiva’s attraction has brought me falsehood.
Having thus held this in mind, the mantra was revealed by Kālī; she is Kālikā, delighting in desire and amorous play, accompanied by Mahākāla.
She alone is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman spoken of by Ādinātha;
she is of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, the form of Brahman, and devoid of qualities.
"O Śiva, the spear fashioned by you has come to heaven;
it was given by me for the sake of accomplishment," thus spoke the illustrious Kālikā. (25)
Sadāśiva, the Supreme Śiva, intent upon his previous practices, thus attained the desired state of Kālī through the cultivation of Śakti. (26)
At the beginning of the Kalpa, the Śiva-śakti who was created by Kālī in the past—Śambhu was filled with excessive pride [thinking], "A second beautiful woman is mine. (27)
The great vidyā Kālī was indeed formerly Sundarikā;
O Goddess, on a single day she was endowed with two powers.
(23) "For Śiva has conceptual proliferation as his root; one should say he resembles a dark cloud.
In the second statement as well, one should likewise say 'he with the terrible fangs. (29)
In the third sentence, O Queen of the Gods, [he spoke] to the second Sundarī:
"O beloved of my life, you are Trailokyasundarī, who possesses my very own form. (30)
Thus addressed, the goddess Dakṣiṇā, who is Caṇḍikā in the form of Brahman and the primordial power (Ādiśakti) of perfect form, became possessed by wrath. || 31 ||
Then the Supreme Goddess, assuming the form of the Queen of the Sovereigns of Kings, bore a most beautiful form, an ocean of loveliness.
Then Paraśiva Śambhu, his eyes filled with wonder,
[realized that] the conjunction of the five [elements] occurs simultaneously in an intense manner.

O Supreme Goddess, she who has been described by the Śāla tree that transcends all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) is indeed the embodiment of the Great Proliferation, the Mistress of ten million cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa). 34.
Then she was born as the sixteen-year-old, the great mistress of the Śrīcakra;
the first is the venerable Dakṣiṇakālī, and the second is Kālabhairavī.
The third is the Vidyā proclaimed as Rājarājeśī;
by her gracious glance, he indeed became Rājarājeśvara.
O Dear One, at that very time, all the networks of nyāsa and so forth, the various mantras of worship, and the six āmnāyas beginning with the Ūrdhvāmnāya [are revealed].
O Priyaṃvadā, the primordial Mūlavidyā consists of the original Prakṛti;
O Parameśvarī, this entire expansion of the sacred tradition was fashioned from that.
O Dear One, the doctrine beginning with *ka* is the *Kādimata*, and the doctrine beginning with *ha* is the *Hādimata*;
for the letter *ka* is considered the first, while the letter *ha* is considered the final one.
The letter *kṣa* is known as Meru, while the sixteen vowels are proclaimed [as its parts]. "Ka-ha" is indeed the great mantra that belongs to the domain of the Uttarāmnāya.
She is the Queen of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), the venerable Mahātāriṇī;
she is Sundarī in the form of Kālikā, the venerable Mahābrahmatāriṇī.
O Goddess, O Beloved, the pair of Tāriṇīs always resides [there];
thus the mantra consists of a couple, having the nature of the Kādi and Hādi systems.
Either the first letter of the *ka*-group or the first letter of the *ha*-group [is used];
the first letter of the *ka*-group is prescribed, while the last letter of the *ha*-group is declared [to be the other]. (43)
O lady of pleasant speech, there is no counting the number of Vīreśvaras. Having been told "So be it," Mātṛkā was thus endowed with those syllables. (44)
O Goddess, the complete Mātṛkā is undoubtedly a Vidyā;
therefore, O lady of sweet speech, this Kādimata is proclaimed as the foremost.

O Bhavini, if the letters beginning with 'ka' and 'ha' are grasped by means of the initial letters [of their respective groups], then, O Maheśvarī, the mantra is everywhere declared to begin with 'ka' and 'ha'. (46)
The letter *ka* is the nature of Brahman, and Sundarī is of the essence of Paraśiva. O beloved, in the Kali age, this meritorious Kādimata alone remains as it existed before.
Thus, in the past, the phenomenal world (prapañca) was created for the sake of accomplishing saṃsāra;
in the Āgama, there are many divisions arising from the six systems of philosophy (ṣaḍdarśana).
O sweet-spoken one, there are indeed millions of other divisions as well:
the Dharmaśāstras, the four Vedas, the Purāṇas, and likewise the Vyākṛti.
Logic, Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta, Sāṃkhya, and likewise Pātañjala—these, as well as many other divisions such as poetry and so forth, are proclaimed to be merely elaborations (prapañca). || 50 ||
O Supreme Goddess, from the moment you assumed this beautiful form,
this phenomenal world has been revolving everywhere ever since.
O Goddess of gods, if the Kādimata alone exists among those who speak the truth, then men are of the very nature of Mahākāla. 52.
Women are indeed the embodiments of Śrī-Kālikā; of this there is no doubt. Thus, for the sake of worldly manifestation, there are indeed the Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, and Śāmbhava [traditions]. (53)
The Gāṇapa, Saura, and Bauddha are declared to be the six systems of philosophy (ṣaḍdarśana);
O Mistress of the Gods, numerous doctrines have come into being. (54)
In the Vaidika [tradition], there would be censure of the Śāstra; in the Śākta, the censure of the Vaiṣṇava;
in the Vaiṣṇava, the censure of the Śaiva; and likewise, in the Saura, the censure of Gaṇapati.
In the Gāṇapatya [sect], there is censure of the Saura; in the Saura, the censure of the Vīra;
in the Cīna [sect], there would be censure of the Jaina; and in the Jaina, that of the Kāpālika. (56)
In the Kāpālika [tradition], there is censure of the Buddhists; the Buddhists are considered to be of various kinds.
Thus, O Śāmbhavī, they speak of these differing doctrines in the Purāṇas and other texts.
Indeed, many branches of the Vedas have been proclaimed;
thus, O Maheśvarī, when censure had arisen and division occurred, [the following took place].
But whose mind is not attached to someone who speaks kindly?
Everywhere, mutual disparagement is revealed through worldly proliferation. (59)
They praise one another's divisions and revile one another;
thus knowledge does not attain perfection, for they behave like Piśācas in their agitation. 60.
If there is mutual censure, then unity is not produced;
therefore, for the sake of successfully achieving unity, Kālikā is your savior.
Furthermore, for the sake of destroying the Daityas, the Great Goddess, the destroyer of all beings beginning with Śumbha, assumed a truly beautiful form.
She who sports upon the hearts of corpses amidst seven corpses reclining on a single royal couch;
she who dwells within the lotus-heart of the white-formed Mahākāla.
The flame of the fire of ten million kalpas is to be served according to the prescribed rite;
she who is the source of all things bestows ten million siddhis.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (64)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Brahman Hero," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā. || 5 ||
The Sixth Chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the definitive determination of the power-triangle (śaktikoṇa)."
Śrī Śiva said:
There are three fires, three villages, as well as three gods and three qualities.
Likewise, there are the three states of being, the triad of powers, and the nature of the three channels;
the triple accomplishment, known as the three principles, and the wondrous triad of vessels.
O Goddess, in the Kali age, Kālī who dwells in the triangle, the perfected one of heroes and bestower of boons, is to be meditated upon and known; never indeed any other vidyā. (3)

The goddess Sundarī is relaxed and characterized by the quality of passion (rājasa); her appearance is hidden, yet she may occasionally become a bestower of boons through the protection of ten crores of progeny.
In the Kali age, Kālī; in the Kali age, Kālī; and in the Kali age, Kālī alone is the sovereign of the illustrious Kādimata, bestowing swift fruits in the Kali age. (5)
One should always worship the Mother Kālikā with the five *makāras*;
for one should not recite the mantra without a *śakti*, nor is there a *śakti* without a cause.
"One should constantly contemplate, 'I am always of fivefold form. Thus endowed with such a state of being, one should be devoted to the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa)."
O Goddess, in the ritual of the ten Vidyās, there is a tenfold differentiation;
O Great Mistress, within the Śrīvidyā, the five groups of six (ṣoḍhā-pañcaka) are proclaimed.
The first is Laghu-Ṣoḍhā, the second is Pūrva-Ṣoḍhā, the third is Mahā-Ṣoḍhā,
the fourth is Mantra-Ṣoḍhā, and the fifth is Guhya-Ṣoḍhakā.
In the *Kālikā*, there is a hexad of sixfold [divisions] through various internal subdivisions:
the *Laghuṣoḍhā*, the *Mahāṣoḍhā*, and the third, the *Guhyaṣoḍhā*.
The sixfold mantra is Śaktihaṃsī; the divine sixfold is named Rasā.
The first wheel of the sixfold is Krodha; that which is consciousness is known as Vahni.
O Goddess, O Śivā, likewise for Śyāmalā and for the others there is a pair;
O Supreme Sovereign, there is a pair consisting of Laghuṣoḍhā and Mahāṣoḍhā.
One should perform each [mantra] with the six seers and the meditations;
O Supreme Goddess, wherever the seer, meter, and so forth are proclaimed, [one should apply them].

p. 27) That very [practice] is declared there; even when not explicitly stated, the visualization (dhyāna), the meter (chandas), and so forth, as well as the hymn (stotra)—all of these are indeed identical to those of the Goddess. 14.
And ten thousand recitations are required for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) according to the method of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Thus, all this has been explained in brief; what more do you wish to know? (15)
The Śrī Devī said:
"Tell me, in due order, the ritual for the worship of Kullukā within the Ten Vidyās.
The Śrī Śiva said:
Kālī, Tārā, as well as Chinnā, Sundarī, and Bagalāmukhī. || 16 ||
Mātaṅgī, Śyāmalā, Lakṣmī, Siddhavidyā, Bhairavī, and Dhūmāvatī—these are indeed the ten Mahāvidyās in their proper order. (17)

The Kullukā mantra is considered to consist of *kāli*, *kūrca*, *vadhū*, and *māyā*, ending with *phaṭ*. Aghora is declared to be its seer (*ṛṣi*), and Virāṭ is proclaimed as its meter (*chanda*). || 18 ||
The deity is Kullukā Kālī; the seed-syllable (bīja) is considered to be that named Māyā.
Likewise, Kāmaśakti and Kūrca are proclaimed as the pin (kīlaka). || 19 ||
The six-limbed nyāsa is proclaimed with the [mantra] enriched by the long *ḍa* and *kāma*;
one should perform all rites such as meditation and worship just as in the case of Kālikā. (20)
Māyā, Ramā, as well as Kūrca, Tāriṇī, and Kullukā are considered [the mantras];
and Virūpākṣa is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of Tāriṇīkullukā. || 21 ||
The meter is declared to be Uṣṇik, the deity is Nīlatāriṇī;
the seed-syllable is Kūrca (Hūṃ), and likewise Māyā (Hrīṃ) is the Śakti, while Vadhū is the Kīlaka. || 22 ||
The six limbs of Māyā are as follows: Sarvanīlā, Sarasvatī, Vajravairocanī, and Saṃbuddhā, together with the armor (varma). || 23 ||
Atikāla is declared the Sage (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be the Metre (chandas);
*ha* is the Seed-syllable (*bīja*), likewise *mu* is the Power (*śakti*), and Rocanī is considered the Pin (*kīlaka*). (24)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the syllable *śiva* joined with the six long vowels;
all [subsequent rites], such as meditation and worship, should be performed according to the *Chinnamastā* tradition. (25)
The first seed-syllable of Saṃpatpradā is in the fire of Śrībhairavī;
Vikarāla is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Paṅkti is proclaimed as the meter (chandas). || 26 ||
The deity is celebrated by the name Bhairavī as Kullukā;
*haḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *sauḥ* is the great power (*mahāśakti*), and *am* is considered the pin (*kīlaka*).
One should perform the ritual assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the seed-syllable enriched with the six long vowels;
all other rites, such as meditation and worship, should be performed just as for the Child-form (*bāla*).
The twelve-syllable Kullukā-devī has been proclaimed by Sundarī;
it consists of the Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, and the Lajjā syllables, which form the station of Tripurā. (29)
Having uttered "Śī" and the Blessed Lady, one should speak two "Ṭha"s at the end.
Ānandabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi) of the Kullukā of Sundarī. || 30 ||
O Great Goddess, Gāyatrī is declared as the metre (chandas), Vāgbhava is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), Lajjā is the power (śakti), and Kāmabīja is the pin (kīlaka). || 31 ||
The deity is Tripureśī; with the two [mantras] known as the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), one should perform all rites such as meditation and worship just as in the case of Sundarī. || 32 ||
Listen to the sequence for Mātaṅgī, Bagalā, Lakṣmī, Dhūmā, and Ucchiṣṭa:
the Praṇava, the Kūrca, and the Nārasiṃhas are considered the Kullukā for these five. (33)
And the sage is named Bhairava, O Pārvatī, as far as the mantras are concerned;
that very deity is indeed the seed-syllable and so forth, according to the sequence of each respective deity.
One should perform all acts, such as meditation and worship, as one would for one's own personal deity.
Thus has it been briefly declared; now hear, O beloved, about the form of Ka. (35)
The Mahāvidyā Kaheśvarī swiftly bestows the fruit of accomplishment;
the two-syllabled mantra "Ka-he" shines within whose mouth. (36)
He himself shall become the form of Kālī and attain the body of Tārā; Kahā is the chief of those possessing flowers—one should always practice all of that.
Having taken her who has bathed at the proper time, one should worship her;
she is known as the Triangle (trikoṇa), and the Bindu residing therein is so called.
O Dear One, [one should worship] her together with her limbs and her enclosures in the middle of the triangle.
Then, having worshipped [the deity] together with the secret [teachings], one should visualize the yantra there;
and having performed the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa-pūjā), O Dear One, whatever [mantra] one recites— || 40 ||
All that, O Goddess, bestows success; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Likewise, whatever is spoken, O Goddess, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, [is likewise effective]. (41)
O Goddess, all of that should be performed with effort by one who desires their own welfare.
Kālikā becomes pleased when she is in the form of Brahman and in the form of the Siddhas.
Worship of the [deity] is the best, while worship of the yantra is middling. (43)
Worship of an image and worship of the feet are inferior and would be in vain.
Within that [body], there exist three principal channels:
the lunar channel flows with water, and the solar channel flows with the essence of flowers.
The seed-syllable flows and is known to reside in the center of the triangle;
having observed the fiery channel (nāḍikā), one should worship it, recite the mantra, and offer libations. 46.
O Goddess, one should always worship Kālikā with Svayambhū flowers.
A garland of skulls should be worn around the neck, and a great conch shell held in the lotus of the hand;
one should meditate on Hālā, the youthful maiden of desire, at your side with a [drunken] face. 48.

A garland of human heads, a garland of teeth, and the cremation ground as the womb-mandala—he who performs [the ritual] in this way, O Goddess, shall attain the siddhi of the triple power (triśakti). || 49 ||
Otherwise, even through infinite recitations and millions of heroic practices (*vīrasādhana*), the three powers (*triśakti*) are not attained; what else do you wish to hear? (50)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Power-Corner," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā. || 6 ||
The Seventh Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear about the auspicious maṇḍala of the Yakṣiṇīs."
Śrī Śiva said:
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Guhyakas, and others [are there]. || 1 ||
O Goddess of the gods, there are many mandalas for these [beings]:
first the yakṣiṇī-maṇḍala, and then the gandharva-maṇḍala. (2)
Then follows a pair of Apsaras and Kinnaris, then a pair of Guhyakas;
then a pair of Bhūtinīs and Nāginīs, and thereafter the circle of Kuṣmāṇḍas.
Through great wrathful power or through the wrathful Śrīpārṣanmaṇḍala,
[the mantras] will not succeed at all otherwise, even in tens of millions of aeons.
The great vidyā and the great yakṣī, the mandala and the perfected mandala;
the great yakṣa and the yakṣiṇīs, and the great yakṣa and the yakṣaka. || 5 ||
Which yakṣa is in which place, and who would be the mahāyakṣa?
Which yakṣiṇī is in which [place], and who would be the mahāyakṣī? || 6 ||
O Goddess, due to ignorance of this, one does not achieve success anywhere;
however, the previously mentioned maṇḍalas are certainly accomplished here through this vidyā.
First is Kālī and her Yakṣī, the supreme Mahāmadhumatī;
the second is Bhrāmarī, who is Surasundarī of Sundarī.
Bhairavī’s wife is Candrarekhā, her sister is Suta,
her daughter is considered to be Śālīkelikuñcī, and her mother-in-law is Śālamañjikā.
The form of the Yakṣiṇī has been described, as well as Mahāyakṣī and Mātṛkā;
Tāriṇī is the Yakṣiṇī of Tārā, while Kiṃkaṭā is Padmanāyikā. || 10 ||
The Yakṣī Lampaṭā belongs to Cinnā, and Viḍālikā to Bagalā;
Dhanadā belongs to Kamalā—now listen, O beloved, regarding Bhuvaneśī. (11)
Listen attentively, O Yakṣī, to the Trailokyamohanī mantra of Mātaṅgī;
it is declared to be Śrīmanohāriṇī. Now listen, O beloved, to that of Dhūmāvatī.
The terrifying Yakṣiṇī has been declared; the tenth maṇḍala has been described.
O Goddess, in the ritual of the ten Vidyās, these great Yakṣīs have been proclaimed. (13)
Whichever Yakṣiṇī belongs to a particular Vidyā is considered her servant;
indeed, for whoever is her worshipper, she will certainly grant success. (14)
If a mortal, while reciting another mantra, should recite any yakṣiṇī mantra, he shall obtain no success in his fruit and shall incur the wrath of the yakṣiṇī. || 15 ||
The divisions of the Yakṣiṇī of the tenth maṇḍala are indeed remembered as being in the tens of millions;
those very divisions of the ten Vidyās are what bring about success, and not otherwise.
The maṇḍala of the spirits is also certainly accomplished here;
for how could a yakṣī belong to one who indeed does not know this? (17)
Then, O Maheśvarī, the eight yakṣī heroines are accomplished here;
thirty-six yakṣiṇīs are here, and sixteen yakṣiṇīs, O beloved, are perfected in the attainment of the vidyā; it is not otherwise, nor shall one meet with destruction.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Maṇḍala of the Yakṣiṇīs," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṃgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā. || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O Lord, tell me: is it not the case that nothing at all is accomplished without the attainment of the Vidyā?"
How could great accomplishments such as those of a yakṣiṇī come into his hand? || 1 ||
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Goddess, by the power of this knowledge everything is accomplished, and not otherwise;
likewise, O Goddess, the host of Apsarases and the host of Kinnarīs [are attained].
O Goddess, there is the maṇḍala of the Gandharvas, the maṇḍala of the Siddhas and Guhyakas, as well as the maṇḍala of the Piśācas and the maṇḍala of the Bhūtinīs. || 3 ||
O Goddess, there is the maṇḍala of the nāginīs and likewise the maṇḍala of the ḍākinīs;
O Goddess, there is the maṇḍala of the kuṣmāṇḍas and likewise the maṇḍala of the śabaras.
By means of the sequence of the ten vidyās, or by the Śrī Krodhamandala,
or through the application of the assembly of attendants (pārṣanmaṇḍala), all supernatural powers (siddhis) are accomplished.
O Goddess, in the three mandalas, the Apsarases and others bestow excellent accomplishment;
through the prescribed method for the accomplishment of mantras, they all become accomplished without exception.
Kālī, Tārā, and Sundarī are certainly accomplished through the threefold union;
otherwise they are not accomplished at all—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Thus has initiation been briefly explained; listen now to that, O beloved, wherein the full initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā) is proclaimed according to the path taught in the Kādi-tantra.
She is described in the Bṛhat-Śrīkrama-tantra as having the nature of the Ūrdhvamnāya,
and in the Sudhāśāmbhava-tantra as being the embodiment of peace and liberation.
The one called Śāmbhavā is proclaimed as taught in the Parātāṇḍava-tantra;
the one called Śāmbhavā is also proclaimed as taught in the Śaktisaṅgama-tantra. || 10 ||
Thorough knowledge of the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya), contemplation upon the supreme grace,
and complete mastery of the Great Ṣoḍhā— these are not the fruit of meager austerity.
The knowledge of synonymous permanence, the worship of both the eternal and the non-eternal,
and the method of reciting the sixty [syllables]— these are not the fruit of minor austerity.

The thorough knowledge of the five and the sixfold [methods], the contemplation on the placement of the powers (śaktinyāsa), that which is called the recitation of names (nāmapārāyaṇa), and likewise the recitation of mantras (mantrapārāyaṇa). || 13 ||
(33) Not understanding the impermanence of the ages is not the fruit of minor austerity;
nor is it [the fruit] when contemplating the Kālikā-mantra with the six complete consecrations. 14.
The ritual for the blue [deity] is not the fruit of meager austerity;
likewise, the meditation on the three feet and the preparatory rites in the Śāmbhava and other [initiations]. (15)
The dharma known as Kālī Tārā is not the fruit of meager austerity;
indeed, there is no knowledge equal to that of Aniruddha-Sarasvatī.
O Maheśānī, what on this earth cannot be accomplished merely by knowing this Śrīvidyā? One should perform the Vīrasādhana within it. 17.
During the Kali age, the star Tārā is well-pleased throughout the day and night;
one who desires success should perform the Nīla-gāndharva rite for Sundarī.
By means of the Great Divine Sequence (mahādivyakrama) and the Great Heroic Sequence (mahāvīrakrama),
as well as the Great Blue Sequence (mahānīlakrama), she consists of the letters beginning with *ka* and *ha*.
O Maheśānī, these indeed succeed through the *paśu* sequence: *e*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ*;
while the others, O Maheśvarī, succeed only through the *divya* sequence. (20)
The practice of Bhairavī-mantra follows the sequence of the Svayambhū-flower; the practice of Bhairavī-mantra follows the sequence of the flower born of oneself. || 21 ||
By means of the yoga of the sequence of the Self-Arisen (Svayambhū), what on earth cannot be accomplished?
Everything indeed comes to pass through speech; therefore, it is celebrated as Vāgbhava.
He who knows the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, which is the form of Brahmā, which is itself Ardhanārīśvara, and which consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti—he is a true practitioner (sādhaka). || 23 ||
O Dear One, the Vāgbhava is the root of all, consisting of the wheel of Śakti;
O Dear One, that bliss which arises in the union with the nectar-like essence of Śakti— 24.
O Goddess of gods, that which is of the nature of bliss is declared to be the Vāgbhava seed-syllable;
it is devoid of qualities, formless, and its very embodiment is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
That which is free from dualities and free from egoism is proclaimed as Brahman;
how, then, can such a Supreme Brahman be uttered by the mouth? 26.
Everything is uttered from the mouth; therefore, the mouth is said to be the source of speech (vāgbhava). By means of speech, the entire world—both stationary and moving—is brought into existence.
O Goddess, the supreme seed-syllable Vāgbhava consists of Śiva and Śakti;
Śakti is said to be conscious, while Paraśiva is considered insentient. (28)

Without power (*śakti*), how could there be the utterance from the mouth of that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)? Therefore, apart from power, everything is considered to be insentient (*jaḍatā*). (29)
Due to the union with Śakti in the mouth, she is designated by the name Brahmā;
Śakti resides eternally in the mouth and is celebrated as Vākśakti (the Power of Speech). || 30 ||
O Dear One, the form of Ardhanārīśvara is proclaimed as Vāgbhava;
it is the beginning of all things, the face, and is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman.
O Goddess, O Beloved, the utterance of all things arises from the mouth;
therefore, it is proclaimed as Vāgbhava (the Source of Speech), the eternal form of Brahman.
Vāgbhava is said to be the mouth, and the mouth is celebrated as Brahman. (32)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Great Siddhis such as Yakṣiṇīs," in the second section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṃgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā. || 8 ||
The Ninth Chapter.
Śrī Śiva said:
Now I shall describe the seats for the sake of accomplishing all purposes and goals.
He was seated upon a soft cushion, likewise adorned with a delicate crest-ornament.
The vulva is the skin mat and the bone is the ground seat;
likewise, O Goddess, there is the kūrca seat and the surata seat.

Likewise, O Goddess, the seat of one severed head (muṇḍāsana), as well as the seat of five severed heads (pañcamuṇḍāsana), or three severed heads, or even one severed head, is proclaimed for the purpose of a seat. || 3 ||
A funeral pyre is also praised as a seat, but the cremation ground is the best of all;
likewise, a tuft of hair and a corpse-seat are so described.
Likewise, the corpse posture (mṛtāsana) is proclaimed, as well as the great corpse posture (mahāśavāsana);
O Maheśānī, there is also the hero posture (vīrāsana) and the great hero posture (mahāvīrāsana). || 5 ||
O Goddess, regarding the seat of the vulva-flower and other illuminated seats,
I shall first explain therein the auspicious characteristics of the *muṇḍas*.
By the mere performance of this sādhana, one becomes directly identical with Śiva.
There are four castes—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—and likewise four types of bone-lineages.
White, red, yellow, black, and that which is considered vaidūrya-colored—thus it has been declared, O Goddess Maheśvarī, in the Muṇḍarahasya. (8)

Listen now to the sequence beginning with the highest [quality]: that which was prepared immediately, that which has remained for three nights, likewise that which has remained for seven nights, and that which has remained for twenty-one nights.
It is indeed of four kinds: superior, middling, inferior, and most inferior;
however, that which is shaven immediately is proclaimed as the superior.
The tonsure performed within three nights is proclaimed as the middling;
the tonsure performed after six nights is proclaimed as the inferior.
That which remains for three weeks is declared the lowest of the low;
however, a shaven head that has been freshly made is prescribed for all rites.
The skull situated within three nights is proclaimed for use with garlands and yantras;
one should prescribe the skull situated beyond six nights for the purpose of a vessel.
That which remains for twenty-one nights within a garland, a yantra, or similar objects is considered middling;
that which remains for six months is declared to be ordinary.
The venerable Goddess said: (p. 36) But in the *Kālikapariśiṣṭa*, it is proclaimed otherwise:
"A severed head (*muṇḍa*) found within a three-night period is proclaimed for the purpose of a garland. (15)
The "shaven" (muṇḍa) [liṅga] that has been kept for six nights is declared to be the "ordinary" (sāmānya);
likewise, the shaven liṅga that has been recently prepared is declared to be the "ordinary. || 16 ||
Śrī Śiva said:
A skull that has been freshly severed is recommended for use in the *mālāyantra*;
for the purpose of accomplishing the vessel’s objective, one from seven nights ago is also praised when [the former] is unavailable.
A freshly cut skull is proclaimed to be for the purpose of accomplishment;
taking an excellent skull, the wise man should dig a pit one cubit deep. (18)
One should perform the recitation (japa) over that [object] at the root of a family tree, or in a cremation ground, or at a crossroads, or in a deserted, empty house. (19)
Having diligently offered oblations (bali) especially to the guardians of the directions,
and having performed the purification of the directions, the dissolution of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and so forth, one should indeed perform the recitation (japa).
Having performed the *mantra* for as many times as required, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number;
O Dear One, having first perfected the *muṇḍa* [mantra], one should then have the rosaries and other implements prepared.
One who died by his own will, one who was two years old, an elderly person, a woman, or likewise a twice-born man;
one who died from lack of food, one with leprosy, or likewise one who has been dead for more than seven nights. || 22 ||
Thus, having abandoned the fear of death, one should perform the heroic practice (*vīrasādhana*);
this is declared to be the "hero's posture" (*vīrāsana*), which brings pleasure to Kālikā. (23)
O Dear One, a corpse that has been dead for more than seven nights, whether it remains suspended in the air or has been impaled on a stake, is praised for the purpose of [obtaining] the vessel.

O Goddess, that which remains in the atmosphere for more than six months is likewise excellent; and that which is situated on a garland is also praised, as is that which has been produced beneath [the ground] for seven nights. (25)
Or on a Saturday or a Tuesday, or when death occurs in the body,
or on the fourteenth day, the full moon, the new moon, or during the festival of lamps (Dīpaka-utsava).
O beloved goddess, likewise on the day of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), on the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī),
during the festival of Durgā, on a "hero's day" (vīradina), and upon the arrival of a hero's battle (vīraraṇāgama).
When a shaven head has appeared, it is declared auspicious; even if it remains fixed upon a stake or similar object, one should strike it with a sword, take it, and perform the recitation.
