Having carefully placed the soft hair-tufts, the skulls, and the fourth [item], which is tender, in the middle portion of the great corpse upon the ground; || 38 ||
Having joined [the breath] sequentially in the directions, one should bring the Śakti there;
then, having provided a seat there, as well as the Great Tiger-Posture (Mahāvyāghrāsana).

Having brought [the materials] over it and arranged them according to the rule, and having prepared a seat consisting of the six touches, one should perform the recitation with undistracted mind. (40)
O Goddess, one who is devoted to the observances and other duties should recite [the mantra] for at least one year;
such a person will become capable of maintaining concentration on a thousand [recitations] and so forth. || 41 ||
Having diligently gathered both saffron and kesara,
and having placed them in the left hand, one should draw the yantra with the right hand.
One should perform the libation with the left hand, either a thousand or ten thousand times;
one should always perform the libation while gazing at the face of the Śakti. (43)
She shall become the sovereign of all accomplishments; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Now listen as the characteristics of Siddheśvarī are being described. 44.
If the maiden whose hand is taken in marriage is a heroic woman,
and if she too should become [a practitioner], then she is considered a Siddheśvarī.
O Great Goddess, even a woman who is a thief of grain and devoted to infidelity may become [worthy] if she is the wife of a man of noble family. (46)
She is renowned as Vāgīśvarī, the supreme Mistress of the Great Seat;
she is the sister-in-law (*śyālikā*), intent upon the tasting of [the nectar] if... 47.
She is called Viśālākṣī, the bestower of all attainments;
she who was the daughter of the brother-in-law became unchaste. (48)
She is to be known as Kāmākhyā, the bestower of all accomplishments on earth;
O Goddess, in the house of her husband, one becomes deaf for a hundred [births].
She is renowned as Mahārājeśvarī, the bestower of success in the three worlds;
she herself is the heroic consort of the hero, proclaimed as the illustrious Maheśvarī. 50.
Her daughter is Śrī Traipurāmbarā, the foremost of the family lineages of knowledge;
her daughter is Bhuvaneśānī, the power (kalā) of the capable Śaṅkara. 51.
Vimalā is declared to belong to Divya, and Kālikā is remembered as belonging to Pūrṇa;
O Supreme Goddess, [this extends] from the top down to the end of Medhā in the Sarvasāmrājya.
O Great Goddess, beginning from Vidyārājñī and ending with Haṃsakālī, the names of their wives are proclaimed in reverse order.
The teacher’s wife is Kāmeśī; his daughter is known as Bālikā; and his daughter-in-law is Lopāmudrā. Now hear the sequence for the four castes.
If she is a twice-born woman, she is called Kulasundarī;
if she is devoted to sexual misconduct, she is called Tvaritā.
The daughter and daughter-in-law of the Kṣatriya, through their union, are the goddesses Kaulinī, Mādhavī, Vārāhī, and Kāmasundarī. (56)
In due order, she is called Mohinī; and likewise, if a Vaiśya woman is devoted to sexual misconduct, [she is called] Vyabhicārakramā. (57)
Svapnavatī, Bhogavatī, Nityā, Klinnā, and Kukkuṭī; Aghorā, Siddhacāmuṇḍā, Sutā, and Snuṣā follow in sequence. (58)
The son of a Śūdra’s wife is Kuñcī; [the goddesses] Vā, Vyabhicārataḥ, Aśvārūḍhā, Dhanadā, Kubjikā, and Śabareśvarī [are likewise]. 59.
Anaṅgamālā and the one named Nīlā have been proclaimed in sequence.
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (60)

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gavākṣa Yoga," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 15 ||
The sixteenth chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the definitive exposition of the Navarātra."
Now that the Navarātra has arrived, tell me what ought to be done.
"What is the name of Navarātrī, how did it originate, and what is its nature?
Śrī Śiva said:
"That which is joined with the nine powers (nava-śakti) is called Navarātra."
O Goddess of the lords of gods, she who is one alone is established in nine ways;
[there is] the period called Śayana and Bodhana, and the Navarātra is twofold.
The sleep [of the deity] occurs in the month of Caitra, while the awakening occurs in Āśvina;
by fasting for both occasions, a man shall obtain all perfections.

Abstaining from food, subsisting on fruits, eating only once a day, firm in his vows, eating only at night, or consuming sacrificial oblations (haviṣya)—he should practice these according to his ability. || 5 ||
One devoted to the Navarātra vow will certainly become a Navanātha;
it may be of various kinds according to the Gauḍa, Kāśmīra, or Draviḍa traditions.
The first lunar day (pratipad) occurring in conjunction with the new moon (amāvāsyā) must not be used for the worship performed at that time;
having performed the rites up to the eighth day, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) on the eighth day.
O Pārvatī, even the Root-Vidyā that arrives at midnight becomes the eighth [syllable], the accomplisher of all undertakings.
O Pārvatī, one should perform the fire sacrifice, worship, and other rites there with diligence;
if it falls on the second day, one should observe a fast on that very day.
If there is not even a small portion of the *pratipad* joined with [the previous lunar day] on the following day,
then one should perform the rite when it is joined with the *amāvāsyā*, excluding the first sixteen *nāḍikās*.
The first sixteen ghaṭikās of each tithi should be avoided;
one should perform the installation of the water-pot (kalaśasthāpana) during the auspicious periods, and prosperity will certainly arise.
One should perform the breaking of the fast on the ninth day and the ritual dismissal on the tenth;
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen with care to the procedure known as Kāśmīraka.
One should remain without food for nine nights and perform the fire-oblation on the eighth day;
on the ninth day, there should be a feeding of Brahmins, and one should break the fast when the piercing of the quarters has occurred.
Fasting for nine nights, free from conceptual construction, and with senses subdued,
one should perform the fire-oblation on the eighth day at the junction of the eighth and ninth days.
On the ninth day, one should feed the Brahmins, and on the tenth day, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa).
This sequence is called the Kerala-krama; listen now to the definitive conclusion, O Pārvatī. (15)
Likewise, when there is a decrease or increase of the lunar day (tithi), according to the method previously described,
one does not incur fault in the case of a "prior-penetration" (pūrvavedha) when the eighth and ninth lunar days meet.
Whatever a person performs on the eighth lunar day at midnight becomes inexhaustible through the practice of the Nine Durgās. || 17 ||
Or, the wise practitioner should perform hymns of praise, recitations, and so forth, increasing them by one each day; or he may perform exactly as much as was done on the first day.
By reciting [this mantra] at sunrise and sunset, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds;
this is so even when a woman is engaged in yoga during the vow of Navarātra.
She alone is the Goddess, of this there is no doubt; by worshipping her in the Kali age, one becomes victorious with betel, agallochum, musk, divine garments, and ornaments. (20)
For the Śaktis, the consumption of betel-leaf is always permitted during the Navarātra and similar occasions, beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise. (21)
Having recited that many times, one becomes free from all afflictions and a master of all supernatural powers;
then, remaining seated in a single posture for nine nights, one should worship Śāmbhavī.
O Goddess, one should take hold of the mudrā, and one shall become a sovereign lord of the nine nāthas;
this should be performed in a house, a garden, or on a solitary mountain.
Or, O Goddess of gods, having covered it with clay, O Goddess, one should place the jar there for nine nights with the opening facing downwards, abstaining from water and food.
Having planted barley sprouts, one should perform the *sāmbhavī* mudrā;
or, maintaining a firm posture or lying down, one should practice as instructed.
This vow of the Kāpālikas and Avadhūtas has been declared by me;
O Mistress of the Gods, when the command is given, one should then observe the fast.
If the command of the village headman, the provincial governor, the brahmin, the priest, or likewise that of women, were not to be obeyed; || 27 ||
Having received the command, O Goddess of gods, and having prayed for a boon, one shall become happy;
Mahādurgā, pleased with her devotee, herself bestows the command.
According to the Vīraśākta rite, one should perform the Caṇḍadarpa vow,
diligently licking the tongue to a length of two times four (eight) finger-breadths.
That tongue returns once more; by that means, one becomes a lord of supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Having arrived on the ninth night, at the onset of the night of the great eighth day (*mahāṣṭamī*)... (30)
Having worshipped the Goddess with diligence and having made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) accompanied by his desire,
he should cut the flower from his head, [measuring] full, middle, or smallest [in size].
Having then offered [the oblation] into the center of the yantra, he will certainly become equal to Śiva;
furthermore, that excellent Mahācīna will have his head restored.
Alternatively, listen as another method of practice is described:
for nine nights, one should remain without food, endowed with faith and devotion.
On the Great Eighth day at midnight, having carefully cut away the flesh from the thumb up to the crown of the head, one should begin the sacrificial pit as prescribed.
O Goddess of gods, by performing oblations there, the Goddess shall become manifest;
indeed, one's own body shall become the body of the Goddess—of this there is no doubt to be made. (35)
Alternatively, listen as another method of practice is described:
for nine nights, one who is devoted to the Guru and observes the great vow should remain without food.
Having specially prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one man's height,
one should there perform the fire-ritual using wood from five types of leafy trees.
The observer of the vow should indeed offer his own body as a sacrificial oblation (homa), from the big toe up to the crown of the head;
or, having prepared a bed of fire, he will certainly behold the Goddess.
And by entering the bower of creepers in this very sequence, the practitioner becomes equal to the wish-fulfilling tree; of this there is no doubt. (39)
Alternatively, listen as another method of practice is described:
for nine nights, one should remain without food, free from conceptual constructions, and with senses subdued. (40)
Whatever mantra one may mutter, as well as leaves, flowers, or fruits; whether it be bathing, a tooth-stick, or even a meal in that person's house—[all these become purified]. (41)
One shall bring the three worlds under one's control; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Alternatively, another method of practice is described—listen.
Remaining without food for nine nights, free from conceptual thought, and firm in his vow,
he shall bring under his control whoever he performs the rite for.
O Goddess, one should bring the food intended for whomever one wishes to subjugate;
one should utter the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), followed by the name of the target, and then say "subjugate" (VAŚĪKURU). || 44 ||
O Goddess of gods, having uttered "svāhā" into the blazing fire of the stomach, one should perform the oblation with effort, O Goddess; thus one shall bring that person's house under control. (45)
Alternatively, listen as another method of practice is described:
for nine nights, one should remain without food, speaking the truth, and having conquered the senses. (46)
O Supreme Goddess, O Goddess, on the ninth day, one should take the Sahadevī plant to the forest and fetch its leaves or a ball of food (piṇḍa) with the previously mentioned mantra.
One shall bring that very person, along with their family, under one's control until the end of life;
or else, listen as another method of practice is described. (48)
Remaining silent for nine nights and seated upon a wooden plank,
O beloved, when the day for breaking the fast arrives, one should have a cow's face fashioned.

O Goddess, one should offer oblations into the digestive fire with the previously mentioned mantra in one's own home for three nights according to the principles (tattva), or in that person's home for three days.
One may bring even a man superior to Mahādeva under one's control from birth until the end of life;
or else, listen as another method of practice is described. (51)
Fasting for nine nights, devoted to the Guru and observing the great vow,
one should remain upon the left big toe for four nights, O Maheśvarī.
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, one should observe the Vedarātra vow upon the right thumb;
on the ninth day, one should perform the breaking of the fast and offer a bilva fruit.
One shall bring the three worlds under one's control; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Alternatively, another method of practice is being described; listen. (54)
One should perform the fire sacrifice on the Mahāṣṭamī and observe the breaking of the fast on the Navamī;
by giving away all one's possessions, one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds.
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described:
O Maheśānī, O Maheśvarī, one should subsist on cow urine for nine nights.
O Maheśvarī, whatever mantra one may recite, one should perform the fire-oblation on the ninth day; on the ninth day, one should break the fast with the offering of cow's products.
O Maheśvarī, may there be a vision of the deity in a dream at night;
or else, listen as another method of practice is being described.
For nine nights, having conquered his appetite, observing a vow of silence, pure, free from dualities, devoid of egoism, truthful in speech, and possessed of great intelligence— (59).
If one desires to attract a king, that king should face the seven directions;
he may break his fast according to his wish, but he should always perform the recitation at night. (60)
The three worlds come under his control; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The Sannyāsī is declared to be Śaṅkara, and the Kāpālī is Kālabhairava.
Digambara shall be Mahākāla, and he shall be a celibate student (brahmacārī) and a youth (vaṭu).
Kṛṣṇa is remembered as being of black complexion, while the best of sages (ṛṣivara) is remembered as fair-complexioned (gaura). || 62 ||
O Maheśvarī, "Nāma" is said to be distinguished by form and fragrance;
one should proclaim the name "Kumārī" according to the distinctions of the classes of forms. (63)
O Queen of the Gods, through the division of the *gandhas*, there are ten types beginning with *vidyā*.
Having understood this, O Śāmbhavī, one should perform the breaking of the fast with diligence. (64)

Thus has the classification of speech been briefly explained; listen now, O Pārvatī, to the accomplishment of speech (vāksiddhi), which is said to be of two kinds: that which bestows curses and that which bestows grace. (65)
The first is proclaimed as having the form of great poetry;
now hear the divisions of the second, which has the form of cursing and favoring.
O Maheśānī, [realization] occurs through the gateway of mantra; the second is through the gateway of dreams;
the third would be direct perception; and the fourth is that which comes within the range of the ears.
That which moves in the sky is proclaimed as being of the measure of an arrow;
it resides in the jar, resides in the mirror, and is situated in the midst of the circle of water. 68.
Thus, O Great Goddess, the eightfold power of cursing and favoring has been described; now listen attentively to its divisions known as poetic inspiration (kavitva). 69.
O Maheśvarī, there is also the Aṣṭadikśatasāhasra, the Mahāśrutidhara,
the Dūtakāvya, and the one known as the Ghaṭikāśataka.
The perfection of speech has been described, O Goddess; now listen, O Beloved, to the form of the creeper.
Enveloped by the great Chinese tree-creeper, the most excellent practitioner [attains this]. (71)
If one recites the mantra at night, she herself becomes a wish-fulfilling creeper;
the wise declare that the moon is in her mouth and the sun is in the parting of her hair.
Kāma is in the two eyes, and Sanatkumāra is in the pair of ears;
the Lord of the Nectar-like Speech is in the lower lip, while Sarasvatī is in the tongue. (73)

In the Kali age, the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) and the cow of plenty (kāmadhenu) are proclaimed to be on the two foreheads; likewise, the wish-granting gem (vāñchāmaṇi) and the touchstone (sparśamaṇi) are [proclaimed]. 74.
The conch-shell turning to the right is proclaimed to be the region of the throat;
the wish-fulfilling gem is in the lotus of the heart, and Śeṣa is established in the braid of hair. (75)
The seven heavens are at the end of his head, the seven netherworlds in his nose,
the incarnations in his feet, and the hosts of deities in his shanks.
Brahmā is at the navel; Sadāśiva, whose nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas), is in the triple line;
and Mahāviṣṇu is in the line of hair; [all within] the sphere of the cosmic egg.
The Rākṣasas are on his backbone; the Fortune of Destiny is on his lotus-face;
the Fortune of Generosity is on the pair of his hands; and that called Compassion is in his heart. (78)
In the Kula scripture, she is the glory of fame; in the Māna, she is known as Khaḍgā. || 79 ||
The many millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) are established in its center;
within the worlds of the principles (*tattva*), fire, the Vedas, and the earth, as well as in the continents and so forth, reside the powers of the worlds (*lokaśakti*).
In conversation, he was the four Vedas; all the scriptures were at his waist; and whatever exists within the cosmic egg or upon the surface of the earth was likewise present [within him]. 81.
All that remains eternally pervading the body of Śakti;
O Śivā, it begins from [the state of] Śakti and extends up to the end of liberation.

O Goddess of gods, everything resides in Krodha; the powers of withdrawal (saṃhāra-śaktayaḥ) reside in Hāsa, as do the great mantras (mahāmantrāḥ), while the great vidyās reside in the side-glances (kaṭākṣayoḥ).
The tree is proclaimed to be the living being, and the creeper is the giver of life;
such, O Supreme Goddess, is the majesty of the Cīna-tree creeper.
O Goddess of gods, listen now with care to this marvel:
it is said that the root of another tree may become the surface of the earth. (85)
The root of this tree, however, shines forth in its middle part;
O Maheśānī, the earth is situated in the center, and the branches are said to be all around it. (86)
With branches below and branches above, its root is in the middle and the ground is there;
O Goddess of gods, water is right there, and that place is celebrated as Prayāga.
O Pārvatī, the cosmic egg is indeed the flower, the fruit, and the seed;
it remains fixed there, O wise one, while the tree moves at all times.
Speech dwells there full of joy, moving according to its own will and unrestrained;
it is proclaimed that the creeper of that speech is of the nature of supreme bliss. (89)
She is known as the nature of great bliss, her form being the bliss of consciousness;
she is the nature of perfect bliss, consisting of the essence of the great state of equilibrium. (90)
O Maheśānī, she whose nature is the bliss of Brahman, who consists of the bliss of the mass of consciousness, and who is the embodiment of the bliss of union, is called the creeper (latā). 91.
She alone gives birth to the three worlds and she alone creates the five elements; she alone is the destroyer, and she is considered to be the very form of liberation.
She herself is indeed of the nature of Brahman, while liberation is fourfold;
by the mere knowledge of its root, O Pārvatī, they abide eternally [in that state]. (93)
Sālokya, Sārūpya, and the third, Sāyujya;
and Sānnidhya shall be the fourth—all these are established in Śakti.
Endowed with the nine powers, it is known as Navarātra;
the year of Kalā consists of the month called Caitra, and that which follows is called Āśvina.
O Supreme Goddess, it is proclaimed that [the period] up to twenty-two years is the Kīrti;
up to thirty-two years is declared to be the Dīpāvalī-kalā.
After that, O Maheśvarī, everything will become terrible; listen, for the night of delusion is proclaimed to last for twelve years. (97)
In union, there is the yoga-sleep; in emission, the great sleep.
O Goddess of gods, it is proclaimed that [the former] is illumined by bliss, while the latter is its opposite.
Endowed with devotion, serene in soul, and a worshiper of deities and guests. || 100 ||
In the lower part stands the root of a tree and another tree;
above are the branches, and there, further up, are the flowers and fruits. 101.
The dry seed is Brahmā, and the basin at the root is Viṣṇu;
water should be poured there [by Śiva], but the tree itself is the lowest of men. (102)
Though intent on protecting others, he does not know his own root; for the root and the watering basin of the Chinese tree and its creeper remain unknown to him. (103)
The flower, the fruit, and likewise the seed all abide in one and the same place;
O Goddess, the drop of water situated within a jar is its own protector.
(82) "The banner should have its stalk [fixed] there; this is the view in brief.
O Maheśvarī, everything is accomplished in one place, yet it is distinct within the tree. (105)
The former tree, O Maheśvarī, was lifeless, whereas this one is endowed with life;
it is declared to be the supreme, all-perfecting tree, O Maheśvarī. (106)
"Thus has it been briefly proclaimed; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the most secret of secrets. (107)
"O Lord, by means of the yoga of that knowledge, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds.
Śrī Śiva said: "Having meditated upon one's chosen deity at the root of the Great Kalpa-creeper... (108)
Having joined the mind with the *manotā*, one should move toward the corner;
being of that very form, O Great Goddess, one should practice the yoga of meditation. (109)
By meditating for five ghaṭikās, a person becomes equal to the wind;
by meditating for ten ghaṭikās, one attains victory over the earth. || 110 ||
By meditating for fifteen ghaṭikās, one is not burned by fire;
by meditating for twenty ghaṭikās, one becomes a performer of all types of attraction.
By meditating for thirty ghaṭikās, one shall attain complete perfection; O Goddess of gods, O beloved, by reciting the root mantra and others for a day and night, one attains success.
By meditating for three days, one obtains the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā*;
having thoroughly practiced the yoga of meditation, one becomes a partaker in the meditation on Kuṇḍalinī.
O Maheśānī, without the path, how indeed could there be movement?
For the purpose of showing the way, the creeper has been described; what do you desire? (114)

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nine Nights," in the second section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 16.
The Seventeenth Chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess of gods, this secret has not been proclaimed to anyone at all.
That very thing is being told, O Goddess; listen attentively as it truly is.
Seizure (grahaṇa), O Goddess, is of two kinds, through the distinction of external and internal. || 2 ||
O Pārvatī, that which is called the "Inner" (ābhyantara) is the body consisting of ten million moons;
even there, it is twofold, through the yoga of being (bhāva) and the yoga of action (kriyā).
The yoga of contemplation (bhāvayoga) occurs within Śakti; it is recorded as the yoga of action (kriyāyoga) in the ritual procedure.
Listen, O Maheśānī, to the external [practice], which is twofold according to the sequence of the Sun and the Moon.
O Goddess, there are three types of solar eclipses and likewise three types of lunar eclipses;
they are known as the eclipse of the sun at sunset, the eclipse at sunrise, and the total eclipse.

In the Moon as well, there is a threefold division, and in the Śakti as well, it is threefold each; that which is swallowed is proclaimed to be two and a half finger-breadths greater than the preceding Tattva.
At whatever time clarity arises when joined with touch,
that time, by its imperishable nature, is for the rite of *puraścaraṇa*.
O Goddess, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, from the moment it is seized until its release,
one should perform the fire-oblation and other rites for as many times as the mantra has been recited.
Its five limbs are as follows: recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) are considered equal;
this is declared in the Siddheśvarīmata, which bestows all accomplishments (siddhis).
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described:
during a solar or lunar eclipse, one should stand in water reaching up to the navel.
O Maheśvarī, one should make the end [of the recitation] free from morsels;
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that, and then three times that tenth part in succession.
The preliminary practice consists of seeing and touching; its completion occurs upon seeing liberation.
By means of this sequential yoga, one becomes a lord of all accomplishments.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, however, standing in water reaching up to the navel in a river flowing to the ocean, or in a pond, or even at a confluence; || 13 ||
Standing upon a single big toe until liberation from the final morsel of food,
one should diligently perform the preliminary rite consisting of five, eight, or ten limbs, O Goddess; thus one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhis*).
Having observed the rites such as bathing and giving gifts through the perspective of the scriptures, || 15 ||
These must be performed with diligent effort; no hesitation should be felt in this matter.
The vision of the scriptures is the preliminary sight, while direct perception is the state of full manifestation.
Indeed, no other time is praised more than the moment of a solar eclipse;
having first performed the purificatory bath that removes all impurities, the man of vast intelligence [should proceed]. (17)
When [the eclipse] is being released, it is dāna (giving) that occurs; when it is seized, bathing is proclaimed.
Having performed the bath as prescribed by the mantras, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) according to one's entitlement.
Having performed the twilight ritual appropriate to that time, one should perform the recitation until liberation is attained;
having recited thus, free from all affliction, one becomes a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 19 ||
Having recognized that a woman has bathed after her menses during the interval between solar or lunar eclipses, one should offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to her upon the arrival of every full-moon day.
This yoga bestows sons upon the barren woman and grants all perfections;
O Goddess of Gods, having bathed during a solar eclipse, one should perform worship. (21)
O Maheśvarī, having worshipped [the deity] along with the limbs (aṅgas) and the enclosures (āvaraṇas), together with the bali offering,
and having performed the worship of the maiden (kumārī), one shall become a master of all siddhis.
O Maheśvarī, when a solar eclipse has arrived, having bathed and performed worship,
one should perform the gift of a balance-scale, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and so forth, according to one's capacity.
Having offered that to the deity, one becomes the master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
O Goddess, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, [one should feed] a hundred young maidens.

O Maheśānī, O Śivā, having worshipped him during a solar eclipse while performing the optional fire-oblation (kāmyahoma), one shall become a master of supernatural powers (siddhīśvara); there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
For one who performs the libation (tarpaṇa), prosperity comes from every direction;
indeed, the ritual rinsing (mārjana) should be performed for the pacification of all suffering. (26)
When a solar eclipse has occurred, if there should indeed be a halo (paridhi), that configuration known as Pāribhadra bestows universal sovereignty. || 27 ||
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, when there is little visibility in the quarters, during the eclipse of the center,
or at the time of liberation from clouds, one should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites.
Only the recitation [of mantras] should be performed during a partial solar eclipse, just as during a total solar eclipse;
likewise when a lunar eclipse occurs, and also during a solar eclipse. (29)
One should perform the recitation (japa) and other rites, and thereafter carry out the worship of Śakti;
one shall become a sovereign of all supernatural powers (siddhis)—of this there is no doubt.
During an eclipse of the moon by Rāhu (Tārāpiṇḍoparāga), one should worship the Guru like a deity;
having satisfied him, his boon should be accepted, and one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (sarvasiddhīśvara). || 31 ||
O Goddess, when the time for seizing the *tārā-piṇḍa* has arrived, the practitioner should bring a corpse and,
O Śivā, recite the mantra upon the corpse-seat through the sequence of *grāsa* and *anugrāsa*.
He shall become a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis) and, at the end of that, attain the state of Śiva.
When a solar eclipse has arrived, one who is pure and has previously fasted— || 33 ||
One should offer the flesh of one's own body into the fire from the first morsel until liberation;
O Dear One, such a person becomes a master of all siddhis and beholds the deity.
The solar eclipse is said to be Śiva, and that called the lunar eclipse is indeed Śakti.
During a solar eclipse, one should perform the initiation of Śakti, but one should not perform the initiation of a paśu (bound soul).
One should not perform the Viṣṇu-initiation according to the Pāñcarātra during a lunar eclipse;
however, an initiation performed during an eclipse of either the moon or the sun is considered auspicious for all initiations.

During a lunar eclipse, the initiation by the Śakti is the most excellent of all initiations; there is no requirement for a specific weekday, lunar day, or asterism, nor any restriction regarding the month.
One should not perform the yoga-observance nor engage in ritual deliberation;
even if an eclipse occurs during the Damanotsava festival or on the Śravaṇī day, [the rite must still be performed].
Even one who lacks the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) succeeds if he possesses the mantra;
no other time is praised as more auspicious than the moment of an eclipse of the moon or sun. (39)
During a lunar eclipse, the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) is considered to grant all accomplishments;
the eclipse begins precisely half a ghaṭikā before [the actual onset]. (40)
At that time, one should perform the ritual bath; while [the eclipse] is swallowed, one should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
One should perform the recitation (japa) until the release [of the eclipse], and when it is correctly known [that the eclipse has ended], one should perform the conclusion.
When the sun has been covered for half a ghaṭikā, one should perform the deliberation;
thereafter, one should bring it to completion, and the mantra will certainly become perfected. || 42 ||
If the yoga has passed due to negligence, one should feed wealthy Brahmins;
for whichever limb [of the rite] might be deficient, the feeding of twice-born men serves to complete that limb.
One should perform the fire-oblation (havana) with a tenth part [of the recitations], the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that;
the sprinkling (mārjana) with a tenth part of that, and the consecration (abhiṣecana) with a tenth part of that. 44.
By feeding one-tenth of that number of Brahmins, a man becomes like a god;
for whichever limb [of the body] may be deficient, the recitation must be doubled that many times.
The *puraścaraṇa* for the Brahmins and the other castes is performed respectively by means of two, three, four, and five [units];
or else, the *puraścaraṇa* is described by another method.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should perform the ritual of Meru;
even a flawed mantra, O Goddess of Gods, will certainly be perfected through this sequence. (47)
Alternatively, another method for *puraścaraṇa* is described:
O Goddess, during a solar eclipse, an ascetic whose inner heart is purified [should perform it]. (48)
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped the Mother of the World,
one should offer the flower from one's head as an oblation to the deity.
When a solar eclipse has occurred, having bathed according to the prescribed method, one will certainly behold the goddess Śivā, who is intent on granting boons.
Having brought the Śakti, one should perform the full array of ritual placements (nyāsa) upon her limbs,
[offering] with liquors, meats, fish, and even with dead bodies.
O Śivā, having worshipped the deity there along with the limbs and the retinue,
and having offered the tongue there, one becomes accomplished in the three times through recitation.
O Maheśānī, having respectfully brought [the materials], one perceives the knowledge of the past and future as well as the present during a solar eclipse. 53.
He shall become a conqueror of the three worlds; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O Goddess, the rule regarding eclipsed sunrise and likewise the determination of eclipsed sunset has already been explained by me previously in the Śaktiyoga-krama, O Śivā.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Planetary Seizure," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 17.
The eighteenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, I now desire to hear the ritual procedure for the marks of worship.
The illustrious Śiva said:
When one, facing the direction of hope, should raise up the king of wheels (cakrarāja), [then he attains success]. || 1 ||
O Maheśānī, that very same direction is remembered as the East (prācī) in the ritual of Tārā-Chinnā;
in the ritual of Kālī, the East is remembered as being between the worshiper and the object of worship.
The minister Purandaramukha should worship the Mother of the World (Jagadambikā) according to the sequence of the Goddess’s names; this is recorded as the procedure for Tārā in the Gauḍa tradition.
In the ritual of Kālikā, according to the sequence of one's own left, Kālī,
and the right, the procedure for the Gauḍa and Kāśmīra traditions begins from the petal behind the Goddess.
At that very moment, O Goddess, the rite of offering (arghya) is twofold according to the sequence of one's own deity;
namely, the arghya and the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), performed when the Siddhas have been invoked.

O Maheśānī, the sequence of the limbs (aṅgakrama) in the various directions should be performed according to the order of Kerala and Kāśmīra, and also according to the sequence of their respective goddesses.
O Goddess, the six limbs are placed in the six corners in the order starting from Agni and Īśa;
likewise, the writing of the seed-syllables is considered to be of three kinds.

The sequence known as Kerala occurs precisely according to the established order of the directions; and the inscription of the seed-syllables is performed in the Gauḍa manner within the conceived directions.
The worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) is prescribed in Kashmir, which is well-known among the cardinal directions;
one should worship the deity according to the sequence of facing them directly.
O Goddess, in the ritual procedure for the fierce [deities], one should worship the four *bali* offerings in the sequence starting from the southeast (āgneyī), having assumed a horizontal posture.
It must be hidden, hidden, hidden again and again;
it is a secret, a most profound secret, a secret beyond the most profound. || 11 ||
"Thus it has been briefly declared; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
"O Śiva, let that very thing which has not been told by you to anyone else be spoken.
Śrī Śiva said: It is a secret, a most profound secret, and a secret even more profound than the most profound. (p. 88)
It is said, O Goddess of the gods; be attentive to that.
There shall be an intermediate space even between the worshiper and the one to be worshiped. (14)
This eastern direction, which is esteemed by Virūpākṣa for the severing of bonds,
is considered the eastern direction between the two worshippers of the gods in the case of Bhairava.
In Kerala, that very direction between the object of worship and the worshipper is indeed the east;
from the path facing the deity, what is to its south is the south.

In the case of Bhairava, the prior determination is according to one's own right-hand sequence; having turned toward whichever direction one faces, one should draw the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja). || 17 ||
That same [goddess] is Prācī in the Gauḍa tradition and becomes Tripurā Muktamālinī in the sequence of the Cīna tradition; she is the mantra whose face is like Indra. 18.
At that time, on the back of the Goddess, the East and the West are considered to be Tripurā;
according to the Vedic tradition, that direction where the sun always rises is indeed the East.
According to another view in the *Sūryasiddhānta*,
the east is that direction which lies directly in front of one’s own face as one proceeds along the path of circumambulation, while the west is behind one’s back.
One should know the left as the right, and the right as the left;
thus is the sequence of the east declared according to the path of the eightfold equality.
In that regard, one should worship the lineage of gurus according to the sequence of the Lords; O Goddess, one should worship the lineage of gurus to the right of the deity.
In the triangle in the midst of the goddesses, according to the Gauḍa tradition, there is the worship of the gurus;
the worship of the gurus proceeds by the sequence of the rows of the right and left thumbs.
O Goddess, the doctrine known as Caitanya is the consensus of the bliss of the three lines;
it is worship according to the path of the Nātha tradition by way of the sequence of the three rows.
The right limb is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), and the left limb is Caṇḍikā in the fire;
for this very reason, O Maheśānī, [the merit of] recitation in the left hand is [greater]. 25.
The dedication is declared to be the bestower of all accomplishments; the dedication consists of reciting the Puruṣa-sūkta with the right hand at the conclusion of the japa.
The lineage of gurus is arranged on the left side according to the previously established order;
thus the sequence for the worship of the gurus has been declared. Now hear the sequence for the two offerings of water (arghya). || 27 ||
(89) O Pārvatī, where both the general *arghya* and the special *arghya* are prescribed, there are four vessels for the general *arghya*, and a jar (*ghaṭa*) is considered essential. (28)
Just as a triangle, O Mistress of the Gods, would be devoid of its central point (bindu), so too, O Goddess, is every form of worship rendered void without the jar (ghaṭa). 29.
Just as a petal separated from its filament is devoid of function,
so too, O Goddess of Gods, the triangle becomes devoid of the *bindu*.
If a yantra is devoid of the *bindu*, that yantra becomes like a corpse;
but if a yantra is endowed with the *bindu*, that yantra bestows spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). || 31 ||
In the same manner, one should carefully fashion a circle above the eight-petaled lotus;
for without the circle, there would be no eight-petaled lotus due to the specific ornamentation of the central area.
O Great Goddess, listen attentively to the determination regarding the two vessels:
the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *pādya* vessel, and likewise the *ācamana* vessel, O Śivā. (33)
O Śivā, the arghya, the madhuparka, and likewise the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
as well as the bathing water and other items, O Maheśānī, should indeed be prepared with the general arghya.
In Kerala, even the worship of Śiva is performed with the ordinary arghya; likewise, among the Gauḍas, the worship of the Bhairavas is performed with the ordinary arghya. (35)
O Maheśānī, there is the special arghya, the vessel for the Guru, and the vessel for Bhairava;
then the vessel for the Vīra, the vessel for the Śakti, and the vessel for the Yogins. (36)
Likewise, O Goddess, one should prepare the vessel for the offering (balipātra) using the Śrīpātra;
this is the Kerāla-krama taught and approved by the venerable Sadāśiva. || 37 ||
The vessel for the bali offering, the vīra-śakti, and the vessel preceded by that of the Yoginī are declared according to the system of Virūpākṣa; now hear the system of Vīrabhadra.
O Great Goddess, there is the general arghya and another, the śrīpātra;
with the general arghya comes accomplishment (saṃsiddhi), and with the special arghya comes worship (pūjana).
O Maheśānī, with the third [mantra] one should offer water for the feet and so forth;
O Śivā, according to the tradition of Vīrabhadra, O Goddess, one should perform the five-limbed rite.
O Goddess, in the opinion of Baṭuka, the *prokṣaṇī* water should be common;
for the worship of the Goddess with the special *arghya*, one should perform everything according to the Tāntrika rite. (41)
One should likewise perform the rites for the Guru, Bhairava, the Vīras, the Śaktis, and the Yoginīs;
everywhere, one should perform the offering of the bali, the pādya, and so forth, with the third [syllable].
The doctrine of Baṭuka has been declared; now hear the doctrine of Ānanda:
in the general [rite] there is the hero’s vessel (vīrapātra), and in the special [rite] the power’s vessel (śaktipātra).
(Page numbers 90, 91, 92, and 93 are missing;
p. 94) One should perform the installation of the vessels according to the three traditions (*sampradāya*), through the divisions of *mahākalā*, *mahānanda*, *vāṇa*, *agni*, and *candra*. (101)
O Goddess, one should install and worship [the deities] according to the divisions of the previous kalpa;
if a vessel is moved from its place in the east among the vessels, [the rite is affected]. 102.
One should again perform the placement of the vessels, beginning from the very start;
O Goddess, let there be no clashing of the vessels through negligence. (103)
Having again arranged the vessels, one should worship the Mother of the World;
once the excellent vessel has been established, there is no discarding of the vessel.
But if one has not performed the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*), one should worship again as before;
O Goddess, one should perform the worship at the three junctions of the day by means of merely placing the vessel.
One should worship Śivā with those vessels placed in a single row;
O Goddess, after the ritual dismissal (visarjana), there is no further dismissal of the vessels.
O Maheśānī, the worship has been performed but the ritual dismissal (visarjana) has not yet been done;
O Deveśī, in this sequence one should perform the worship according to the Gauḍa tradition.
Having first performed the rite of setting out the vessels in the sequence of worship,
and having fully worshipped the deity Tārā, one should perform the dismissal of the vessels.
Having again arranged the vessels, one should perform the midday worship;
having performed the dismissal once more, and having set them up again, one should worship them thoroughly.
This sequence known as Caitanya has been proclaimed in the tradition of Mahābhairava.
O Goddess of the gods, by means of this sequence, it shall bring about the attainment of perfection for the vessel. 110.
O Śivā, one should behold the vessel made of the divine, containing the special arghya;
the hero’s vessel for the heroes, and the power-vessel for the Śaktis. (111)
O Maheśānī, the vessel for those who are not heroes is said to be that of the Yoginīs;
the vessel for the Śrī-gurus is the Guru-vessel, and that for the ascetics (yatins) is named Bhairava.

The skull-bowl is proclaimed to be the primary vessel for offerings among the Kāpālikas; however, in its absence, Śūdras should drink water. In the absence of all [such vessels], one should drink water. 113.
The divine drink is for the front of the Goddess, and the heroic drink is for the assembly of heroes;
otherwise, the drink of the animal-sacrificers is proclaimed to be for the sake of hell. 114.
Having merged the general arghya and the special arghya together, one should drink it oneself;
as for the substance in the jar, in the absence of heroes, the heroes themselves should drink it.
One should place [the offering] for the sake of the beggar into the vessel designated as "the beggar.
They know that vessel which is for the sake of the beggar to be the "beggar-vessel" (yācaka-pātra). || 116 ||

O Supreme Goddess, O Auspicious One, having rotated the special *arghya* water at the edge of the wheel upon the pedestal of the Goddess—which is in the form of a wheel—one should [place it] in one's own mouth. (117)
O Goddess of gods, one should first carefully collect [the water] oneself and then cast it [into the vessel];
with the water of the ordinary *arghya* alone, one should offer the water to the Goddess. || 118 ||
Having recited the Brahma-mantra, one should offer everything to the Goddess,
O Maheśvarī, perceiving the vessel as consisting of the great divine nectar.
Having meditated upon that as having the form of the Goddess, one should personally receive it with reverence;
and with the root mantra or other mantras, one should sprinkle it upon one's own head.
O Śivā, having poured that water upon moist ground, one should draw the *māyā* [mantra];
O Goddess of the Gods, by means of this mantra, one should certainly apply the *tilaka*. 121.
Whomever he touches with his two hands, whomever he beholds with his eyes, that very person falls into servitude—even if that man were equal to Śakra. (122)
Having understood all this according to the prescribed rule, one should cause the rites to be performed.
Thus has it been briefly declared; what else do you wish to hear? (123)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Worship and Symbols," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 18.
The nineteenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the definitive rule regarding the ritual waving of lamps (ārārttika)."
The illustrious Śiva said:
[It is performed] with ten, twenty, five, or nine long [vowels].
The wise one should perform the waving of lights (ārārtika) with eight lamps corresponding to the number of principles (tattvas).
He should draw a triangle and a hexagon, and place a dot (bindu) in the center.
With various yantras consisting of the respective vidyās, or with a special arghya-yantra,
one should first display the Bhairava-yantra and the cakra-mudrā.
O Goddess, together with your entire retinue within the circle of all the Yoginīs,
accept this waving of lights for the sake of your pleasure.
O Goddess of the Gods, with this mantra, the wise one should perform the ārārtika offering using black gram,
sesame seeds, rice, wheat, or even barley.
One should carefully prepare lamps made from rice-paste, sugar-candy, turmeric, saffron, the eight fragrant substances, and molasses.
With lamps that are red and yellow, the result is known as subjugation and immobilization.
Thus has it been briefly explained; what else do you wish to hear? (7)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the characteristics of the perfected vessel (*pātrasiddhi*).
Śrī Śiva said:
One should perceive the vessel as consisting of radiant energy; this is the characteristic of one who has attained mastery over the vessel.
By receiving the drops from that vessel, one attains the nature of the deity;
by the mere touch of the vessel, there shall be an ascending progression higher and higher.
O Goddess of gods, even one who is as if dead comes back to life by the touch of a worthy vessel;
for wicked people see the vessel of Vidyā like a lamp.
One should behold the vision of the deity’s hand resembling a great flame;
one should also perceive the six limbs there within that emitted radiance.
O foremost of practitioners, they arise in the midst of light;
O Goddess of gods, the vessel moves with great reverence before the deity. 12.
O Goddess of the gods, she utters a supreme speech consisting of a hymn of peace;
O Goddess, [she effects] the blinding of the wicked with *māṣa* and *karavīra* flowers. (13)
O Goddess, in the sacrifice, liquors attain the state of milk, fish the state of radish-roots,
Bhairava the state of [the deity], and the Śakti the nature of a lamp-flame.

O Goddess, this accomplishment of the vessel (pātrasiddhi) is considered to consist of the nature of the sacrificial fire-pit (homakuṇḍa), the nature of the reality of the path of mantra (mantrādhvatattva), and the nature of the deity. 15.
O Goddess of gods, having brought forth the vessel, one should place the yantra upon the pedestal;
for if the yantra is devoid of its seed-syllable (bīja), that yantra becomes like a corpse. || 16 ||
That which is joined with the seed-syllable (bīja), possesses the form of accomplishment (siddhi), and is endowed with life is proclaimed as such.
O Goddess, just as the wheel of life (jīvacakra) is living, so too is the yantra living.
In Kerala, the engraving of seed-syllables follows the well-known eastern tradition;
the scripts of Gauḍa and Kashmir are likewise conceived according to that very same ancient sequence.
The merging of the seed-syllables into consciousness occurs precisely through the sequence of their mutual presence;
the script [is established] in Nandanātha according to the sequence of the divisions of one's own left and right. 19.
Through the sequence known as the right and left [channels] of the deity, one attains the Bhairava who is a mass of consciousness;
thus, by knowing the order of writing and by worshipping therein, one achieves success.
O Goddess of the Gods, that Great Vidyā in the form of meditation, having attained a divine form within the Bindu, remains eternally wherever she may be.
Whatever is accomplished merely by writing it down, that alone bestows success;
this is the perfection of the *yantra*, O Goddess, through its characteristics moment by moment.
The forms of accomplishment arise as the foremost means for achieving the perfection of the body;
treat the secret, the ultra-secret, and the secret itself like a womb.
Thus has it been briefly explained; now hear, O beloved, about the accomplishment of the jar (ghaṭasiddhi), by the mere installation of which the deity becomes present in one's hand. 24.
One should perceive, without interruption within the vessel, the auspicious Ānandabhairava, who is the entire wheel, all forms, and composed of all the gods. 25.
The jewel named Vāñchā, whose nature is splendor, consists of the wish-fulfilling creeper;
it is speech composed of the essence of nectar, a cascading torrent of ambrosia. (26)
O Goddess of gods, he utters speech through the petition of the deities;
O Goddess of gods, he acts himself, for he is himself a jar equal to Nīla.
O Goddess, by going to that house, the mute speaks Śāradā;
and the water-jar becomes a great retainer of scripture, with a hundred thousand streams. (28)
This accomplishment of the vessel (ghaṭasiddhi), which embodies all the scriptures, has been declared;

likewise, the accomplishment of the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and the accomplishment of the sacrificial offering (balisiddhi) exist within a single hand, O Goddess. What else do you wish to hear? 29.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled “The Determination of the Offering of Lamps,” in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*,
in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā.
The twentieth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O Master, the ten Vidyās and so forth are indeed the ten Śaktis."
O Lord, they have already been described; now, please tell me their sequence.
Śrī Śiva said: Out of devotion for you, I shall speak that which is a secret and even a greater secret: Kālikā, through the Mahānīla-krama, is the bestower of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
O Goddess, the Mahānīla-krama is proclaimed to be of two kinds:
with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). Listen to that sequence, O Pārvatī. (3)
With a sword in hand and his head shorn, his hair was always loose;
his eyes were perpetually rolling from the intoxication of meat and liquor in his heart.
How can that man who does not apply a tilaka of vermilion on his forehead nor [anoint it with] the essence of wine be a worshiper of me? (5)
How can that man who does not wander about at night nor perform worship at night be considered my worshiper? (6)
How can that man who acts in such a way be a worshiper of me? || 7 ||
A dot of vermilion on the pair of eyebrows, a leaf-mark of *svayambhū* (musk) from the sage’s leaf,
and likewise a *tripuṇḍra* made of red sandalwood— after that [he should apply these].
O Maheśvarī, a drop of collyrium should be applied to false sandalwood;
one should cause it to be placed upon the site of the *sattva* for the sake of the *tripuṇḍra* made from incense embers.
O Goddess, in the Mahānīla-krama, the sectarian mark (tilaka) is thus proclaimed:
one who sleeps in the cremation ground, who eats meat, and whose mind is filled with the bliss of pure consciousness.
O Goddess, having made a rosary with teeth, using the uppermost tooth as the central bead (meru),
one should recite the mantra while always chewing betel, O Goddess.
Always chewing betel-leaf after having worshipped the skull-bowl;
devoted to the practice of *vīrasādhana*, he worships the skull-bowl. (13)
Adorned with a garland of skulls and intent upon that [practice], he has a vermilion tilaka on his forehead and the essence of wine in his hand. (14)
(100) O Dear One, the bliss of power (*śaktyānanda*) resides in the lotus of the eyes, in the mouth, in wine, and in the courtyard of the house;
it is said to be twofold—red and white—arising from red sandalwood or from *svayambhū* flowers, and also produced from the skull, bone, or tooth, O Beloved. (16)
The substance of power (śaktidravya) is not something to be refined; all this, both moving and unmoving, is it.
Unchanging, joyful, devoted to women, and having conquered his senses—such a man, O Goddess, is considered fit for the Mahānīla rite. (18)
A rosary made of human teeth, or one derived from a donkey, camel, or horse, belongs to those who are unattached;
it is the "partless" (niṣkala) type. Listen to its sequence, O Pārvatī. (19)
Having drunk the milk from Vijayā, with a mind established in existence, consciousness, and bliss,
one should perform the recitation while wandering and holding a crystal rosary.
In this case, there is no restriction of direction or time, nor is there any rule regarding staying in one place and so forth;
there is no restriction of time for the recitation when practicing the great mantra.
Whatever practice is found in a particular mantra, such is the dharma therein;
one should not entertain doubt regarding that, for it leads to either heaven or even liberation. (22)
The sequence of the five wheels (pañcacakrakrama) should be performed according to the order of the Guru’s command;
O Goddess, it may be soft and delicate, with a crest-lock (cūḍaka) or without a crest-lock (acūḍaka).
The corpse posture, the hero’s posture, and indeed the vulva-skin posture; the posture of assuming any form at will, O Goddess, and the posture of sexual union. || 24 ||
O Goddess, there is the seat of vermilion, the seat of the mountain,
the lotus seat, O Goddess, as well as the sesame flower and the wagtail.
The moon-disk, the female serpent, and the kambalāsana as well;
O Goddess, the prayāgāsana and likewise the mahāprayāgāsana. || 26 ||
The Municūḍāsana is for subjugation (vaśya), and likewise the Sparśaṣaṭkāsana;
O Goddess, there is also the Jihvāsparśāsana or the Vāyusparśāsana.
O Goddess, there is the seat of embrace (āśleṣāsana), as well as the seat of the shaven-headed one (muṇḍāsana);
or else, the blissful union with the illustrious Muṇḍa (śrīmuṇḍasurata) or the blissful union with the illustrious Vīra (śrīvīrasurata).
O Goddess, the five heroic seats (pañcavīrāsana) are located in the directions starting from that of Indra [the East] in sequence:
Āvantī, Mathurā, Kāśī, Prayāga, and likewise [the fifth] seat.
(101) The seat of licking and touching, and indeed the seat of the triple Prayāga;
each of these is a seat, as is the seat attached to the hips. || 30 ||
One who is young, handsome, brave, standing face-to-face on the battlefield, devoid of flight, yet overcome by fickleness and the like. || 31 ||
[He saw him] young, handsome, and brave, standing face-to-face on the battlefield, devoid of flight, yet overcome by fickleness and the like. || 31 ||
O Pārvatī, having brought corpses that have been dead for three nights— whether on a Saturday or Tuesday, or even on the fifth day of the lunar fortnight— one should [proceed] immediately.
One should diligently establish [the deity] in Śivā according to the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions,
in an empty house, on a mountain, at a solitary liṅga, or at a crossroads.
Having reached such a place where the linga indeed faces west and is devoid of the bull, one should adopt the attire of a hero.
O Pārvatī, having diligently offered a bali-oblation to the deities of the cremation ground and to Mahākāla, one should then present a bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions.
Having carefully washed the corpses according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should be fully equipped with all necessary implements and keep the higher practitioners at a distance.
O Dear One, having brought from a distant land such practitioners who are authorized and skilled in the ritual of consecration, and who are equipped with weapons, [one should proceed]. (37)
Having established ten stakes, one should indeed drive them into the ten directions with the Vīrārgala mantra or the Aghorāstra mantra, O Dear One.
Having performed the binding of the directions (digbandhana) with the mantra known as Jayadurgā or with the Vidyāmaṇḍalaka, one should then partake of liquor, meat, and other such substances.
There, one should perform everything— including the fish-offering (*matsya*) and the ritual gestures (*mudrā*)—
according to the procedure prescribed in its own respective ritual manual (*kalpa*), provided with the necessary materials for the sacrificial offering (*bali*).
O beloved, having brought together groups of elephants, horses, buffaloes, goats, rams, mice, cats, and so forth, or else [images] made of flour, || 41 ||
O Pārvatī, having carefully placed one's own neck [as a support], and having made everything like a cremation ground, including the binding of the topknot and so forth; || 42 ||
A horseman, having stationed himself there in due order, should perform the recitation (japa),
beginning after the first watch and continuing until the end of the third watch.

(102) O Dear One, for mantras consisting of one, two, three, or more syllables, such as the *mālāmantra* and others, one should worship Śiva within the *śaktiyoni* according to the path described, O Goddess of the Gods. (44)
O Maheśānī, one should perform the recitation (japa), and the deity will become a granter of boons; yet, fear arises there in forms numbering millions upon millions. (45)
O Maheśvarī, having rendered everything false, one should perform the recitation;
O Goddess, if by the power of fortune the [mantra] consists of refined syllables in the form of a woman. (46)
O Goddess, she who speaks sweetly is indeed called Maheśvarī;
O Maheśānī, from the middle part [of the body], the Brāhmaṇa should speak in Sanskrit.
O Maheśānī, he who is celebrated as Bhairava arrives;
O Pārvatī, O Goddess, whatever is requested by her there must be granted.
She should say, "Choose a boon according to your own desire; speak your wish.
O Maheśānī, that shall happen exactly so; there is no doubt.
One should practice the direct perception of that reality which is the source of power;
having become a lord of all accomplishments, the person shall become the very form of Kālī. || 50 ||
O Goddess, whatever Siddhis exist anywhere upon the surface of the earth within this cosmic egg, they all reside in his hand.
She herself becomes Kālī, O Goddess; no deliberation is required here.
Abandoning delusion, O Maheśānī, perform every rite, O Maheśvarī. (52)
How can he who has the delusion of impurity regarding what is pure be my worshiper?
For one who has such delusion regarding drink would surely feel disgust [toward it]. (53)
How can a man who acts in such a manner be my worshiper?
O Maheśānī, whatever he may obtain, he should offer all of that [to me]. (54)
In the Niṣkala [state] and on the path of Nīla, one should perform the tilaka and other rites as before;
having consumed betel, one should always partake of the milk of consciousness (saṃviddugdha).
"O Goddess, upon seeing a woman, one should mutter [the mantra] and collect the ashes of a corpse;
thus devoted to this practice, the illustrious man becomes the very form of Kālī. (56)
With fifty blades of kuśa grass, one forms the *brahmā*; that which is above it is known as the *viṣṭara*.
A wise man should have the *viṣṭara* fashioned with exactly one hundred blades of kuśa grass.
Having performed the deposition of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa) there, one should perform the recitation (japa) over it;
[one should also employ] betel, the yoni-cakra, a garland of severed heads, and a corpse-seat.
O Goddess, vermilion, the small sword, consciousness, and the essence of wine—whosoever worships Kālī without these shall go to the Raurava hell. (59)
"By adhering to the family tradition (kulācāra), one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (sarvasiddhīśvara).
Thus has it been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Sequence of Worship for the Ten Vidyās and Others," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 20 ||
The Twenty-First Chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear about the supreme Mahācīnakrama."
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Goddess, the Mahācīnakrama is being described by me briefly.
Tārā bestows swift results precisely through the Mahācīna method;
there are the Brahmacīna, the Divyacīna, and the Vīracīna as the third.
Mahācīna and Niṣkala are known as the fivefold Cīna;
O Goddess, the Mahācīna-krama is proclaimed to be twofold.
He is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). The one with parts is the object of the Buddhists; the one without parts belongs to the Brāhmaṇas. Listen to the second [point]. || 4 ||
It should not be said that there is anything more essential than the essence within the three worlds;
for some are gods, some are humans, and some are dānavas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
The world of the Nāgas, the Kinnaras, and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases;
or whatever beasts, wild animals, and birds there are, and all those who have come into this world.
All these are extremely dull-witted, mutually malicious by nature; they are all devoted to evil doctrines and eager for the vision of wrong paths.
O Maheśānī, they do not know the realization of Brahman, which is bliss, nor the joy of the consciousness of Brahman; how can I explain that to you? (8)
That vow was proclaimed for him whose nature is eternally liberated;
forgive me, O Goddess of beautiful limbs, for it must not be spoken by me, O sinless one.
The Goddess said:
Salutations to you, O Lord who bestows boons; salutations to the treasury of compassion.
Even those who are devoted to other deities are seekers of your feet.
For those very devotees of mine, a superior fruit is established;
as for those who are lions, tigers, and the like, and those who act as obstacles— [11]
Likewise, enemies, evildoers, and whatever other wicked creatures there may be—
all of them go to their destruction like moths in a fire.
O Lord, this house, with its flames of lamps visible even to wicked beings, is seen only because of you alone, the all-pervading Master, through your affectionate disposition. (13)
Or else, having become composed of a corpse, do the five deities on the seat proceed? Does the earth attain insentience, and does that which is insentient become full of light? (14)
Fire, wind, earth, and space which illuminates them—[all these were subdued by him], as were the Dānavas, Rākṣasas, mortals, and whatever other hosts of deities there may be. || 15 ||
All the kings as well as others who follow in his footsteps obey his command; if even the Gandharvas do so, how much more so the Narakas and Kinnaras?
Wherever there may be a desire, there success rests in the palm of one's hand;
speech always follows that [desire], remaining perfectly steady.
Having abandoned the state of duality, what is the use of further talk? One who seeks liberation attains liberation; one who seeks wealth attains wealth.
But at the end, he is born in the world of Gaurī like another Śiva;
through devotion to me, he becomes a perfected one (siddha)—this has been told by me to you. (19)
It must not be spoken to one who is not a devotee, nor to one devoted to another, nor to a sinner.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, the Mahācīnakrama has been indicated previously as being of two kinds.
O Goddess, the Mahācīnakrama is proclaimed to be of two kinds; therein, O Mistress of the Gods, it becomes divided through the three qualities (guṇas). (21)
Bathing and other rites are mental purity; recitation is supreme when mental; worship is divine when mental; and the offering of libations and so forth is likewise mental. (22)
The mental observance is declared to be the mental cleansing of the teeth;
every time is auspicious, for no inauspicious time exists anywhere.
O Great Treasure, there is no distinction between day and night, nor at the twilight;
mental purity is the true cleansing of the body, not merely water for the limbs. (24)
One should not seek purification here; one should practice with a mind free from conceptual construction.
Here there is no requirement for purity, nor is there any defilement by what is considered impure. || 25 ||
For one who thus recites the mantra with these observances— which grants the fulfillment of all desires—
eloquence consisting of both prose and verse arises for him in the assembly.
By the mere sight of him, disputants are considered to be deprived of their luster;
even kings submit to servitude—what then of other people? (27)
One should always worship the Goddess even while unwashed or after having eaten;
at the dead of night, in a pure place, one should cause an offering (bali) to be presented with the mantra.
One should never harbor hatred toward women; rather, one should especially honor them.
Having placed a large conch shell upright in the place of recitation, one should perform the *japa*. (29)
While approaching, touching, or looking at a woman anywhere—even where there is no water for rinsing—one may consume betel, other edible substances, and whatever foods one desires. (30)
Having eaten meat, fish, curd, honey, fermented liquor, meat broth,
or any other foods that have been mentioned, one should perform the recitation of mantras while consuming only permitted food.
There is no restriction regarding direction or time, nor any restriction regarding staying in one place and so forth;
there is no restriction of time for recitation, nor for worship and other rites, nor even for offerings.
In this practice for the accomplishment of the Great Mantra, there is no restriction regarding one's own will;
[one may proceed] with water [for purification] in relation to clothing, seat, house, body, touch, and so forth. (33)
O Goddess of the Gods, having anointed [the image] with oil, one should always offer betel;
having put on various garments, one should wipe the body with a cloth. (34)
O Goddess, one whose mind is always absorbed in me should perform the mantra-bath;
O Goddess, in the Mahācīna-krama, this constitutes the bath of a Brahmin.
One should not perform purification here; rather, one should practice with a mind free from conceptual construction.
One should worship with fragrant white and red flowers and leaves. || 36 ||
One should offer auspicious leaves such as bilva, maruvaka, and others, excluding tulasī;
however, one should carefully avoid the bilva leaf and diligently avoid the maru.
O Goddess, one should always nourish the hair, keeping it adorned with oil,
especially on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days and on auspicious festival days.
O radiant one, no unrighteousness exists here, nor does any great dharma;
this is declared to be the discipline of self-will, and one should conduct oneself with a joyful mind. (39)
Considering his purpose accomplished, he remains satisfied within his own mind;
he would not utter the name of Hari, nor would he touch a leaf of tulasī.
One should not engage in thinking of anything else, nor ever censure anything else;
one should not mutter any other mantra, O Goddess, but should always remain free from conceptual construction.
O Goddess, one who enjoys dalliance with Mātaṅgī women should drink liquor immediately; O Beloved, when one has become Brāhmī in conduct through intoxication, what distinction can there be?
O Goddess, [the marks] are the pair of eyebrows, the earrings, and thereafter the vermilion.
O Śivā, thereafter one should apply false sandalwood paste as a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) along with saffron;
a garland of severed heads should be worn around the neck, and a skull should be held in the hand. (44)
Thus, always devoted to right conduct, one should become a follower of the Mahācīna-krama; with a heart of constant bliss, one should always serve with devotion. || 45 ||
That which is situated between the ear and the eye is proclaimed as the *mahāśaṅkha*.
A rosary made of fifty gems, or of the bones of cows, men, or horses [is likewise prescribed]. (46)
O Maheśānī, a garland should be fashioned; one shall become a lord of the sixty siddhis.
That very [garland] is Tārā, O Maheśānī; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (47)
The Goddess said: O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, O Lord of the Universe, O Eternal Savior of the universe!
How could a Brāhmaṇa practice those religious duties that are devoid of the Vedas?
The illustrious Śiva said:
"Excellent, O Goddess, my dear life-partner, you who are so beloved by the practitioner!
O beloved, one should act with that very disposition, having arrived at that state of contemplation."
O Goddess, just as meat is proclaimed to be the primary substance in the ritual of ancestral offerings (śrāddha),
it is forbidden for Brāhmaṇas in the Kali age, O Maheśvarī.
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, having killed animals, one becomes an animal; as many hairs as there are on its body, so many births shall one undergo.
O Pārvatī, I have also declared its secondary forms (anukalpas) as the māsas;
I have explained everything, but now listen, O Pārvatī, to the partless (niṣkala) form.
O Pārvatī, there is no fault in practicing that [meditation] in such a manner;
O Śivā, the hands should be below the wrists and the feet below the ankles.
O Goddess, one should wash the face; this is known as the Cīna-bath.
Having placed both knees upon the ground, one should bring the head down to the earth. (54)
O Goddess of the gods, I have described to you those salutations according to the Chinese path; O Mistress of the Gods, Śakra is my representative for the former sequence.
Having performed bathing, giving, and likewise worship and other rites, O beloved, there is no bathing for me, nor do I have a body, nor indeed does sin belong to me.
What is bathing, and whose is the bathing? For one who has not bathed, food is already taken;
for everything is established within me, in the lotus of the heart.
Having known me, O gods who bestow boons, the perfection of my mantra has been attained;
she who assumes that very nature is Tāriṇī, whose form is the splendor of the entire universe. (58)
Having brought about contact with that splendor, one should perform the recitation;
having come under the power of meditative visualization, the yogi becomes a great poet. (59)
For a Brāhmaṇa, however, the liquor should be made from molasses and fresh ginger;
O Goddess, in its absence, one should perform the worship after consecrating water.
With his heart always near that state and his mind ever fixed upon it,
having abandoned the sense of duality, he shall become a lord of all accomplishments.
Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and other lords of sages constantly worship Śivā by means of the path of the partless sequence (niṣkalakrama).
O Great Goddess, those who are devoted to Tārā are indeed proclaimed to be Brāhmaṇas;
the Brahmavidyā, the Mahāvidyā, is difficult to obtain everywhere in the Kali age.
This is the most secret of secrets, to be guarded in the presence of the uninitiated;
thus it has been declared in brief. What else do you wish to hear? 64.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Great Cīna Tradition," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*,
within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 21.
The twenty-second chapter.
The venerable Goddess said:
"O God, my beloved, tell me the sequence known as the Gandharva."
Śrī Śiva said:
According to the sequence known as the Gandharva, such a beautiful woman is difficult to find on earth.
O Goddess, the sequence known as Gandharva is now being told; listen.
O Goddess, [place] saffron between the eyebrows, and at its end, Malaya aloe-wood.
A man adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made from the eight fragrant substances, with musk applied in the center, and decorated with fragrant white and red flowers, [is purified]. || 3 ||
Situated in a place marked with svastikas, enclosed by a red rampart,
and adorned with various fragrances through incense made of the eight perfumes.
Wearing red garlands and garments, adorned with a necklace of pearls, he has received the full consecration upon his head; therefore, there is no shaving of the head there.
O Goddess, one adorned with fragrant oils should cause the hair to grow long,
providing various fragrant foods fit for a king, O Maheśvarī.
Water is pure by its very nature; how much more so when heated by fire?
One should always bathe in warm water, or in the absence of that, in whatever water is available.
The house should be decorated with various paintings until it resembles the interior of a mirror;
it should be enriched with canopies and banners as ornaments and graced by the resonance of bells.
It was accompanied by the five kinds of musical instruments and endowed with various sounds;
it was adorned with extremely fine garments and embellished with gold leaf and other ornaments. || 9 ||
He was always adorned with ornaments consisting of necklaces, bracelets, and finger-rings,
and [served] with various sweet foods and many kinds of milk-based preparations.
Endowed with various enjoyments, there arises the sequence known as the Gandharva;
thus it has been briefly explained. What else do you wish to hear? (11)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Sequence Known as Gandharva," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahotārā. 12.
The twenty-third chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, tell me quickly the sequence for the ritual procedure of Chinnamastā.
Śrī Śiva said:
According to the very method of the divine Cīna [tradition], Chinnamastā bestows the fruit [of practice]. (1)
O Great Goddess, the two sequences have already been revealed previously. O Goddess, her tilaka is on the forehead and red sandalwood paste is on the pair of eyebrows. (2)
At its end, O beloved, one should cause a mark of three lines (*tripuṇḍra*) to be made with divine pigments upon a leaf of *rocanā*, and a drop of cremation-ground ash should be placed in its center.
O Śivā, one should recite at all times while placing mouth to mouth;
O Goddess, this specific method for the drinking of the essence of Śakti has been described.
Thus has it been briefly declared regarding Bhairavī; listen, O Pārvatī, how Bhairavī is difficult to attain on earth through the yoga of the sequence of one's own flowers (svapuṣpakrama).
O Goddess, listen now as the sequence known as Svapuṣpa is being told:
[one should contemplate] a young woman, beautiful and charming, whose very form is the nectar of youth.
Then, O Maheśvarī, having brought her—who was full of longing, whose mind was intent on [him], and who was endowed with mantras and yantras—[he approached her]. (7)
And mutual glances must also be exchanged with one another.
One should always remain in his company; water prepared by his hand, food prepared by his hand, and ground prepared by his hand [should be used]. (9)
One should offer to the deities the flower fashioned by her hand;
for women are the gods, women are life, and women alone are indeed the ornament.
Women are the creation; women are the emanation; everything is established in them.
One should never harbor hatred toward women; rather, women should be especially honored.
One should avoid striking them or acting with crookedness in every way;
for he who does so out of negligence will meet his downfall.
O Goddess, when one who dwells in the house of a beautiful woman beholds such a sight and remains free from agitation, he is worthy of the practice; otherwise, he is not.
And when one perceives it as a state of modification, O Maheśānī, the practitioner perishes in an instant; and that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) likewise becomes [destroyed] in an instant.
Nevertheless, she should not cause any alteration to her own body,
O Goddess of the lords of gods, so that she may indeed remain free from modification.
p. 111) Within her there exist three principal channels:
the lunar channel flows with water, and the solar channel flows with the flower.
The seed flows; the channels are to be known as threefold and fiery.
O Goddess, one should forcibly obtain the flower by means of the Puṣpiṇī mantra.
O Goddess, one should lead [the disciple] by force with the Drāviṇī mantra and a glance;
having grasped both, O Maheśvarī, one should perform the recitation (japa). 18.
That which becomes a flower by itself is called "svapuṣpa" (self-flower);
