likewise, O Great Goddess, it should be performed through the recitation that brings about stability. 19.

O Goddess, both the Śakti and the practitioner are considered difficult to find as a couple, even with great effort among the Bagalāntā mantras, O Queen of Devas, including those beginning with the Kalpa-mantras. (20)
This sequence should be properly applied; no hesitation should be felt here.
O Goddess, due to the influence of the defects of the Kali age, this yoga will not come to pass.
Therefore, O Śivā, let the Bālā be accomplished through the ritual procedure for the bound soul (pāśava-kalpa);
for regarding the Bālā, the dual practice (ubhayācāra) is indeed primarily the right-hand path (dakṣiṇa).
And if one desires swift accomplishment, one should practice the Gavākṣa-yoga wherever there is a gathering of women, or by a river, a stream, or the ocean. (23)
Wherever they perform their ablutions, one should have a window constructed there;
having observed them, one should diligently perform the recitation (japa) without interruption.
O Goddess, O beloved, one should satisfy them all with gold, garments, and other gifts;
thus has it been briefly declared. Now hear, O Pārvatī, concerning the *tilaka*.
Having carefully brought saffron in the left hand,
O Pārvatī, one should go with effort to the bank of the Śaktisnapana.
O Śivā, having carefully inscribed the yantra on the palm of the left hand,
O Supreme Goddess, one should apply the remaining paste as a tilaka.
O Goddess, one should apply a drop of musk on the forehead, a leaf-pattern of excellent sandalwood paste, and a decorative streak of saffron on the cloth. 28.
In the center of that, there should be the divine white [syllable] and so forth, as well as the hair and so forth, as before.
O Goddess, the two sciences of the ten Vidyās are said to be the "hair-increasing" [mantra].
Thus it has been briefly explained; what else do you wish to hear? || 29 ||

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Sequence of Chinnamastā," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 13.
The Twenty-fourth Chapter.
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the definitive teaching on the sequence of Vagalā.
Śrī Śiva said:
By the very sequence of good fortune, Bagalā becomes swiftly visible. || 1 ||
The minister wore yellow garments, was adorned with yellow ornaments, wore yellow garlands and clothes, and resided in a yellow house. || 2 ||
He is declared to be devoted to yellow worship, his mind delighted by yellow food,
a consumer of yellow substances, and provided with a yellow seat.
Performing oblations with yellow substances, using yellow flowers, and endowed with a yellow power,
he should bestow yellow pigment (rocanā) upon the earth, as well as saffron and *munipatra* leaves.
O Śivā, one should apply a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with turmeric and place a piece of khadira wood in its center;
O Supreme Goddess, it should be fumigated with incense made of yellow sandalwood.
Having accomplished everything indeed, one should be devoted to the path of the gradual stages;
for in the Kali age, there are threefold types of worship: creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
The worship of emanation alone proceeds according to the sequence of the Garbha and Kaula Āgamas;
however, in the Gauḍa country, the worship follows the path of maintenance (sthitimārga), while in Kumārikā it follows the path of withdrawal (saṃhāramārga).
The ritual procedure for the worship of the Gauḍa country is called Guptakaulāgama;
that for the worship according to the sequence of reabsorption (saṃhārakrama) is called Kāmarūpāgama.
And likewise, the sage Sāṃkhyāyana, relying upon the Gauḍa Āgama, spoke concerning the worship of the image during its installation in the Āgama; listen to this, O son.
One should seek out the daughter of a Brahmin who is beautiful in all her limbs, lovely, adorned with every part of her body, recently married, and in her menses.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the fourteenth, or on the full moon;
or else on a Tuesday or a Friday at night, the youth [should perform the rite]. || 11 ||
Likewise, one should perform an anointing with oil from a young woman;
then, having brought a mattress and bed, one should spread them out facing north.
Having spread over that [the ground] with *śevanta*, *jāti*, and *campaka* flowers, as well as sandalwood mixed with camphor and musk; (13)
The wise man should perform an anointing of all her limbs with the Lakṣmīsūkta;
he should place that maiden, who has been smeared with sandalwood paste, upon a couch.
With the mantra "dhruvā dyauḥ," the boy should place the girl, who is facing southward,
upon the bed of Unmīkhī while reciting the Śrīsūkta.
Having extended her [the tongue], one should perform the worship;
having performed the two-fold sixfold placement (*nyāsa*), one should then place the fivefold Bagalā-mantra. || 16 ||
One should likewise place the maiden while recollecting each of those respective limbs;
then, one should purify the foot and the city of Japa with the root mantra.
One should apply musk ointment with the mantra "Gandhadvārā," and one should properly offer a garland of flowers with the root mantra. || 18 ||
One should offer the purification of the substances and perform the recitation right there;
one should recite this king of mantras one hundred and eight thousand times.
During the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), on each day of the lunar month,
or alternatively on the full moon day, one should perform the worship for good fortune (saubhāgyārcana).
This bestows the perfection of practice upon men and is the supreme means for achieving mantra-siddhi;
O Goddess, without this sequence, the practice will never succeed anywhere.

Therefore, O Goddess, with every effort on this earth for the sake of accomplishment, one must practice the sequence known as Saubhāgya; O Goddess, without it, there is no success even through ten million [other means]. (22)
Having abandoned the eightfold pride, having indeed abandoned the three defects,
and having abandoned attachment to the five senses, one should practice the sequence of auspiciousness.
Having made pleasure and pain equal, gain and loss, victory and defeat,
and having established equanimity toward cold and heat, one should practice the sequence of auspiciousness.
He who performs worship on this earth without knowing the two groups of six becomes fallen;
such a man shall go to the Raurava hell.

O Goddess, without the knowledge of the distinction between the external and the internal, the sequence of the yellow [syllables] must not be performed; otherwise, one incurs the curse of the deities. (26)

Having abandoned both conceptualization and discursive thought, one whose mind is established in pure consciousness should then perform the sequence of drinking; otherwise, he will certainly fall from his state.
O Śivā, one who has conquered the senses may perform the sequence of drinking after having first attained bliss;
however, he who performs it for the sake of mere pleasure shall incur the curse of the deities. (28)
O Supreme Goddess, O Devi, he who performs worship without knowing the procedure for one's own immersion (āveśa) does not become a fallen Brahmin. || 29 ||
But he who causes agitation in the mind of the maiden during the auspicious sacrifice shall immediately become distracted in mind, like another Vācaspati.
One should not produce pain in either the body or the senses;
the man who causes such pain shall become fallen. || 31 ||
One should worship one's own wife, or the wife of a brother, or even the wife of a guru—provided she is endowed with youth—as prescribed by the Sāṅkhyāyana school. (32)
One should respectfully [invite] a washerwoman residing in the initiation hall, or the daughter of a potter, or even the daughter of a Pulinda, or a Mṛducūḍaka.
One should worship the wife of the Ṛṣi, endowed with the characteristics previously mentioned;
the worship according to the prescribed rite is the method of Durvāsas for the offering. (34)
O Śivā, one should worship the flowering [plant] endowed with all auspicious marks;
this was spoken by the sage Mataṅga and brings immediate success upon the earth. (35)
O Goddess of the Gods, this is the sequence for attaining accomplishment; there is no accomplishment without a guru.
Therefore, with every effort, one should be a follower of the guru’s command. (36)
O Goddess of the gods, one becomes accomplished; there is no need for deliberation here.
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (37)

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Sequence of Vagalā," in the second section of the Northern Portion of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 24.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O God, tell me the sequence of the Mahārāja."
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Goddess, the sequence of the Mahārāja is now being told; listen.
In a wonderful pavilion adorned with various and variegated staircases, graced by lofty palace towers, and furnished with canopies and banners; (2)
It was endowed with various groves, beautified by swans and peacocks,
delightful with various variegated mansions, and resplendent with elephants and horses.
It was adorned on all sides with various ornaments,
filled with the fragrance of incense, and embellished with diverse lamps.
Upon a beautiful jeweled lion-throne, adorned with precious ornaments and graced by the fragrance of jasmine, campaka, punnāga, and ketakī flowers.
Adorned with camphor, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment, saffron,
as well as the juice of jaṭāmāṃsī, he was embellished by the fragrance of perfumes.
Accompanied by the resonance of bells, always pure in mind,
his heart immersed in bliss, he was adorned with divine garments.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with celestial raiment,
his mouth filled with betel and resplendent with the beauty of his teeth.
With vessels for the gods, vessels for dance, vessels for enjoyment, and musical instruments,
as well as with dances, songs, and instrumental music, he was proclaimed by twenty-four [bards].
It was adorned with songs, melodies, and rhythmic beats; with resonant sounds and the languages of various regions, both in prose and verse.
Adorned with various and manifold ornaments, the supreme practitioner [becomes] the queen of kings, because she deludes all royal conduct. (11)
O Goddess, the Śrī Mahārājamātaṅgī, who deludes all the gods—her *tilaka* is now being described; listen. 12.
O Śivā, one should apply *kucandana* between the eyebrows, *aguru-sāra* in the space between them, *kastūrikā* as the *tripuṇḍra*, and *keśara* in the middle of that.
O Goddess, the sequence of the Mahārāja has thus been told by me to you;
or else, O Sovereign of the God of Gods, one should personally become intent upon singing.
Thus it has been declared in brief; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Sequence of the Great King," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 25 ||
The twenty-sixth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
Speak the sequence of the venerable Bhuvaneśānī, which is most difficult to obtain.
Śrī Śiva said:
Through the sequence of divine states alone, Bhuvaneśvarī swiftly bestows accomplishment.
The syllable *ha* is the very form of Śiva, and the syllable *ra* is the destroyer of sins.
The letter *ha* is proclaimed to be the form of *māyā* because it takes on any form at will;
O Goddess, this entire universe is enveloped by *māyā*.
O Goddess, without whose Māyā nothing at all shines forth; and that which is devoid of her light never shines anywhere.
O Goddess, this world shines forth accompanied by that light;
O Maheśānī, without her, the world would become like an insentient object. || 5 ||
Contemplating with his intellect the unity of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra, and then unifying the three energies (tejas), he should then conceive the Form (mūrti) therein.
Having meditated upon her together with her limbs [aṅgas] and her retinue (āvaraṇas), one should become identical with her in form;
the Goddess is known to be the form of the Guru, and the Guru is the form of the Goddess.
The self should become the form of the mantra, and the self should become absorbed in that;
O Goddess of the Gods, in this manner, one should always have the mind fixed upon that through this sequence.
One shall become a conqueror of the three worlds; there is no need for hesitation here.
O Goddess, listen as I describe with diligence the tilaka of this [mantra]. 9.
One should apply a drop of white sandalwood paste in the center of the forehead;

at its edge should be the *gandhasāra* [sandalwood paste], and from it the *tripuṇḍra* of divine color. Red *akṣata* grains should be placed in its middle; by this, one becomes a lord of supernatural powers (*siddhīśvara*).

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Sequence of Bhuvaneśvarī," in the second section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 26 ||
The twenty-seventh chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the definitive teaching on the sequence of Kamalā."
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, [apply] saffron on the pair of eyebrows, and after that, vermilion.
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, there is a white triple-line (tripuṇḍra), and in its center is the filament;
having bathed, wearing white garments, and adorned with white garlands and unguents.
Adorned with white ornaments, he should perform his ablutions at the three junctions of the day;
the man should subsist on sacrificial food (havis), sleep upon the ground, and be fond of sweet foods.
Starting from the first Friday,
one should always worship the Virgin Goddess on each subsequent Friday, following the sequence of increasing days.
Starting from the second Bhṛgu, one should cause [the disciple] to swallow [the mantra] with an increase of one syllable per day;
O Goddess, one should worship [him] every day amidst the sounds of various musical instruments.
One should perform this every day until the sixteenth day;
then again, O Maheśvarī, beginning from that day, one should continue until the end of that same day.
One should worship daily with a restrained mind, intent upon the nature of the deity;
circumambulation should be performed according to the sequence of the parts of the body.
Lamps should be offered there according to the sequence of increasing digits (kalās),
and one should daily feed Brāhmaṇas according to the sequence of the presence of those digits.
Thus, devoted to right conduct, the illustrious man shall become Viśvarūpa;
with self-restraint, he should always worship all the royal insignia.
"He shall undoubtedly become the lord of all imperial sovereignty;
the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) shall reside in his home, and the King himself shall become his servant.
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? 10.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sequence of Kamalā," in the second section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 27.
The twenty-eighth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Śiva, I desire to hear the sequence of Dhūmāvatī."
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen as the sequence of Dhūmāvatī is being told. 1.
O Goddess, there should be collyrium between the eyebrows, a drop of ash within that;
there should be a tilaka of clay on the forehead, and human ash within that. || 2 ||
Wearing garments of black cloth, adorned with black perfumes,
wearing smoke-colored robes, and decorated with garlands of dhattūra flowers.
Combined with incense made from *gulā* and seated upon a cremation ground,
one should worship the entire smoky-colored world as a mantra consisting of smoke.
The seat should be a crow’s wing-feather, and one should whiten the teeth black;
he should be a celibate student, moderate in diet, free from conceptual construction, and a master of his senses.
Speaking the truth, moderate in diet, sleeping on the ground upon a mat of kuśa grass,
he should perform ablutions three times a day, being intent upon the rite of eradication.
"By making one's own mind like a crow, one will certainly cause the world to vanish.
A mortal devoted to this practice thus enters the stage of the Smoke-colored Sequence (dhūmrakrama).
This is declared to be the Crow Sequence (kākakrama); what else do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure of Dhūmāvatī," in the second section of the northern portion of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 28 ||
The twenty-ninth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Śiva, I desire to hear the sequence of the path of Brahman."
The illustrious Śiva said:
Collyrium should be applied to the eyes, and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be made with vermilion.
One should apply turmeric to the pair of eyebrows and fashion a white petal; with a red drop in its center, one should always remain absorbed in that. || 2 ||
One should always recite [the mantra] while eating, while lying down, at night, and at all other times.
O Goddess of Gods, when one's hands are soiled with food remnants, one should offer the bali-oblation with those remnants.
O Maheśānī, while consuming the remnants of the Śakti at all times, one should perform japa; indeed, one should practice japa specifically at night.
Having consumed betel, one should offer betel-leaves as oblations;
one who eats betel is like a meat-eater, and having eaten, one should not perform purification.
Having carefully smeared the house, one should perform the sweeping with a broom; O Goddess, one must recite the mantra with diligence, for otherwise success is certainly not attained.

O Goddess of the gods, one should always sprinkle one's own body with the hand still holding the remnants [of the offering]. Reciting the mantra with the hand still holding the remnants is proclaimed as the path of Brahman.
O Goddess, the sequence of the path to Brahman has been told by me to you;
by another sequential yoga, one becomes established in the sequence of the path to perfection.
The perfected Vidyā becomes gracious, manifest, and bestows boons;
even the Lord of the Gods becomes a servant—what then to say of human beings? (9)
"The secret has been told, O blessed one; it must be guarded like one's own womb.
Thus it has been declared in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (10)

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Sequence of the Path of Brahmā," in the second section of the latter part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 29.
The thirtieth chapter.
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the definitive teaching on the Kramamālā.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Maheśvarī, hear now the garland of the vidyās according to the sequence previously described. || 1 ||
The rosary called "tooth" (dantākhyamālā) has been described, as well as the "great rosary" (mahāmālā); O Goddess, in the ritual of Vindhyavāsinī, there is likewise a rosary of human bones.
A garland made of red sandalwood is prescribed for Tripurā; that known as the self-arisen flower is prescribed for Bhairavī. (3)
A garland of guñjā seeds is prescribed for Mātaṅgī; for Dhūmrā, one made from donkey teeth; and the garland known as haridrā is proclaimed for Vagalāmukhī.
One made from ivory, one made from human bone, and likewise one made from coconut shell—
between these two, O beloved, there is no difference, just as there is none between Śiva and Śakti.
The garlands of Mahālakṣmī are proclaimed to be made of lotuses;
O Śivā, for the rite of the Siddha-vidyā, the garland of Bhuvaneśī should be made of crystal.
A rosary made of *guñjā* seeds is highly recommended; now hear of the powers of those vidyās.
Mahāvidyā is proclaimed through the distinctions of fragrance, form, and species. (7)
O Goddess of the gods, listen now with diligence to that sequence;
O Maheśvarī, one should assign the names according to the sequence of form and fragrance.
O Pārvatī, having diligently set aside the name given by one's mother and father,
one should indeed bestow upon oneself a name according to what is appropriate, O Pārvatī.
That which is the first power, O twice-born ones, is pure in her inner being;
she is pure, with stainless and beautiful limbs, possessing a divine fragrance and enchanting to the mind.
For that goddess is like a dream, revealing all accomplishments;
she who is black, with a dark-blue luster and honey-brown eyes.
Desiring the heart of the practitioner, possessing a human-like scent yet smelling foul, she is to be joined with Kālī; she is proclaimed as Kālī.
She who is the third, fair-limbed and anointed with fragrant honey-scented unguents,
is the goddess named Tripurā, the one who accomplishes her own flow of consciousness through the sequence of her own blossoms.
But that woman who has the scent of rut, who is slow-moving due to stumbling from intoxication, and who is endowed with the scent of raw flesh, is Mahiṣāsuramardinī. (14)
A woman who has the scent of liquor, with red eyes and being exceedingly harsh, is proclaimed as Mahogratārā, the destroyer of great sins. || 15 ||
A woman who possesses aśvagandhā, who has long shanks and is captivating, whose eyes are tremulous with fear, and who is mounted upon a horse, shall be a bestower of boons. (16)
With a stench like raw meat in her mouth and a putrid odor from her joints, she is said to have dark-blue hair; she is Durgā herself, intoxicated with passion. 17.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, filled with various fragrances, beautiful, with lovely hair, long-eyed, and captivating. (18)
Skilled in various graceful charms, she deliberated upon the family scriptures;
she pressed against the chest of her guru, appearing slender at the waist.
That beautiful woman shall be fair-complexioned, the promoter of all undertakings, possessing a divine complexion, a slender frame, and anointed with divine perfumes. (20)
Bhuvaneśī has been described by me; now hear about Kamalā, O Pārvatī.
She has beautiful limbs and lovely eyes, and she sits in the lotus posture with her knees slightly raised.
Kamalā is described as having her limbs adorned with golden ornaments;
she is richly decorated with necklaces of gunja berries and possesses dark, flickering eyes.
O Maheśvarī, the Mātaṅgī-vidyā known as Cāruhāsā has tawny eyes, tawny hair, a small mole, and a very broad smile. (23)
She is called Dhūmāvatī; O beloved, listen to this perfected vidyā:
she is always addicted to food and is very fickle due to eating much. (24)
She whose form deludes the three worlds is proclaimed as the perfected Vidyā;
she has a hanging face, pendulous lips, is yellow in color, and is motionless. 25.
O Maheśānī, O lady of noble vows, she is celebrated as Bagalā;
these ten Vidyās, O Pārvatī, are renowned as being the very form of Śakti. (26)
O Maheśānī, they constantly sport with the threefold state—consisting of mothers, wives, and sisters—in the form of the Vidyās themselves; of this there is no doubt, O Goddess. (27)
O Great Goddess, one should diligently perform the ten sequences within the ten Vidyās in every way, O Goddess; otherwise, it cannot be accomplished even in ten million aeons. (28)
For indeed, O Goddess of gods, they do not attain success by means of ten million recitations;
therefore, with every effort, one should practice the sequence of one's own respective vidyā.
O Goddess, the *svayambhūkusuma* is proclaimed to be of three kinds in the Kali age; furthermore, according to the Gauḍa and Kāśmīra traditions, it is indeed of six kinds.
The flower of a maiden who has not been married before the age of sixteen is declared to be the best;
the flower taken by force is declared to be middling. (31)
O beloved, O Goddess, the youngest [lineage] is proclaimed for one born through the Rajas-yoga; now hear the sequence of the Puṣpa [lineage] according to the tradition known as Kāśmīra.
The flower of a maiden who has not yet reached sixteen years of age is said to be the best; the flower obtained by force is said to be middling.
Through the Rajas-yoga, that which accords with one's own will is proclaimed as the lowest;
this "triple flower" is said to be difficult to obtain in the three worlds. (34)
The flower known as Anaṅgagandha is the secret and the most profound secret; it must never be spoken of. || 35 ||
"It must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret again, O Śivā!
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (36)

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Garland of the Sequence," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Prajñātārā. || 30 ||
The thirty-first chapter.
The venerable Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, the ten stages and the powers have been described by you."
O Lord, in what length of time does the fruit of those successive stages arise?
"O Lord of the gods of gods, how was all that form and action in the past?
Śrī Śiva said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this secret in your presence. (2)
O Śivā, on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
one should by all means perform the rite of the Nīla-sādhana.
O Goddess, let this be performed every day; in its absence, on the Mahā-aṣṭamī.
In the Satya age, [the goal is reached] in ten years, and in the Tretā age, in one year.
In the Dvāpara age, that same period is two months; in the Kali age, it is a single day and night.
O Goddess of the Gods, spiritual accomplishment is attained especially on the Nīla path.
Having abandoned the entire day,
and having avoided the final watch of the night as well as the first watch, [one should practice] during the two middle watches.
In the midst of that, within the four channels, Kālikā becomes the bestower of boons;
she is endowed with sixteen steps and accompanied by various hosts of elemental beings.
In the midst of those nine staircases, crowded with the seventh,
Mahākālī stands there together with her hosts of attendants.
Her heart is desired by the practitioner; she is joined with Vahni and Vetāla, and is endowed with the armor and enclosures as taught in the venerable Uttara-tantra.
Endowed with the states of the arts (kalā), she herself proceeds beyond that;
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, hear now the enumeration according to the Mahānīla-krama. 10.
In the Kṛta age, [the goal is attained] in twenty years; in the Tretā, in two years;
in the Dvāpara, in six months; and in the Kali age, in two months and more.
The ritual procedure for Chinnamastā is remembered as being exactly according to this same sequence;
however, there is indeed this much distinction: her constant association with Śakti is remembered.
O Pārvatī, listen attentively to the number in the sequence called Gandharva, starting from twenty-one, ten, four, and seven, O Pārvatī. (13)
One should perform the rite of *vīrasādhana* with the four mantras.
O Pārvatī, listen attentively to the number [of repetitions] according to the sequence known as *puṣpa*. (14)
It is accomplished through the path of yoga involving the Ṛṣis, Vedas, Vahnis, and Yāmas;
O Pārvatī, listen with care to the number [of repetitions] in the Mahācīna-krama. 15.
O Śivā, listen to the sequence of the Great Kings, from Satya up to Kali, occurring over thirty-six days known as thirty-six, ten, and four [i.e., forty]. 16.
Listen now to the sequence of the state of Brahman, from the Satya age up to the Kali age, according to the progression of eighty, sixty, twenty-six, and seven years. || 17 ||
O Pārvatī, [the number] is one thousand less by one hundred for each sixty-year period;
O Goddess, listen with diligence to the count according to the sequence of the worship of the digits (kalā). 18.
O beloved, listen now to the state of Dhūmra, who is sixteen years of age, possesses one thousand six hundred Vedas, and is skilled in the true sequence [of the scriptures]. (19)
One thousand, six thousand, one thousand, and twenty-five thousand [years],
O Maheśānī, are the durations in the absence of Brahmā during the Kali age, totaling three years.
For ten years and six months, the deity shall be a granter of boons;
O Goddess, I have declared this number to you regarding her direct manifestation.
O Maheśānī, a mantra becomes perfected through the previous yoga;
O Maheśānī, the prior sequence is proclaimed to apply to every mantra. (22)
O Goddess of gods, even a wicked mantra is accomplished through the previous sequence;
this is a secret, a most profound secret, and must be guarded like one's own birth-vagina.
"By keeping it secret, one attains success; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus has it been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (24)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Fruits of the Krama," in the second section of the *Śrī Śaktisaṅgama-tantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣa and Ugratārā. || 31 ||
The thirty-second chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the symbolic gestures (mudrā-saṅketaka) were previously indicated by you."
O Master, what have you concealed? Tell me now.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Śivā, out of love for you, I shall tell you this secret which is more secret than the most secret, the essence of essences; O beloved, one should guard this secret.
The Kerala, the Kāśmīra, and the Gauḍa as the third—these are declared to be the three traditions (sampradāya), each of which is manifold. (3)
It is proclaimed as ninefold through the divisions of pure, secret, and fierce; [the lineages] are the Divine, the Siddha, and the Human Oghas, along with Dakṣiṇāmūrti and Śaṅkara.
Ānandabhairava and Kāla, and by the sequence of time as well;
in the tradition of Ānandabhairava, there is a lineage of eighty-five gurus. (5)
Through the realization of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, there is indeed a triad of divisions;
furthermore, ten divisions were previously taught according to the sequence of the ten Vidyās.
From another [perspective], Śiva-nirvāṇa is attained through the sequence of the six Śāmbhava [methods],
and indeed by the sequence of *ka* and so forth and *ha* and so forth, according to the distinction between the rays (*raśmi*), the Person (*puṃs*), and Power (*śakti*).
Six thousand and one hundred and sixty-four [verses] are proclaimed;
while the primary form (prakṛti) exists, the modified form (vikṛti) is not more powerful.
O Goddess, there are three traditions within the sphere of the abodes of Prakṛti;
through the division of the Tattva-mudrā known as Makāra, there come to be this triad.
O Goddess, eating eggplant with milk, or consuming surana, milk, and meat,
is proclaimed to bring death for a maiden at the end of five sets of five years (at age twenty-five).
In the case of a young girl and a young woman, having worshipped the young girl, [one attains] the fifth.
Liquor, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual union—these are declared to be the five "M"s that bring pleasure to the deity. (12)
O Goddess, the juice of jaggery and raw ginger is considered the first mudrā;
oil-cake and salt, O Goddess, are proclaimed as the second. (13)
Garlic and tamarind are proclaimed as the third;
[the first] resembles the solar disc, and [the second] is like the lunar disc. (14)
The fourth is Sundarī, produced from wheat and beans;
the fifth is Śaktyālāpa. These are proclaimed as the five mudrās. (15)

The Goddess said: What is the origin of that which is called "mudrā"? What is its essential reality (tattva) named? And what is the nature of the syllables beginning with "ma"? O Śaṅkara, tell me everything.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, listen now with diligence as the secret is told—
how it was spoken by the Great Goddess and how that form is described.
Because it maintains that form, it is called a *mudrā*; from that form, transformation occurs.
O Maheśānī, how could there be movement without the path? (18)
O Goddess, because the path is shown, movement is seen everywhere; indeed, for the purpose of showing that path, the five *makāras* have been proclaimed. (19)
Having known this, one attains the fruit; there is no need for deliberation here.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Sadāśiva [are attained]. || 20 ||
These five "M" syllables are the five types of names;
they know that the fifth is the all-pervading, auspicious Self-knowledge, which is complete.
O Goddess of the gods, the five principles (tattvas) are proclaimed in Kerala;
they are the foundation of the five mudrās, which consist of bliss—listen as I speak of them. 22.
Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, Īśvarī, and Śrī Sadāśivā—these are declared to be the five mudrās, O Śivā, who hold the essence of reality within their mouths. (23)
Having gratified the power Kuṇḍalinī by means of the fivefold ritual of the mudrās—
with wine, meat, fish, and the supreme mudrā of union— 24.
Wherever the five things beginning with "ma" are found, there the Goddess resides; of this there is no doubt.
There is no middle way [without them]: the wine of Mādhavī and the power arising from the essence of wine.
Susumna, Shankhini, Mudra, Unmani, the unsurpassed Rasa, the blissful nectar of Samarasya, Maithuna, and Sadashiva. (26)
O Maheśvarī, the power Mahākuṇḍalinī was taught by me for the sake of union with that [Śiva];
O Maheśānī, this power was not spoken of by me for the sake of worldly enjoyment.
The self-arisen liṅga (svayambhūliṅga) is proclaimed for the sake of the state of equilibrium with Kuṇḍalī;
through the yoga of practicing this, one becomes possessed of the essence of Kuṇḍalī. || 28 ||
"O Lord, what is Kuṇḍalī like, and what would her essence (rasa) be like?
Śrī Śiva said:
"I shall speak of that which is unspeakable, and how her essence truly is. (29)

In that same way, O Goddess of gods, the essence of the bliss of the equality of flavors has been proclaimed by me, whether through ignorance or even through the latent desire for worldly enjoyment. (30)
O Goddess, the fruit born of saṃsāra manifests in the form of the embryo;
having understood this, one attains the fruit and becomes a conqueror of the three worlds. || 31 ||
Therefore, this fifth mudrā has been proclaimed by me to you through the union of the nectar of conjunction, for the purpose of raising Kuṇḍalinī.
When it goes into the lunar vessel (cāndrapātra), that is proclaimed to be in its center;
when it has gone into the ten-petalled maṇipūra within the suṣumnā, [that is the next stage].
Indeed, because of its union with the nectar produced by that [action], it is proclaimed as the second [channel].
Within the twelve-petaled heart-lotus, however, resides Śaṅkhinī, situated like a tortoise. (34)
In the *Sudhāsāgarakrīḍā*, the fish (*matsya*) is proclaimed there;
the third mudrā is thus described, while the fourth is on the sixteen-petalled lotus.
The fourth [mudrā] is circular, with the moon, sun, and fire conjoined within it, containing a central bindu, and joined by chickpeas known as the "vulva-banner. 36.

The five mudrās have been taught by me for the sake of attaining the fruit of the meditative realization of liberation; through the five [syllables] beginning with *ma*, knowledge of this arises. (37)
"The form of the letter *ma* has indeed been proclaimed by me to you as the path;
thus it has been explained in brief. What else do you wish to hear? (38)

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Secret Sign Language of Mudrās," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 32 ||
The thirty-third chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the secret [teaching] previously mentioned."
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen to the primary convention within the convention known as the five mudrās.
Drink is said to be of five kinds, distinguished as Mahādivya and so forth: Mahādivya, Divya, Vīra, and Mahāpaśu. (2)
It is proclaimed to be fivefold: Paśubandha and Paśu;
Prāṇāyāma, which is the coordination of prāṇa and apāna; Pratyāhāra, which is the steadying of the mind; and [Dhāraṇā and Dhyāna]. || 3 ||
Having pierced the solar orb and entered the center of the lunar orb,
she constantly draws down a stream of nectar through the path of the Suṣumṇā.
This is declared to be the divine drink, supreme and bestowing all accomplishments;
this is declared to be the great divine [rite]. Listen to the divine [instruction], O Maheśvarī! (5)
Before the Goddess, he partook of the divine and supreme drink, the *vīrapānaka*;
he whose accumulation of impurities and latent tendencies had been uprooted by abandoning all mental dispositions.
One should satisfy [the deities] through the yoga of the Kaulika conduct by means of the five principles (pañcatattva);
one should offer the substance accompanied by mantras according to the sequence of the six chakras.

The supreme state of heroic drinking is the condition of being intent on meditation and worship; O Goddess, that which follows the ritual dismissal [of the deities] is called heroic drinking (vīrapāna).
The drinking of heroes (vīrapāna) is said to be of two kinds; hear now about the drinking of the bound souls (paśupāna), O beloved.
In the drinking of heroes, the former is a hero, while the latter is a bound soul.
Attachment and greed are hypocrisy; however, [hypocrisy] regarding the meaning of the mantra arises from lack of application.
A lustful person is one who directs his desires; that is called "drinking like a beast. (10)
O Goddess, when those born of noble lineage, remaining full of pride, consume the drink without performing worship,
that is called the drinking of cattle (paśupāna).
Listen further, O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, to the procedure for the drinking of animal spirits (paśupāna):
he who drinks liquor alone, O beloved, and he who consumes the Śakti alone.
If one never associates with a devotee of Maheśvara, this is called "drinking the beverage of cattle," which bestows great poverty. (13)
O Dear One, that drinking which is performed with the mouth without mantra and without initiation from the mouth of the Guru is known by the wise as the drinking of a beast (paśupāna). || 14 ||
In the Bhairava [Tantra], the bound soul (paśu) is said to be of three kinds, along with the former;
one who is solitary and devoted to drinking is designated as a paśu. || 15 ||
The one who is initiated but is a reviler is proclaimed as the second;
he is uninitiated, devoid of ritual action, and bereft of mantra and tantra. (16)
He is called Mahāpaśu; now listen, O beloved, to [the description of] Kaula and Vāma.
To the left is the woman (rāmā) joined with passion (rati), while the vessel for the offering (balipātra) is on the right.
O Maheśānī, the Mahākaula practitioner, while offering libations with his left hand from the drinking vessel, should place it upon the ground and perform the libation, O Maheśānī. (18)
O Goddess, if [the hands] are held with both hands together, it is called Kaula;
by reversing the left and right hands, it is proclaimed as Vīra-kaula. || 19 ||
One should satisfy [the deity] with the right hand using the vessel of wine held in the left hand;
that which is held in the left hand is declared to be Gaudī, and it is indeed called Caitanya.
O Great Goddess, having placed [the vessel] upon the ground, one should offer libations with both hands;
this is proclaimed as the "Bliss" (Ānanda) and is designated as the "Left" (Vāma).
O Goddess of the gods, in Kerala, worship is performed with the right hand;
in Gauḍa, however, I perform worship and libation with the left hand alone. (22)
I satisfy, I worship, and I likewise offer salutation in three parts—
at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end— or separately, O beloved, at each stage.
O Maheśānī, I worship and offer libations using only the right hand;
having said this, one should recite [the mantra] at the beginning and end with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
O Maheśvarī, these traditions have been proclaimed by me here;
the one named Siddhacaitanya and thereafter the one called Vilāsa. (25)
The one named Satyacaitanya is next, followed by the one called Siddha;
then comes Caitanyādivilāsī, and after that, the one designated as Siddhaprajña. || 26 ||
And then there is the one named Siddhaprajña, followed by the one named Divyānanda;
then the one known as Siddhabodhānanda, and the one known as Divyacaitanya. || 27 ||
p. 131) Therefore, the perfected awakening is proclaimed as that which is designated as divine consciousness (*divyacaitanya*);
it is called the Lord of Divine Wisdom (*divyaprajñānanātha*), and it is the eternal divine non-duality (*divyādvaita*). || 28 ||
Then there is the one named Śāmbhavādvaita and the one called Medhādvaita;
these sixteen are proclaimed solely according to the sequence of libations (tarpaṇa).
Other variations have been proclaimed in detail in the *Rahasya*;
it must be kept secret, kept secret, like one's own womb or another woman.
Thus, the supreme convention of the *mudrās* has been briefly explained. (30)

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Convention of Drinking," in the latter portion of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Mañjudakṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 33 ||
The thirty-fourth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Universe, I desire to hear about the supreme secret convention of the creepers."
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, listen now with diligence to the secret convention of the creepers (latā-saṅketaka).

O Goddess, without the initiation of wisdom (medhādīkṣā), there can be no practice of the creeper (latāsādhana). I have described to you that which is called the creeper as consisting of the phonemes from 'ka' to 'ha' and the kalās.
O Maheśvarī, [the lineage] beginning with Bālā and ending with Śāmbhavī has been revealed starting from Medhā; and beginning with Śrī Sparśakālī and ending with Guhyāmbā.
O Maheśānī, the initiation of wisdom (medhādīkṣā) exists both in the Kādimata and the Hādimata;
however, O beloved, the wisdom of universal sovereignty (sarvasāmrājyamedhā) arises from the union of these two.
One should apply [the practice] starting from Maṇipūra up to the cavity, beginning with Bālā; and one should apply it starting from Maṇipūra up to the cavity, beginning with Sparśa. || 5 ||
Alternatively, O Goddess who resides in the gods, according to the path of withdrawal and emission:
when emission begins with the letter *ka*, O Goddess, it falls within the scope of withdrawal.
O Pārvatī, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sarvātīta, Kālī is the source of emanation (sṛṣṭi), and she becomes the end of dissolution (saṃhāra) through the sequential order starting from Parā.
Having known that [the state] which reaches the end of the Śāntyatītā [kalā], one should awaken it by means of the power of Śiva;
or else, by the piercing of the phonemes (varṇavedha), one should awaken her who is solely of the nature of piercing.
One should perform [the rites] starting from the initiation of the Cakṣuṣmat and ending with the Sāmrājya;
for those endowed with wisdom and the other [qualities], the tonsure is not required.
O Goddess, one should always nourish the hair by applying oil;
O Goddess, one should not shave the beard until the piercing [of the central channel] is clearly perceived.
Vāgvedha (piercing by speech) and Śrutivedha (piercing by hearing) are mentioned, with Dṛṣṭivedha (piercing by sight) as the third;
Sparśavedha (piercing by touch) would be the fourth, while Kriyāvedha (piercing by action) is the fifth. || 11 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, they are born in succession through the process of spiritual practice;
whatever exists within the sphere of the cosmic egg and upon the surface of the earth, [all arise from this]. 12.
All accomplishments stand before that practitioner;
they arise through the sequence of practice merely by his glance.
(133) They come before him of their own accord; what need is there to mention Jayā and the others?
Acting according to his instructions, they behave like servants. (14)
Success consisting of his every desire shall always be his servant:
the power of atomization (aṇimā), the power of moving through the air (khecarī), the power of vision (vīkṣā), the medicinal pill (guṭikā), and the power of assuming any form at will (kāmarūpitā). 15.
Alchemy, vetālas, yakṣiṇīs, longevity, entering the bodies of others, and so forth—these are the attainments of the city of the moving and the unmoving. (16)
One shall become a master of the sixty siddhis; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Great Goddess, the six rites come into being through a mere glance.
One should practice continuously for as long as it takes to reach the various stages;
once a stage has been attained, one proceeds from that point along the path of the Gandharvas.
O Goddess of the gods, there is no doubt that one is indeed Śiva by way of the Gandharva path;
for one endowed with imperial sovereignty and wisdom should practice the sādhanā of the creeper (latā).
"But he who acts otherwise will meet with downfall.
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? || 20 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Convention of the Creepers," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 34.
The thirty-fifth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear with reverence about the form of the creeper."
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Maheśānī, the form of the creeper was already described by me previously.
I shall speak in general; be attentive in mind.
[She was] a young woman, possessed of great beauty, lovely, and charming in her demeanor. (2)
Fickle-eyed and lotus-eyed, sixteen years of age and yet not having reached her bloom,
she was a beautiful woman who struck with side-long glances, fragrant and enchanting to the body.
Having observed her in such a manner, one should always seek union with her;
her kissing should be performed with a mind free from agitation.
If a man remains free from transformation even after gazing intently at a woman, he is steadfast;
however, if a transformation arises, the practitioner is certainly destroyed.
But always gazing upon her, listen quickly to the yoga thereof:
having drunk again and again from her feet up to her root, one should drink once more.
The tips of her nails shall dispel the inner darkness with their moonlight;
she shall have the shape of a tortoise-shell due to the beauty of her elevated forefeet.
The hero, with a supple inner heart, should always remain free from conceptual construction;
he is beautiful with well-rounded knees and the support of shanks, thighs, and hips.
The line of hair at the navel, the chest, the full breasts, the neck, the eyes, and the tips of the hair standing erect—[all these were visible]. || 9 ||
Until he is filled with the intoxication of honey by boundless glances of feeling,
his senses become tender, he is satisfied, and he is endowed with the four aims of life.
And again, O Maheśvarī, at the time of cessation, beginning from one's own face which has the form of a drop, [one should contemplate it] as full with the nectar of rebirth.
He is called the "supreme practitioner" (sādhakottama); having meditated upon, touched, or seen these four verses while endowed with this Kāmakalā, [he attains success]. || 12 ||
Having reflected upon this for a moment there, the accumulation of states is conquered;
and having transformed it into the form of that *kalā* within the auspicious lineages. (13)
How one is born with effort into such a family—how shall I tell you that?
For it is in such a family that the reality (tattva) itself is directly realized through the contemplation of reality. (14)
Therefore, it should be worshipped with great effort by those who know the scriptures of that lineage (kula),
provided that his family deity and personal deity remain steadfast.
That man is blessed in the world, and his rise is indeed unshakable, in whose family there is the initiation of the lineage; therefore, he alone is truly that [initiation].
From association with families that have not received initiation, the loss of siddhi arises;
as does listening to their talk or going to their beds. (17)
O Goddess, how can he be of noble birth? How can he be my worshiper?
One may assume a name according to one's own desire, in accordance with one's scent, form, or appearance. (18)
A name given by one's mother or father should be diligently avoided;
one should know that another's wife increases attachment, whereas one's own wife increases affection. (19)
Upon his arrival, one should offer a welcome according to one's own desire through the application of playful grace;
then, rising from one's seat, one should take him by the hands and lead him to sit down.

Having meditated there upon Kāmakalā, who is seated on the left side, golden-hued, and able to assume any form at will, one whose body is filled with the *bindu* and other [energies] should contemplate her.
One should employ the hair-arrangement, forehead mark, pearl necklace, armlets,
and lac-dye at the beginning of the performance of all arts and rituals, as these are the substances belonging to the Kula.
Having given and then consumed betel-leaf accompanied by the causal [mantra],
the practitioner should behold her path of the Kula, both mundane and supramundane.
Flowers that bloom spontaneously are prescribed for the Kula and other traditions;
one who knows the Kula does not use them, for even Śiva would surely perish [if he did].
Having observed faults and the like therein, one should not instruct out of mere affection;
nor indeed should one speak with harsh words, for if [the instruction] is given thus, it becomes fruitless. || 25 ||
O beloved, since the secret of the Kula scripture is the very root of the Kula, it is better to abandon the Kula doctrine than even the Kula teacher. (26)
O beloved, I do not abandon my own family out of fear of even perceived faults;
established as the tree of my lineage, I nourish my own kin.
Therefore, with every effort, one must protect [the lineage] with diligence;
for if, through the conjunction of fortune, there should be an abundance of offspring within one's own family, [it must be preserved]. (28)
The wise person should establish equality and abandon all contrariety;
there is separate meditation, a separate location, separate worship, and separate praise. (29)
This must be done with effort; what is the use of these many words?
O Goddess of gods, I shall remain in the lineage—of this there is no need for deliberation. (30)
By betraying them, that very land perishes;
yet from joy, there is no doubt that for me there will be the account known as "Amṛta. (31)
Born of noble lineage, I am the one who makes the sound of the slapping of arms heard in great battles;
I do not desire mere fault, for it is from me that the world falls [into ruin]. 32.
Hatred for one's husband, harsh speech, quarrels and the like, and even the company of the base—such things do not exist there; indeed, I certainly do not dwell in such a place. (33)
By the shattering of the vessel of the cosmic egg, he shall live endowed with supernatural powers;
without the Kula, perfect accomplishment is not found anywhere at all.
Following the instructions of the Kulālāpa and having discerned the form of the Kula,
one should dwell during the day and likewise at night, intent upon the practice of attraction (ākṛṣṭi).
O Maheśvarī, having brought all the women born of the eight castes, one should assign them names according to the sequence of the fragrances.
Or else, having first stated its own nature as being of a single birth, one should join that mantra to it and perform worship by means of that very [mantra]. (37)
Having worshipped with pure flowers and food offerings mixed with salt and honey, one should accomplish one's own spiritual practice as before.
One should worship that Kālī with offerings of those very flowers;
O Goddess, one should worship her named Tripurā with red flowers. (39)
Endowed with the previously mentioned qualities, they may be of various or of a single species;
they are possessed of color and fragrance, as was previously stated according to their names. (40)

Having thus performed [the rite] in many ways according to the distinction between the seen and the unseen, O Goddess of Gods, there is indeed a specific excellence here; what is the use of further prolixity? (41)
Having concealed her own self through illusion and assumed the form of her own wife, O Goddess, she comes; by that very means, she is surely seen. 42.
Therefore, O Goddess of the Suras, one who desires success should perform this in one's own country; or else, one should strive for the sake of the destruction of desire.

Having taken up the rod of ritual action (karmadaṇḍa) and having established equality with Śiva, one performs a sevenfold wrapping of that body with the thread of the [inner] wheels (cakrasūtra). (44)
"O highly fortunate one, you have been created by the Self-born for the protection of all beings; let a firm bond be established. (45)
Having thus addressed that sūtra, which is a limb of Śiva and encircled by serpents, one should recite it ten times over; then, having approached, one should recite one's own mantra.
The three *praṇavas* encased within the *saṃhāra-svaprabodhinī* [mantra] are declared to be the "sleeping mantra," which is like a wild beast among all living beings.
Having done this, the Lord himself becomes even greater than Maheśa;
yet, if within the Kula there should be one who is fickle in yoga and lustful for Smara. (48)
Then protection must be provided; wise men should never perform [any other rite].
O Varāṅga, listen to my words, which are the cause of auspiciousness for both of us. (49)
"Having accomplished this task, your endeavor must be performed.
Having spoken thus and having carried out their own duties, the best of practitioners [proceeded]. (50)
O Maheśvarī, one should not engage in the practice of Kulayoga with the wife of a hero, the daughter of a hero, or the excellent woman who is the consort of a hero. (51)
Practitioners should not perform the act of drawing [the deity] until there is stability of the mind;
for if agitation of the mind arises therein, whatever fruit was obtained through the root-yoga [is lost].
That fruit arises, O Goddess; it is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.
For you yourself, O Maheśvarī, are the supreme wife of a hero.
She is remembered as the primordial and ancient mother of the family vidyās;
O Supreme Goddess, she is their consort and the awakener of all mantras. (54)

Whether by right means or by wrong means, O Goddess of gods, if the wife of the guru is [approached] as if she were the guru himself, one becomes an accomplisher of all aims merely by looking [at her].
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? 55.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Form of the Creeper," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 35 ||
The thirty-sixth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Śaṅkara, O Śrī Mahādeva, O Lord, tell me of the worship performed at night.
The illustrious Śiva said:
"Indeed, worship at night should always be performed with its underlying purpose."
Having personally assumed the form of Bhairava and taking his own Kula [with him],
he performed the extensive ritual placement (nyāsa) upon her body, [visualizing] the Kula as having the form of Bhairavī.
Having performed the complete ritual placement (nyāsa), including that consisting of the nine triangles, in the midst of a flower-couch strewn with a profusion of blossoms; || 3 ||
Having drawn the yantra with family materials upon a surface strewn with various fragrances,
one should worship it in a conch shell, preceded by the ritual installation of the water jar (ghaṭasthāpana).
Having drawn a hexagon on one's own left side with the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) in its center,
one should place there a pitcher made of gold or likewise of silver.
O Goddess, one should place [the image], whether made of copper, or even devoid of metal, into the jar along with a portion [of the deity] and well-scented with perfumes.
One should fully worship the causal substance according to the distinctions of Brahmā and the others;
having first inscribed the mantra there, which originates from one's own lineage.
Having meditated there upon one's chosen deity, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
then, displaying the dhenu-mudrā, one should contemplate that [mantra] as nectar.
Seeing the vessel of offerings, the Bhairavas, the Mothers, and the Gaṇas dance;
all the gods, beginning with Indra, dance, longing for the honey.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others dance, intent on joy;
having divided the vessel of the *arghya* offering into two parts, one portion is given to the Guru.
Having taken up one guru, with one [hand] performing the libation to the deities, O Goddess, having drunk the kula-nectar while adorned with various ornaments; || 11 ||
If the Guru is not personally present, then one should cast [the offering] into the water;
having become one whose nature is bliss, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
One should worship [the deity] in their respective yantras according to the procedure prescribed for each;
then, having performed the ritual dismissal (visarjana), one should subsequently recite the mantra.
For that nectar is consumed by me according to its own natural flavor; through the tasting of the essence of the cakora bird, its true flavor is perfectly brought forth. (14)
(139) Merely by grasping its fruit, one ascends the peak of Mount Sumeru;
merely by embracing its creeper, one becomes a lord of the earth washed in nectar. || 15 ||
When the root-yoga has been performed there, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
then, taking the sacrificial substance purified by recitation, one should perform the libation.
O Goddess, having performed the libation (tarpaṇa), followed by circumambulation and prostration,
one should then please her by reciting the hymn prescribed in the Kalpa.
Therefore, having made the *kula* thus suitable with effort, one should perform recitation (*japa*).
*Kula* is declared to be power (*śakti*); its worship and so forth are now described. (18)
That is to be known as the family tradition (kulācāra), which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
since it is from this that one is born noble-born, how can I describe it to you? (19)
Since that reality itself truly abides manifest within the family (kula),
[it consists of] liquor, meat, as well as the mudrā and sexual union.
Worship performed with these very [substances] is proclaimed as the family tradition (kulācāra);
therefore, it should be diligently worshipped by those who know the scriptures of that family. || 21 ||
He whose lineage or even his own family remains steadfast is blessed; he is truly wise, and he alone possesses the true form of his lineage.
The family-initiation (kuladīkṣā) which exists in the lineage of the Yoginīs is proclaimed as Śiva;
as is Kālī, so is Tārā, and as is Śrī Bhairavī, so [is she].
All ritual applications, such as worship and the like, characterized by their formal performance, as well as the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas, are as clear [and accessible] as courtesans. (24)
But this Śāmbhavī Vidyā is secret like a woman of noble family; the deities bestow their grace upon one who keeps the Kaulika conduct well concealed. (25)
They grant the fulfillment of desires, yet they cause destruction when revealed;

For the planet of the householder certainly afflicts the eleventh [house];

These faults arising from women have been described to you;

Having given them [the offerings] with this mantra, one should present the bali-oblation into the six vessels.
