The thirty-ninth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
Tell me, if I am dear to you, what is this "shaven-headed seat"? || 1 ||
The illustrious Śiva said: Out of affection for you, this most secret of secrets is revealed:
the Moon, the Three, the Five, the Skulls, and those known as the Vasus and the Cavities. (2)
O Goddess of gods, O Parvatī, having fixed ten skulls— the skulls of Rudras— by means of the conjunction of the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should perform the practice.
In the center is Mahāmuṇḍa, surrounded on all sides by a multitude of heads;
O Goddess, this occurs on the day of Kālarātri as well as on the day of Vīrarātri.
O Goddess, on the day of Moharātri, as well as on the day of Śivarātri, and on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights; || 5 ||
Having performed the practice with a shaven head, one should employ a rosary, a vessel, and so forth;
or, O Goddess, one should have a yantra made, and one will become the sovereign of the three worlds.
One should accomplish the Heroic Sadhana by means of the method without a crest-lock, by the sequence of the Hero’s Posture, and also by the sequence of the Corpse Posture.
The soft seat (mṛdvāsana) should be in the eastern part, the tufted (cūḍaka) in the south;
the tender (komala) is said to be in the west, and the shaven (muṇḍa) belongs to the northern region.
Having performed the *vīrāsana* in the middle portion and having recited [the mantra], the Leader of the Three Worlds [attains] the Single Hero,
the Triple Hero, or the Five, Eight, or Nine Heroes.
One should arrange ten heroes for the seat, with Rudravīra as the foremost;
O Goddess of the Gods, even in the case of the Muṇḍa-pakṣa, there is a most excellent hero in the center.
Through the application of the mild, medium, and other [intensities], one becomes a vessel for the non-differentiation of the means of accomplishment;
likewise, a cremation ground, a funeral pyre, or a seat of bone-ground is recommended.
O Goddess, the vulva-skin is the seat for ten days after death;
in this manner, O Mistress of the Gods, there are many seats in succession.
Having performed any one of these, one should propitiate Kālī or Tārā in a solitary place,
an empty house, on a mountain, or in a forest grove.
In a wilderness, in a place devoid of auspiciousness, in a mother’s house, on a riverbank, at a solitary linga, in a desolate region, in a cremation ground, or on a battlefield. || 14 ||
(154) At a family tree, a solitary tree, or on a spot marked with various designs; at the source of the Gaṅgā, at a crossroads, at a junction of three paths, or in a temple of the deities. || 15 ||
Or, O Mistress of the Gods, one may accomplish the Vīrasāgara [rite] in a brothel;
having carefully driven in the stakes, one should offer an oblation to the guardians of the directions.

Having gone himself to the site of the stake, the most excellent hero [prepared] the milk of consciousness, the invincible offering (bali), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise the essence (rasa).
O Goddess of gods, having taken up the sword, one should perform the cutting oneself;
staying there and performing the recitation (japa), one should thereafter accomplish the three worlds. || 18 ||
Thus has it been briefly declared; what is the use of further prolixity?
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the secret that was previously indicated. (19)
The illustrious Śiva said:
"Now listen as I speak of that which is the most secret of secrets;
[it concerns] the Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, Cāndra, Saura, and likewise the Ārhata [traditions]."
O Goddess Pārvatī, the application of food offerings (naivedya) in Vaiṣṇava, Vaidika, and Devī rites includes gold, gems, and various other garments.
One should offer that which possesses manifold flavors to the Guru;
one should also offer it to the Guru’s son, his wife, and his daughter. || 22 ||
It should be given to a Brāhmaṇa; however, in his absence, one should cast it into water.
O beloved, one may also cast it into a well, a forest, the middle of a cave, or a pond.
The food offering (naivedya) of Mahādeva attains the status of a sacred remnant (nirmālya);
for to a devotee, the food offering is proclaimed to be of the nature of nectar (amṛta). || 24 ||
One may eat or cause others to eat the food offering (naivedya) of other [deities] as well; however, there is no fault whatsoever in consuming the naivedya from a Śāligrāma or a Bāṇaliṅga.
O Goddess of gods, one should cause the materials for the bali offering to be prepared in two kinds;
O Goddess of gods, at the time of the ritual application, the observer of the vow should worship the Brāhmaṇas.
One should not weave even for a moment until success is attained;
having completed the work from beginning to end, one should thereafter perform an expiatory rite.
Having established the relationship of primary and subordinate parts, the practitioner of the vow should accomplish everything;
furthermore, O Śivā, within the course of a ritual action, there may again arise the state of being primary and subordinate.
O Goddess, having first understood the eastern seat and having diligently dispelled the obstacles, one should accomplish the rites; otherwise, one will become a denizen of hell. (29)
When another task has been commenced, one should certainly not perform that [other] task;
having understood the judicial proceeding, preceded by knowledge of the preliminary framework (pīṭhikā). || 30 ||
Having first understood the relationship between the primary and secondary parts [of the ritual], one should accomplish all undertakings;
for indeed, there can never be the commencement of rites without [knowledge of] the rites themselves.

Furthermore, the undertaking of ritual actions shall proceed through the relationship of primary and subsidiary limbs. O Goddess of the Gods, even when the rite has been completed, one should perform the twilight worship (sandhyā).
"O Supreme Goddess, may he be an obstacle to [your] resolve; otherwise, it would be so.
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (33)

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Muṇḍāsana," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 39 ||
The fortieth chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
Now, O Pārvatī, listen as the procedure for the rosary (mālā) is being described.
Garlands are said to be of many kinds, distinguished by the great conch-shell and other materials. || 1 ||
A garland made of great conch shells, a garland of teeth, and likewise a garland of colored beads, O Goddess, spontaneously produced, accomplishes all purposes and goals. (2)
The rosary of letters is said to be threefold; listen to its sequence, O Pārvatī.
A rosary made of fifty gems corresponds to the fifty phonemes.
Having extracted these two [syllables] in both direct and reverse order,
the garland consisting of one hundred [syllables] is proclaimed, which bestows all desired results.
The eight groups are proclaimed as: a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and śa.
Having thus arranged the eight groups, there shall be one hundred and eight [syllables].
A rosary of one hundred and eight beads grants success in all undertakings;
it is proclaimed that there should be five for the Guru and three for Gaṇeśa.
One should give the remainder to the chosen deity; by that, one becomes a master of supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
O Goddess, three [offerings] are prescribed for the Guru, and three for the devotee of Gaṇeśa (*gāṇapa*).
In the case of a deficiency or a surplus, one should apply the two remaining [counts] to the desired number;
thus, O beloved, the garland of one hundred and eight beads has been described to you.
By means of the forward and reverse order, there shall be one hundred syllables of the Mātṛkā;
this is through the union of Māyā, Vāk, Kāma, and Śrī, and by virtue of the conjunction with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
In both direct and reverse order, there should be one hundred and eight;
by joining the beginning and end with the *māyā* [syllable], one should apply the supreme seed-syllable (*parābīja*).
The garland is said to be of five kinds, bestowing all accomplishments:
those that are bound by seven nails, those that are obstructed, those that are severed, and those with disordered origins.

Even those who are enemies of the wealthy, spendthrifts, destroyers, or even those with physical defects such as being one-eyed or lame—these too certainly become accomplished; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (12)
A rosary made of great conch shells as well as one called "tooth" (danta) must not be given to just anyone; it should be kept secret like the child of one's mother.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Rosary," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 40 ||
The forty-first chapter.
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the definitive rule for stringing the rosary."
By what [means] is what to be accomplished? And which mantra is not to be recited? (1)
"Tell me everything, O Lord of Gods, if I am dear to you.
Śrī Śiva said:
"The stringing must be done by Dhruva, one bead at a time in succession. (2)
The supreme rosary consists of all mantras and bestows all accomplishments;
having meditated upon the form of the deity within that mantra inside the rosary. (3)
All mantras should be recited for the sake of accomplishing all tasks;
or else, O Dear One, one should cause them to be strung together with the Mātṛkās.
A garland made of fifty jewels has the letter *kṣa* as its central peak (*meru*);
when arranged in both direct and reverse order, the garland becomes one of a hundred [syllables].
Having first arranged the eight groups [of consonants], one should perform the recitation of the garland of one hundred and eight [syllables];
the recitation of the Mātṛkā-garland is praised in all circumstances.
O Śivā, having diligently gathered rudrākṣas, crystal beads, and so forth,
one should carefully perform the stringing with the mātṛkā letters.
The supreme garland, composed of all the gods, brings about swift accomplishment;
having meditated there upon the Goddess who consists of their respective mantras, one should perform the recitation.
One should perform the recitation with diligence; no hesitation should be felt in this matter.
This supreme rosary bestows all accomplishments and accomplishes every purpose.

O Śivā, having strung together the Śiva-mantra with the Śakti-mantra, one should recite the Śiva-mantra; O Śivā, having strung together the Śakti-mantra with the Śiva-mantra, one should recite the Śakti-mantra.
O Dear One, through the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti, the supreme garland (mālā) is effective in its function;
it consists of that which is called "tooth" (danta), that which is called "skull" (muṇḍa), and also the "jewel of the fish" (matsyamaṇi).
The threading of the beads must be performed; this rosary is considered to consist of the three powers (triśakti).
Kālī, Tārā, and Chinnamastā are the supreme forms of the rosary.
The supreme ground is the pinnacle of all accomplishments and consists of all the gods; O Goddess, one should recite that very mantra which is not bound by anything at all.
(158) And as it was said by me previously, "O beloved, have you forgotten?"—now you have spoken otherwise; O beloved, I have a doubt.

This has not been stated regarding the *mālikā* [rosary] for those who have distinguished between the *mātṛkā* and the *tāra*, nor for one devoid of Śiva and Śakti; this is the view concerning other types of rosaries. (15)
In any manner of stringing [the beads], one should perform the stringing with whatever method; one should recite that very mantra with which one performs the stringing.

Even in the case of the Mātṛkā and other [mantras], one should meditate upon the rosary as having the form of that mantra within Śiva, and then project the individual soul (jīva) [into it]; otherwise, it will cause an obstruction to success.
"Thus it has been briefly told; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear a most wonderful secret. (18)
"O Maheśvara, tell me the supreme secret of the rosary.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Parameśvarī, in the absence of the aforementioned gems," 19.
Gems of fragrance and form, as well as those originating from ivory and crystal—gems such as these should be prepared with great care by those desiring all spiritual accomplishments. (20)
In the absence of skulls, [the beads] may be made of coconuts, or alternatively, gems placed beneath the skull;
or they may be made from elephant tusks, deer hooves, swords, gold, conch shells, or horn. (21)
Those made of silver, copper, bell-metal, lead, and indeed of tin, as well as gems in the form of smooth stones, are remembered as bestowing all accomplishments.
Now, the goddess Mālikā, who consists of knowledge, accomplishes all tasks;
the gems known as vaidūrya and nīlakāca grant the fulfillment of every purpose. (23)
The jewels of the seed-syllables (bīja), the spikes (kīlaka), and the powers (śakti) bestow swift accomplishment.
O Goddess, the Kullukāmālikā Vidyā is remembered as that which brings about subjugation (vaśyakarī).
Beginning with the seed-syllables (bīja), they are prescribed for the accomplishment of valor; for the purpose of pinning down, they are known as "nails" (kīla).
Endowed with power (śakti), they lead to all perfections (siddhi); [the practitioner] should hold a living being, a bone, and a skull.
A garland made of bones and skulls bestows the form of Śiva;
that which is distinguished by their specific shapes accomplishes various tasks and grants desired boons.
The garland consists of Tārākālī, or it is supreme as consisting of Tārā and Chinnā;
or it may consist of Kālī and Chinnā—this triad is born from the seed-syllables of Muṇḍa. (27)
The ground of all supreme accomplishments is the unceasing Sarasvatī;
the garland consists solely of jewels, arising from nothing but jewels. (28)
That which arises from red sandalwood and the head, as well as that produced from the head of the eight fragrances—thus has it been briefly explained. What else do you wish to hear? (29)
The Goddess said:
"Tell me, you have indicated the garland whose form consists of the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Śrī Śiva said:
I shall also declare the secret, according to the nature of the phonemes, seed-syllables, and vowels.
O Śivā, one should have a rosary fashioned in the form of the letters of the Mātṛkā;
by means of it, the recitation (japa) must be performed, for it embodies the nature of all the gods.
The Mātṛkā, the garland of letters, may be produced from gold, copper, silver, iron, ivory, gems, or crystal. (32)
A garland made of gold grants all supernatural powers (siddhis); one made of silver bestows all desired objects;
a garland of copper is for all-encompassing peace; and one made of iron grants liberation to the ancestors.
A rosary made of elephant tusks bestows success; one made of bilva wood grants wealth;
and that produced from the wood of the arka tree is foremost for the rite of eradication of enemies.
Having thus prepared the garland, one should recite the mantra and offer it to the deity;
especially so for the image of the deity, the yantra, and the divine wheel. (35)
When the image and the yantra have been worshipped, O Auspicious One, two types of dhāraṇīs should be worn:
one made of jewels should be worn on the finger, and one made of gold and jewels should be worn on the heart.
Having fashioned it in the form of a seal or the form of a necklace, one should wear it with diligence;
one shall become a master of all accomplishments—of this there is no doubt. || 37 ||
In that regard, O Pārvatī, hear the names of the deities of the offerings:
Lakṣmī is the deity of food, while Prajāpati is the deity for Vaiṣṇava offerings. (38)
Gold has Agni as its presiding deity; silver has Candra as its presiding deity;
diamond is to be known as belonging to Varuṇa; and among liquids, the earth is traditionally held to be their deity.
Varuṇa is the deity of water; Vāruṇeśvarī is the goddess of heroic powers.
Ramā is the goddess of *kṛsara*; Kālikā is the goddess of supreme food (*paramānna*). (40)
In a ghee lamp there is Mahāviṣṇu; in a floor-lamp, the Lord of Forests (Vanaspati);
likewise, a Gandharva is in incense; and ghee has the Sun and Fire as its presiding deities. || 41 ||
Honey is indeed to be known as belonging to Varuṇa; curd and milk belong to Maheśvara; the great flower belongs to Vanaspati; and the green fragrance belongs to Vaiṣṇava. || 42 ||
Likewise, Durgā is present in a garland, or indeed everything is composed of the Goddess.
One should worship the image with this knowledge; otherwise, it creates an obstacle to success.
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? 43.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Stringing of the Garland," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 41 ||
The forty-second chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear by what means one may become identical with the Goddess."
The Lord said: This most secret of secrets is now being told; listen.
In the Kali age, worship performed according to the sequence of the ten sciences, through the path of the five abodes, and likewise by means of the path of vision, bestows spiritual accomplishment.
O Goddess, one should diligently display the weapons, mudrās, and seed-syllables (bījas) of each respective deity; one should be devoted to that practice.
The Sarvatobhadra pedestal is proclaimed as the pedestal of the Goddess;
there is one lotus for the vessel of the Yoginī and five lotuses for the Kṣetrapāla.
A nine-petalled lotus is prescribed for Gāṇeśa, and for Baṭuka, it is marked with a liṅga;
O Maheśvarī, there are five types of mandalas here on the seat of worship.
O Śivā, one should write the single-syllable *sparśamaṇi* mantra, which is dark-colored, illusory, and adorned with a drop and a moon, upon the forehead.
O Śivā, one should write the single-syllable Sparśamaṇi mantra— consisting of the body of Tārā (TĀM), the Bindu, and Māyā (I), adorned with the Moon (the Bindu)— upon the forehead.
With the *krodha* [syllable] *chinnā*, one becomes the single-syllabled mantra adorned with the *bindu* and the moon;
[one should take] the *māyā* [syllable] adorned with the *bindu* and the moon, which destroys the three worlds. (8)
One should always write the single-syllable Sparśamaṇi on the forehead,
or else one should write the triad consisting of Kālī, Tārā, and Chinnā.
Two or one [of these] should be written; by that, it becomes possessed of that form.
Lakṣmī and Hara have their heads adorned with the Bindu, Māyā, and Kalā.
One should always write the single-syllabled Sparśamaṇi on the forehead;
one should always write the beautiful Sparśavidyā, "Sauḥ," on the forehead.
One should always write the *aiṃ* syllable, Bhairavī, and the Sparśamaṇi on the forehead;
one should always write the smoke-colored (*dhūmra*) Sparśavidyā on the forehead. (12)
One should always write the syllable *vlū*, known as the "Stream of Wealth" (*vasordhārā*), upon the forehead;
one should always write the *vidyā* *drīm*, which is the attractor, upon the forehead. (13)

One should always write the *vidyā* that brings about prosperity (*sampatkaraṇī*) with the syllable *ā*, the *kalā* that effects subjugation (*vaśyakāriṇī*) with *hrīḥ*, and the *vidyā* that performs summoning (*ākarṣakarī*) upon the forehead. (14)
One should always write the *vidyā* that causes paralysis, beginning with *hrīḥ*, upon the forehead;
one should always write the supreme sixteenth *vidyā*, beginning with *hsauḥ*, upon the forehead. (15)
O Goddess, in the ritual procedure for any other mantra, one may likewise write the seed-syllable (bīja) and the power-syllable (śakti);
[this applies to] Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Sundarī, and Bagalāmukhī. 16.
O Goddess, if a guru who lacks initiation performs the ritual of the five sciences, he should,
upon seeing one who has received the full consecration, perform the initiation again.
O Priyaṃvadā, if one who is endowed with the Ūrdhvāmnāya should attain [this state],
O Goddess Pārvatī, he should undergo initiation once again, even if he is already perfect in form.
When one who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa has arrived, one should perform the initiation in every respect;
even those devoid of qualities attain [the goal] when joined with the sixfold Śāmbhava [initiation]. 19.
Having performed the initiation of the Śāmbhava type, a man becomes the very form of Śambhu;
otherwise, he would become poor and crippled—of this there is no need for deliberation.
One endowed with the initiation of *medhā* is indeed rare in the Kali age;
O beloved, whether such a person is found or not is uncertain.
Endowed with the initiation of *medhā*, he is considered superior even to Śiva;
joined with *medhā*, he is a sovereign ruler, certainly composed of Kālī and Tārā.
If great fortune is attained here by the practitioner, he will certainly become eternal, possessing the nature of Brahman and endowed with divine sovereignty. 23.
In whatever region he shines, endowed with divine intellect and the end of his life, that region is equal to Kālikā; Tārā herself dwells right there.
O Goddess, if [the fruit] were to perish in an instant upon reaching him, then what could be said regarding the fruit of penance in Śiva?
It cannot be so said; Śiva knows otherwise. || 25 ||
"It must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret with great effort.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (26)

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Accomplishment of Worship," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 42 ||
The forty-third chapter.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, O Lord of Umā, O Master who is dearer than life itself, you have previously indicated the determination of the perfection of the vidyās.
"Tell that to me, O Lord of Gods, if I am dear to you.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Goddess, this is the essence of essences, a secret even though it has been concealed."
Out of affection for you, O Great Goddess, I shall now speak; listen.
Kālī, Tārā, and Chinnamastā [are attained] by way of the practice of Vīrasādhana.
They are accomplished in a mere watch (yāma); there is no need for deliberation here, O Goddess Śivā, even for one devoid of formal practice within two hundred thousand recitations of the syllables.
Kālikā is declared to bestow success in the Śrī-Śaiva-tattva, while Tārā does so in the same;
Chinnamastā, however, is accomplished through six million four hundred thousand recitations. || 5 ||
Sundarī bestows success in some cases through eighty-four hundred thousand recitations;
Bālā by half a crore of recitations; and Bagalā by seventy-five [thousand]. (6)
O Great Goddess, the illustrious Mahārājamātaṅgī is accomplished through one hundred thousand recitations according to her color;
this perfected vidyā is accomplished in one million recitations.
O Dear One, Mahālakṣmī, Bhuvanā, and likewise Dhūmāvatī—
by means of the application of the qualities of the Vidyās, these are indeed perfected, and not otherwise.
O Great Goddess, by means of the application of the syllables of the Vidyās,
and indeed through that which is composed of the letters of the Mātṛkā, one should become a vessel for virtues.
O Maheśānī, by one hundred thousand [recitations], one certainly attains success and not otherwise;
indeed, through the yoga of Bhairava, the Śāvara [practice] bestows accomplishment.
O Goddess, by the nine emanated lords, Bhairava is indeed the primordial lord;
in the sequence of the ten Vidyās, the fruit is said to be tenfold.
If one person is perfected, then all [others] are givers of perfection;
through the fifty-six different regions, there is a variety of divisions within the Śavara tradition.
Through union with Bhairava, the Śābara [mantra] bestows success;
likewise through union with Mahākāla and by means of yoga with Vaṭuka. || 13 ||
O Goddess, that Śāvara [tradition] which bestows success is indeed of two kinds:
that spoken by the Nātha and that proclaimed by Śambhu. That spoken by the Nātha is also of two kinds. || 14 ||

In that case, within Śiva—who is designated as the Lord (Nātha)—according to the divisions of forms spoken by Śiva, there are two types: that which was spoken by the eighty-four Siddhas and that which was spoken by the Lord. (15)
If one deity is perfected, then the three worlds are perfected;
therein too, by means of the boy (Baṭuka), all that is stationary and moving is perfected.
Now, the first is known as Hetubaṭuka; the second is remembered as Baṭuka; and the third is proclaimed as Tripurāntakabaṭuka. || 17 ||
Vahnivetāla is proclaimed as the fourth Baṭuka;
now Agnijihva is proclaimed as the fifth Baṭuka. (18)
O Goddess, there is Śrī Kālabaṭuka, as well as Karālabaṭuka;
likewise Ekapādabaṭuka and Śrī Bhīmabaṭuka. || 19 ||
Trailokyabaṭuka and likewise Śrīsiddhabaṭuka—these ten are indeed renowned as Baṭukas who bestow manifest siddhis in the Kali age. (20)
The Baṭukas, known by the names Mātṛkā and Suta, were previously described;
through union with Mahākrodha, the hosts of Kinnarīs attain accomplishment.
In Kālikā, Mahākāla and Akṣobhya follow Tāriṇī;
in Tripurā, however, Rājeśa [is the lord], and in Bagalā, Trayambaka.
O beloved, Maheśa [is the deity] in Mātaṅgī, Maheśvara in Bhuvaneśī,
Nārāyaṇa in Mahālakṣmī, and likewise Mahādeva.
When [the power] is severed, it is Karāla; when perfected, it is Kukkuṭeśvara;
and when smoky, it is Aghora—this is the teaching in brief. (24)
In the subtle Śiva, without Śakti, neither name nor abode exists;
and in the digit of consciousness (citkalā), without Śiva, there can never be the state of being a digit (kalātva).
O Goddess of the gods, by virtue of the principle of the seed and the sprout, the Great Light, whose nature is Śiva and Śakti, is eternally awake, manifesting in various forms.
In the case of Sarvabhāvā, however, [the deity is] Baṭuka and likewise Mahākāla;
in Tāriṇī, Baṭuka is proclaimed, and in Kālī, Kāla is celebrated.
O Goddess, the Śrī Krodhamaṇḍala belongs to the tradition of Pātāla;
just as, within the Parākhya mantra, there is the Great Splendor consisting of the nature of Śiva and Śakti.
O Goddess of gods, she who pervades the entire circle of the cosmic egg remains eternally awake;
endowed with the Bindu, she is the Śiva-power known as Śakti, existing until the end of creation. (29)
But when conjoined with the emission of the *bindu*, the digit (*kalā*) consisting of Śiva and Śakti always remains, remains—by virtue of the principle of the seed and the sprout. (30)
Even one who is lax attains success through the path of *vīrasādhana*,
whether it be in the *śakti-mantra*, the *śambhu-mantra*, the *śābara*, or likewise in the *gāṇapa*.
O Pārvatī, [this applies] in the Kaula, Buddhist, and Vedic traditions, even in the case of cruel mantras;
likewise, O Goddess, in the sequence of the Mahāvidyās and in the sequence of the Siddhavidyās.

O Goddess of Gods, even in the sequence of knowledge, everything is accomplished through the path of heroic practice (vīrasādhana); O Goddess of Gods, no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (33)

Just as a lifeless body becomes alive again through the process of the *mṛtasañjīvanī* [resuscitation] spell, so too may it become alive once more through the application of this spiritual practice (*sādhanayoga*). || 34 ||
Everything is accomplished, O Goddess of gods; there is no need for deliberation here.
O Maheśānī, one should perform the *vīrasādhana* upon the mantra alone. (35)
One should perform the heroic practice (vīrasādhana) with the mantra of Baṭuka, Hanumān, Gāruḍa, Ceṭaka, Vetāla, or Dhūmavetāla.
Thus it has been briefly declared; what else do you wish to hear? (36)

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Accomplishment of Vidyā," in the second section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā.
The forty-fourth chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the sequence for the practice (*sādhana*) of Sundarī."
The illustrious Śiva said: This most secret of secrets is being revealed out of affection for you.
It must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret like one's own womb.
Having become intent upon the perfected mantra, one should perform the heroic practice (vīrasādhana). || 2 ||
O Goddess, for all living beings who are devoid of life, this shall be the producer of fruit;
there is nothing else that bestows accomplishment, O Goddess, apart from the heroic practice (vīrasādhana).
O Goddess Pārvatī, in the Kali age, Śrīvidyā will certainly become lax and difficult to accomplish due to the paucity of conduct, the nature of the times, and the resulting moral decline.
In this Kali age, which is filled with evil, whose mind indeed remains unshakable?
For one who is beset by all defects, even when engaged in the heroic practice (vīrasādhana). || 5 ||
O Goddess, he alone is the bestower of accomplishment; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Indeed, there is no accomplishment, truly no accomplishment, without the heroic practice (vīrasādhana).
Even one joined with great sins, if engaged in the practice of *vīrasādhana*,
becomes the bestower of success in this world and is honored by all the gods.
Through the yoga of heroic practice (vīrasādhana), perfection is attained in a mere watch (yāma) on both the eighth and fourteenth days of each fortnight.
O Goddess, after half a watch has passed, one should perform the heroic practice (vīrasādhana) with a youth,
a handsome hero who is present before one and full of passion.
One should carry away the corpse of a great hero, devoid of any attempt at flight—whether pierced by a spear, impaled on a stake, bitten by a snake, or dead from drinking water. (10)

O Goddess, one should abandon the previously mentioned eight types of corpses— those killed by a sword or poison, those pierced [by weapons], and those overcome by outcasts (cāṇḍāla) and the like— which grant swift accomplishment.
Having assumed the attire of a hero, one should practice the conduct of a hero;
having applied the forehead mark (tilaka) as before, one should collect the materials for the bali offering.
"Either I shall accomplish the mantra, or I shall cast off my body"— having made such a vow, he gathered the materials for the sacrificial offering.
Rams, buffaloes, cats, goats, cocks, and elephants;
molasses, milk-rice, and a profusion of sweetmeats, cakes, and *laḍḍuka* balls.
O Goddess, bring various sweet fruits such as the jambīra and panasa, along with betel leaves and other accompaniments, O Parvati. (15)
Clove leaf and its fruit, kaṅkola, as well as vijayā, musk, saffron, and so forth, along with whatever edible substances there may be. || 16 ||
Having gathered all those [requisites], one should practice in the place as described:
at the root of a bilva tree, in a wilderness, in an empty house, or on a riverbank. (17)
In the ocean, in a terrible forest, likewise in a cremation ground or at a crossroads;
within the womb of the Gaṅgā, in a pond, and even in the circle of amorous women. || 18 ||
Especially at a solitary linga, and particularly in the middle of a forest,
having assumed the attire of a hero, one should perform the heroic practice (vīrasādhana).

Having placed a perfected mantra before him and being eager for the vision of the deity, O Goddess, he should perform the heroic practice (vīrasādhana) after one and a half watches of the night have passed. 20.
O Śivā, one should remove [obstacles] with eight stakes of *khadira* wood or other such materials;
O Goddess, one should cast [offerings] in the ten directions and present the *bali* offering to the guardians of the quarters.
Having performed the binding of the directions according to the sequence of the imperial mandala, by way of the path of the Vidyā-maṇḍala, and through the path beginning with Mahāvidyā; || 22 ||
One should indeed cause an offering (bali) to be given with diligence to the deities of the cremation ground;
then, one should cause an offering to be given with diligence to the Lord of the Kings of Kings. || 23 ||
Then [offer] to Śrī Kurukullā, and immediately after that to Caṇḍālī; then to the forms of Baṭuka, Yoginī, Kṣetrapāla, and Gāṇapa.
The deity is the Lord of Lalitā; one should offer bali to all [the deities].
Having worshipped them during the offering of bali, one should perform the vīrasādhana.
Having carefully washed the Vīra, one whose forehead is marked with vermilion should apply collyrium,
ointment, oil, and musk combined with saffron.

O Goddess of the Suras, one should perform the ritual disposal of the betel leaf and the remnants from the mouth with milk; having carefully washed the hero [the Linga] with water, O Sovereign of the Gods. (27)

O Goddess of the gods, having diligently offered the month-preeminent food offering (naivedya), as well as the fish and seal gestures (matsyāmudrā), together with cloves, cardamom, and other ingredients; || 28 ||
Incense scented with camphor, along with perfumes and the eight or five [offerings];
[the incense] may consist of sixteen ingredients, ten ingredients, or be endowed with eighteen.
O Goddess of the gods, incense made from *śrīkhaṇḍa* as well as that produced from *aguru*, *guggulu*, *lohabāṇa*, *rāla*, and *devadāru* [are used]. (30)
Or, O Goddess, lac mixed with molasses; or cow's ghee with sugar;
or, O Goddess, spikenard and claw-nail; or even camphor alone. (31)
One should also [use] śrīkhaṇḍa, aguru, gandhasāra, śilārasa,
and the essence produced from Malaya, according to the twofold division of the vidyā.
I have thus proclaimed to you, according to the sequence of the ten sciences, this incense made of *devadāru* wood, which destroys all malevolent beings. (33)
Having thus performed the incense offering, he should certainly proceed with a sword in hand on a vehicle;
with disheveled hair and wearing the quarters as his garment, he should remain far from the superior practitioner.
Having carefully lit the lamp and being untroubled by obstacles,
one should place the Hero in the center and perform the binding of the *jhuṭikā*.
One should draw the yantra on the back and perform the binding of the feet;
having applied the binding of the mouth to the mouth, one proceeds according to the method for mounting a horse.
It should be without a crest in the eastern part, soft in the southern region, tender in the west, and possess three tufts of hair in the north. (37)
Then one should worship the corpse in due order with the Vīra, Argala, and Aghora mantras, as well as the Cakra, Pāśupata, and Astra mantras. (38)
The mantra known as Jayadurgā is also a hymn for the prayer of heroes; indeed, the mantras beginning with "Tilo 'si" and those called Yava are thus proclaimed. (39)
One should assign [the mantras] to their respective places according to the prescribed path;
having understood the seers, meters, and so forth, one should perform the meditation as described. (40)
O beloved, having worshipped one's own chosen deity along with the limbs and the retinue,
or having honored them with the five offerings, one should perform the recitation with undistracted mind.
One should not feel fear, O Goddess of the Gods; one should contemplate the world as being like a dream.
[This includes] the deities, the sky-goers, the Siddhas, the Bhairavas, and the Yātudhānas.
They come for the purpose of causing harm; one should not entertain fear therein of tigers, weapons, serpents and the like, scorpions, or cruel beasts. (43)
Crooked and cruel forms, the falling from the ocean or into heaven, all deceased ancestors, and likewise the tortures of the king—[these he beheld]. (44)
O Goddess, whether one obtains blue [sulfur], or a cock, or even nectar—regarding all that as mere straw, one should remain endowed with firm resolve. (45)

O Goddess, if one recites [the mantra] according to the prescribed measure, the deity will become a granter of boons; she who speaks in Sanskrit before [the practitioner] is proclaimed as a goddess. (46)
That auspicious goddess Śivā spoke three times to accept his boon;
that Brāhmaṇa spoke in Sanskrit and was proclaimed as Bhairava. (47)
O Goddess, whatever is requested as an offering by her, those—men, elephants, and buffaloes—one should then give to her, O Goddess. (48)
Having made [the offerings] from rice flour and also from barley meal, one should give them on the following day; having accepted the boon, he shall become happy.
One should cast all the equipment, beginning with the hero, into the middle of the pit;
there a heroic battle shall take place, and the man therein shall become firm. || 50 ||
One should personally guard [the secret] for as long as twenty-one days;
by hearing the song, one becomes deaf, and from sexual union with women, one becomes subject to disease.

If the fire-oblation is deficient, there shall be no success; if the feeding of the twice-born is omitted, O Goddess, one will become poor. However, if everything is performed correctly, one will certainly accomplish all goals.
Having drunk water infused with bilva leaves, one shall certainly accomplish everything;
O Goddess, the eighteen-fold descent of power (śaktipāta) arises.
He shall become the lord of the sixty siddhis; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He will be the master of the eight siddhis beginning with aṇimā, righteous, and accomplished. (54)
O Goddess, whatever Siddhis exist anywhere upon the surface of the earth, even as far as the shell of the cosmic egg, they all abide at his feet.
The Bhairavas, Khecaras, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and hosts of Apsarases;
likewise the Yātudhānas, Nāgas, Dānavas, Daityas, and Rākṣasas. || 56 ||
And likewise the Kuṣmāṇḍas, Bhūtas, Viśācas, and the various classes of Pretas; as well as the Nivātakavacas and others, and the Brahmarākṣasas. || 57 ||
Likewise, the Vetālas, Sādhyas, Siddhas, and hosts of Yakṣiṇīs;
the multitudes of Rākṣasīs and Kinnarīs, as well as the Bhūtinīs, Ceṭakas, and others. || 58 ||

The "Great Indra-net" (mahendrajāla), born of Indra and the other gods, shall come under one's feet; having attained the release of the divine liquor, by that means one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhīśvara). || 59 ||
Even liquor made from molasses and ginger is forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa;
it must be concealed, concealed, concealed, like one's own birth. (60)
It is a secret, a supreme secret, and the most secret of secrets;
one may give up one's life, one may give up one's head, but the excellent means (sādhana) must never be given away.
Thus has it been declared regarding the ritual of knowledge (vidyā-vidhi), specifically for Śrīvidyā,
as well as for Baṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, Gaṇapati, and Śaṅkara.
This sādhana has been proclaimed by me; it should be kept secret like one's own private parts.
Thus it has been spoken in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (63)

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Sadhana of Sundarī," in the second section of the latter part of the glorious *Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the illustrious Akṣobhya and Mahogratā. 44.
The forty-fifth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, O Master, O Supreme Cause of the gods and others!"
You previously indicated the determination regarding the selection of the excellent seat.

O Goddess, [I shall explain] the invocation of the deities, the determination regarding the two types of birth-impurity (sūtaka), the determination regarding the vitalization of the yantra, and the determination regarding the ritual dismissal (visarjana). || 2 ||
The determination of the tradition is according to the sequence of Śiva and Śakti;
the determination of the ten incenses is according to the sequence of the ten Vidyās. || 3 ||
O Lord, that which was previously indicated has not been revealed to me;
tell all of that, O Master, if I am dear to you.
Śrī Śiva said:
"How can I tell you this most secret of secrets?
Nevertheless, out of affection for you, it is being told; listen now."
Because the *sūtaka* (the newborn) is the primordial form of all things, its determination is explained;
listen as everything regarding the excellent seat and other matters is related.
Birth-impurity (sūtaka) occurs at the beginning [of the mantra], and death-impurity (mṛtasūtaka) at its end;
a mantra joined with these two types of impurity will certainly not attain success.
Birth-impurity (sūtaka) occurs at the beginning, and death-impurity (mṛtaka) at its end;
a mantra joined with both types of impurity will certainly not attain success.
In the meditation on the Guru-kuṇḍalinī, the marriage is proclaimed;
the twice-returning is the bath, and their union is the libation.
The offering of *arghya* constitutes the embryo; the *gāyatrī* mantra represents the eighth month.
From the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) up to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the conceptualization of the limbs [of the deity] takes place therein.
O Maheśānī, the attainment of a body is said to be from the mother, while breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the purification; meditation and recitation are declared to be the birth of the child.
O Goddess, that which arises from the utterance of mantras is called *jātasūtaka*;
O Maheśvarī, it is for the purpose of pacifying the defect of *jātasūtaka*.
One should recite ten, twenty, or fifty times according to one's capacity, O Śivā;
indeed, O Śivā, there are ten purificatory rites for the preliminary practice (puraścaryā), beginning with the ten ancillaries (daśāṅga).
This and what follows has been instructed by me; now hear the final [instruction]:
there are seven and nine latent impressions (saṃskāras), as well as dullness (jāḍya) in the heart, O Śivā.
(172) With palms joined in devotion, that wheel is likewise the means for attaining its siddhi;
it is the state of "I am He," the attainment of the Mātṛkā, and the union of the five consciousnesses. || 14 ||
The knowledge of the limbs and identity are said to follow immediately after that;
O Great Goddess, dismissal is declared to be the impurity of death and birth.
For the sake of pacifying the impurity caused by death or birth, one should recite [the mantra] ten or twenty times;
by that, its cessation certainly occurs, there is no doubt. || 16 ||
The Kerala, Kāśmīra, and Gauḍa traditions constitute a threefold path;
it is taught that within these three lineages there are three triads each.
O Goddess, the Śaiva-Kerala, the Śakti-Kerala, and that which is called the Śiva-Śakti-Kerala—this triad is thus proclaimed. (18)
In Kerala, it exists in nine ways through the divisions of Śuddha, Ugra, and Gupta;
likewise, Kāśmīra is ninefold, and Gauḍa is also ninefold. (19)
O Goddess, there are three types known as Vilāsa, and there are other divisions as well;
in the tradition known as Kerala, the dismissal [of the deity] takes place in the heart.
One should perform the dismissal of the deity Manu-hṛd-Śambhu into the thousand-petaled lotus;
in the tradition known as Kāśmīra, the dismissal takes place in the thousand-petaled lotus. || 21 ||
O Maheśānī, in the Gauḍa tradition, the dismissal (visarjana) takes place in the heart;
this is declared to be the dismissal as well as the definitive rule regarding birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Listen with care, O Goddess of Gods; a secret is being told by me:
that which is declared to be the impurity (sūtaka) of a mantra is like that of a human being. (23)
At the beginning there is birth-impurity, and at its end there is death-impurity;
O Goddess, during both types of impurity, one should not perform the recitation of mantras.
O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the mental twilight worship ending with the offering of water (arghya);
O Beloved, one should never touch a Śāligrāma stone or an image.
"By touching [it], a man becomes even more sinful; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (26)

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of Impurity," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 45.
The forty-sixth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
Tell me that, O Lord of Gods, which was previously indicated by you.
O Lord of Gods, O Maheśāna, you previously stated that poverty results from abandoning a mantra; therefore, after initiation, one should recite the mantra every single day. (2)
Even at the cost of one's life, it must never be abandoned; by abandoning it, one incurs a curse.
Therefore, one should always diligently perform worship with recitation and the practice of *japa*.
"O Lord, you have stated that at the conclusion of worship one should recite the mantra, but not recite the mantra alone; how then can that mantra be abandoned? (4)
Śrī Śiva said: The previous ritual for the bound souls (paśus), and especially for the Vaiṣṇavas, was declared to be the Vedic twilight rite (sandhyā); however, yours is likewise mental.
O Maheśvarī, one should perform the Tantric rite at the three junctions of the day for a mantra of Śakti;
however, for one who lacks the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), the worship consists of the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra).

Having worshipped with the various offerings of worship— O Dear One, O Goddess— upon the lamp, the wall, the water, the mirror, and the venerable Guru, one should direct this mind toward the beasts and birds.
Endowed with the complete consecration, he indeed becomes the embodiment of perfection.
Who is the embodied being, whose is the body, and to whom do pleasure and pain belong?
Who is born, who has died, O Goddess? Everything is of the nature of Brahman.
O Goddess, there is the recitation of names (nāmapārāyaṇa) as well as the recitation of mantras (mantrapārāyaṇa).
O Goddess, there is the complete study of the channels (nāḍī-pārāyaṇa), likewise the complete study of the wheels (cakra-pārāyaṇa),
the complete study of the diagrams (yantra-pārāyaṇa), O Goddess, and the fourfold twilight rites (sandhyā-catuṣṭaya).
The thousands known as Prastāra, those in the form of Upasthāna,
and the thousands known as Āvarṇa— these are the Vidyā-kalpalatā composed by me.
The garland of steps for initiation follows precisely the sequence of twenty-two;
he who knows the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya) is a follower of the venerable Mahāpañcikā-krama.
The Lord of the Mothers, beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, is indeed free from birth-impurity (*sūtaka*);
likewise, O Goddess, is the follower of the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*) and one initiated into the *caraṇas*.
Endowed with the four feet and likewise following the sequence of the six lineages,
he is further joined with the initiation of wisdom (medhā-dīkṣā) and the wisdom of sovereignty (sāmrājya-medhā).
The one who possesses the knowledge of the Śrīguru’s sandals, as well as the Śrīmahāpādukā;
the one who possesses the knowledge of the Nirvāṇapādukā, as well as the Śrīmūrtipādukā. || 15 ||
O Goddess, [he is] endowed with the sandals of Vārāhī, likewise the sandals of Mātaṅgī, and the sandals known as Śāmbhavī, together with the sandals of Śrī Medhā. || 16 ||
Where is his impurity (sūtaka)? He alone is indeed in his complete form;
for at whatever time, O Goddess, there occurs a forgetting of the deity of the mantra. (17)
At that very moment death is proclaimed; yet it is not truly death. Indeed, life itself exists at that time when there is agitation. (18)
O Queen of Gods, the four Vedas exist as stupas at the gateway of the Śrīcakra in whatever place a master of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) resides.
That region extends for ten million yojanas in every direction and attains prosperity;
there is no disease, nor indeed death, nor enemy, nor fear anywhere.
Śiva is declared to be one whose form is complete; he is indeed Śiva himself, there is no doubt.
What more need be said of a man who possesses many mantras? He is Śiva himself. (21)
O Queen of the Gods, the one who has received the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is prescribed for the ritual of the ten Vidyās.
In the Hādima system, there are four divisions beginning with the letter 'ka' within the division of the fourth [tattva]. 22.
The Mistress of the Five Jewels (Pañcaratneśvarī) is twofold: by the sequence beginning with *ha* and by the sequence beginning with *ka*.
The fierce one (*ugrā*) is indeed by the sequence beginning with *ka*, and the gentle one (*saumyā*) is by the sequence beginning with *ha*.

In the auspicious Śivā, who possesses both the fierce and the gentle aspects, consecration performed according to the sequence beginning with *kāduha* is declared to be propitious and bestows universal sovereignty. (24)
The Śrī Devī said:

"Tell me, how does it become for one who is devoid of consecration (abhiṣeka), who has followed the sequence of grasping [the mantra], and who has applied himself to the preliminary rite (puraścaryā)? (25)
Śrī Śiva said:
Indeed, no other time is praised as more auspicious than the time of a solar eclipse;
whatever is performed or caused to be performed during a solar or lunar eclipse [yields great fruit].
That [offering] becomes inexhaustible; it is considered to bestow the perfection of knowledge.
O Pārvatī, for one who has undergone purification after birth or purification after death, there is no [need for further] ritual during an eclipse.
O Maheśānī, the impurity of the sun does not affect anything else anywhere;
[therefore, one may perform] bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, sprinkling, and likewise libations.
O Supreme Goddess, the feeding of the twice-born should be performed according to one's capacity;
however, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, accomplishment is attained through mere intention alone. (29)
The initiation-yoga, the recitation at the sacred seats (pīṭha), and likewise the complete recitation of the mantra;
there shall be the procedure for the complete recitation of the names, the channels (nāḍī), the wheels (cakra), and the mantra. || 30 ||
The initiation for the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka-dīkṣā) indeed takes place during an eclipse of the moon or sun, O Śivā;
it occurs even during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), for how could there be impurity for that which is already complete? (31)

O Supreme Goddess, at the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), the silent recitation (mauna) is remembered as the substitute for the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites; [this applies] to Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, and Sundarī.
Due to this distinction, there is no impurity from birth (sūtaka); one should recite the mantra of Śivā at all times.
Through consecration (abhiṣeka), one becomes pure, possessing all forms, and eternal.
The consecration (abhiṣeka) is complete in form and bestows the fruit of all accomplishments;
indeed, the consecration is proclaimed through manifold sequences of yoga. (34)
O Great Goddess, even if he be an outcaste, if he is endowed with the full consecration, he becomes a Brahman-sage; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (35)

O Pārvatī, even this best of sages, if devoid of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), is declared to be the lowest of Brahmins; yet through that consecration, he becomes the most excellent of the twice-born.
O Lord, one who is superior by virtue of initiation is not necessarily so because of the advanced age of his physical life;
for an elder may lack initiation, whereas a youth may be fully endowed with it. (37)
One who is complete in form becomes the most excellent; in this matter, age is not the cause.
Furthermore, even one belonging to the outcaste (caṇḍāla) class, if endowed with the complete initiation (dīkṣā), [attains excellence]. || 38 ||
He alone shall be of the nature of Śiva; no deliberation need be made on this point.
[This applies even to] recitation, worship, austerity, fire-offerings, as well as the feeding of Brahmins. (39)
O Goddess, one should perform this with diligence and not allow any obstacles to arise;
first, the mental worship, and thereafter the great external worship.
O Goddess, one should perform this with effort; there is no need for deliberation here.
For those bound souls (paśus) who are devoid of the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), there is only the recitation of mantras (japa). || 41 ||
O Maheśānī, it has been stated in some places that such recitation is indeed useless,
even if one is a knower of the three periods of time and capable of attracting the three worlds.
Nevertheless, one should not transgress worldly conduct even in thought;
O Maheśvarī, for him who is thus intent on reflection, there is worship. (43)
One should diligently receive [the mantra] from the hand of the Guru, from the hand of a brother of the Guru, or from the hand of an Ācārya; one should not merely recite the mantra on one's own.
The mere recitation of the mantra is what is called "japa.
It must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret like one's own private parts.
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (45)

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Recitation of Mantras," in the second section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the illustrious Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 46.
The forty-seventh chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the determination regarding the installation of the yantra."
Śrī Śiva said:
O beloved, one should have a yantra made of crystal, gold, or silver.
The yantra is said to be the house, and the yantra is proclaimed to be the sacred seat (pīṭha);
O Goddess, when worshipped in the yantra, she becomes pleased instantly.
O Maheśvarī, in the case of a Śāligrāma, a Bāṇaliṅga, a Jīvacakra,
a fixed yantra, or an image, there is neither invocation nor dismissal.
Having established the great machine, one should not abandon that machine;
having secured the installation of the machine, one should meditate upon the Vidyā therein.
Having performed the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa) there, one should contemplate the Vidyā right there;
having first performed the consecration of the Yantra, one should install the Deity therein.
At that time, there is neither dismissal nor invocation;
having properly placed the internal time, one should thus consecrate the yantra.
Having meditated upon the form residing in one's own heart within that [image], and having worshipped it, one should perform the dismissal (visarjana);
however, if it is the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of a deity, then there is no dismissal at all.
Thus has it been briefly declared according to the sequence of the ten vidyās;
O wise one, listen now to the ten incenses and be attentive in mind. (8)
O Goddess, the sixteen-ingredient incense called *lohabāṇa* is prescribed for the Śrīvidyā;
in the ritual of the Kālīvidyā, however, it is *aguru* consisting of ten ingredients.
O Goddess, in the ritual for the Tārā-vidyā, eighteen-part śrīkhaṇḍa is prescribed;
likewise, in the ritual for the Chinnā-vidyā, five-part guggulu is used.
Black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) is the yellow essence that falls within the range of the Brahma-weapon;
having stirred this agallochum incense, it is proclaimed for Mātaṅgī. (11)
Musk and camphor, as well as the eight fragrances, O Goddess, are prescribed for Bhairavī, but not without the essence of realgar (śilārasa).
O Śivā, I have declared that in the ritual procedure for the Siddhavidyā, śrīkhaṇḍa is used with Bhuvaneśī and kamalā with Manu, while lākṣā and guḍa are used with Dhūmrā.
All incenses have thus been described; now listen, O Goddess, to the excellent seats.
O Queen of the Gods, the excellent seats are being told—be well-disposed. 14.
Arrows, kettledrums, lutes and so forth, drums, musical instruments, flutes, conchs, bells, banners, and the like—three hundred and twenty-five [instruments]. (15)
Indeed, the practice of using an excellent seat is considered difficult to find everywhere;
so too are the recitation of hymns, the armor-verse (kavaca), and the thousand names. || 16 ||
O Goddess, worship and recitation are likewise proclaimed for the Varayoga;
O Pārvatī, whenever a task arises, it should be performed wherever that may be.
O Goddess, in some cases there may be recitation (japa), and in some cases there may be fire-offerings (homa) and worship (pūjā).
O Goddess, wherever one obtains [a particular practice], one should perform that very thing there.
In some cases, the libation (tarpaṇa) must be performed; in others, there may be the recitation (pāṭha).
In some instances, worship and fire-offerings (pūjā-homa) are to be done; in others, the feeding of Brahmins (brāhmaṇa-bhojana). || 19 ||
It should be performed according to whatever materials are available, especially in the case of the Śābara and other traditions;
O Goddess of Gods, when employing a boon, the arrangement of the seat may be of two kinds.
O Goddess of the gods, O Great Mistress, the seats of the body and the seats of technical terminology, such as Bhadra and the others, are born from the body.
A tiger's head, blankets, skins, medicinal herbs, and objects shaped like camels, goats, and humans, as well as *kuśa* grass and so forth, in their proper sequence. (22)
I have described to you only the general designations of the seats; O Maheśvarī, each of these seats has a twofold division.
They may be lifeless or living, and they grant all accomplishments;
however, O Maheśvarī, in the absence of living ones, lifeless ones are used.
But the primary secret means, O Maheśvarī, are those involving living beings:
the horse, the elephant, the palanquin, and likewise the human. (25)
The buffalo, the bull, the wild cat, the forest-dweller (bear), the tiger, the horse, the jackal, O Goddess, and the ram and goat, O Supreme Lady—(these are the sacrificial animals). 26.
The camel, the species of deer, and that which has the nature of *kuśa* grass or clay;
the dog, O Goddess, the cock, the crocodile, and likewise the reed. (27)
The gavaya, the śūkara, the śivira, and the śabara are recorded;
as well as the taraṇi, the ratha, the śaṅkaṭa, and the sukha-āsana. || 28 ||
The staff-bearer’s [seat], the swing-wheel, the wheel-swing, the one called the house, the footstool, the ascent, and likewise the coconut-seat. (29)
The betel-nut tree, madhuka, ākara, vaṭa, aśvattha, satālaka, date palm, pippala, plakṣa, śamī, and likewise the jambu tree; || 30 ||
Tārā, Kālī, Chinnamastā, and Śrīvidyā born from the Kalpavṛkṣa; the dog, the tortoise, the rhinoceros, and the one called the elephant as a comfortable seat (sukhāsana). (31)
O Goddess, there was the elephant-throne, and likewise the boat-chariot, O Śivā;
and those called the bull, the horse, and the buffalo, O Pārvatī. (32)
The Nara-yāna, the Rāja-yāna, and the Chatra-yāna, O Pārvatī; likewise the Narapati-yāna, and that which is called the Aśvanātha-yāna. (33)
O Goddess, that which is named Gajanātha, as well as the chariot called Sāmrājya—these excellent seats have been described by me to you, O Queen of the Gods. (34)
O Goddess of gods, O beloved, hear now their seven thousand one hundred divisions;
they are fourfold according to the distinctions of the castes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
O Maheśānī, O Maheśvarī, hear the enumeration according to the different regions:
horses are said to be of five types, and eighteen breeds are traditionally recorded. (36)
The Vahlīkas, the Kāmbojas, those born in Koṅkaṇa and Rāka, and those born in Vanaja are the fifth; hear from me, O beloved, their castes.
All the horses of the Sun may indeed become planets through a difference in color:
the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, and Jupiter. (38)
Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu is remembered as the ninth;
[they are assigned] according to the sequence of nine colors and the sequence of five colors.
Due to the individual combination [of these], there are ninety; the deficiency of the moon consists of twenty-five divisions according to the sequence of the five colors. (40)
The number is one hundred and twenty-five from the combination with the black-eared horse;
through mutual cross-breeding, there are three hundred and seventy-five varieties. (41)
O Maheśānī, their fruit is now being told; listen.
Having mounted a chariot with the color of the sun, one should recite [the mantra] twenty thousand times. (42)

One shall become victorious over the three worlds; there is no need for deliberation on this point regarding the armor-verse (kavaca), the recitation of the hymn, and likewise the Thousand Names (Nāmasāhasraka). || 43 ||
The number has been stated generally as one thousand times the Gajantaka;
having mounted a chariot with the color of the moon, one should recite the Śivā-mantra a thousand times for each direction.
One shall become the lord of fame and fortune; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having ascended the earth-colored [seat], one should mutter the mantra three thousand times. (45)
Even a poor man shall become rich; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having ascended the station of Mercury, one should perform thirty thousand recitations. (46)
The sick shall be liberated from disease, and the poor shall obtain wealth;
having ascended a high seat, one should recite the Navasāhasraka.
One shall become the lord of the nine treasures; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having ascended the letter of Bhṛgu (the letter 'B'), one should perform the recitation (japa) one hundred thousand times.
One shall become the lord of all accomplishments; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having assumed the color of Saturn, one should always recite [the mantra] three thousand times. (49)
Freed from all afflictions, that man shall become like a god;
having assumed the form of Rāhu, he remains so for seventy thousand years.
The man who recites this twenty-five thousand times, having mounted the color of Ketu, shall become the lord of Lakṣmī.
The man who recites [the mantra] shall become a conqueror of enemy kingdoms;
mounting a white-colored [vehicle], he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Having completely conquered the enemy army, a man shall become an enjoyer of his kingdom;
having assumed the posture of a horse or a tiger, he should perform a thousand-fold recitation of the mantra for each direction.
O Śivā, whatever hymn, armor-verse, or name one may recite with the desire for a specific wish, that man shall become a conqueror of the three worlds.
O Goddess of gods, these certainly become seats of life;
whatever desire one may long for, that one certainly attains. (55)
Having prepared a white silver seat for mere recitation, mere study, burnt offerings, and so forth, the omnipresent Lord should perform three hundred thousand recitations.
Having conquered Indra and the other gods in battle, he becomes victorious on earth;
having fashioned a white-colored seat with the brilliance of a thousand suns, [he attains this]. (57)
O Śivā, by making a white variegated seat and reciting the mantra alone, one becomes a king who conquers the three worlds and a master of treasures.
Standing in a red-colored [mandala], a man should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day;
standing in [a mandala of] an enemy army, a man should recite it a thousand times every day. || 59 ||
Assuming a black complexion, one should recite the five-thousand-verse [mantra];
by the grace of Kālī Tārā, enemies will fall into servitude. (60)
Assuming a yellow complexion, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
the person shall become a king of kings—of this there is no doubt to be made. (61)
Having mounted a blue-colored horse, one should perform half a lakh of recitations;
one shall become a master of all supernatural powers—of this there is no doubt. (62)
Standing upon Haritāśva, a person should recite this [mantra] two hundred thousand times;
having attained the status of a lord of the earth, he shall become a partaker of the enjoyments of the three worlds. || 63 ||
By relying constantly upon five thousand grey horses for only a month, a vetāla certainly becomes one's servant.
The man who, having attained a dark complexion, recites [the mantra] forty thousand times, becomes Viṣṇu himself; of this there is no doubt. (65)
Mounting a tawny horse, the lord of the earth recites the mantra one hundred thousand times;
standing upon a horse with discolored limbs, a man may bring the three worlds under his control. (66)
Having mounted a swift horse, one conquers the entire universe through recitation;
by reciting it three hundred times daily for just one month, one achieves perfection.
Having mounted a smoke-colored [horse], the practitioner becomes omniscient;
by standing upon one of various colors, a man [should practice] a mere hundred times every day.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred times, the Goddess grants boons within a month;
having stood [in the prescribed posture], one should recite it ten thousand times with the six syllables of the Vedas, the three, the five, and the six.
Wealth, enjoyment, as well as sovereignty, lordship over the world, and power—O Supreme Goddess, these indeed are said to be the fruits in successive order. (70)
O Goddess, if the yoga of the four seats were indeed present everywhere at all times for the practitioner, what would there be that was not already within his grasp? (71)
By means of the eighteen-fold [recitation], one shall attain perfection of speech;
O Goddess of gods, by mere intention, perfection certainly arises. (72)
O Śivā, the fruit of the Ślakṣṇaśvānas has been declared, as well as the fruit of the Koṅkaṇas;
this indeed has been proclaimed by the proponents of the doctrine of emptiness (Śūnyavādins), O Supreme Goddess. (73)
O Goddess, for the Kāmbojas, success is achieved merely by recitation within a fortnight;
for the Bāhlīkas, O Goddess, the fruit is attained within the scope of three days.
O Goddess, for the inhabitants of the mountains, the fruit [of their practice] certainly occurs within a month;
however, for the five castes, O Queen, it is joined with a year.
By the movement [of the breath], there is a fivefold division of the mountains specifically;
multiplied by the number five, they amount to thirty-three thousand. (76)
Thus, O Maheśvarī, I have declared the number of eighteen;
however, in the Kali age, due to the various divisions of the sacred sites (ālayas), they are said to be as numerous as ten million (arbuda).
O Goddess, the horses were described by me, and then their wings were clipped;
the armor, the recitation of hymns, and the Thousand Names were proclaimed.
This should be performed even during mere recitation by those desiring all perfections;
for in this very way, the fruit of the Śaṅkaras will certainly be attained. (79)

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Consolation," in the second section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 47.
